In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says.

In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature, researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it.

If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement.

"It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position."

Location is a basic layer of security. Banks, power grids and government agencies often limit access to sensitive systems to people who are physically inside a secure building. But classical (nonquantum) ways of proving location remotely, which time how long signals take to travel, can be spoofed by hackers working together. Quantum physics can close that security gap, because a single quantum particle can't be copied.

"Is this call coming from my bank, or is it coming from someone in North Korea or somewhere else?" Krister Shalm, a quantum physicist at NIST who led the team, told Live Science. "That's really powerful if you can anchor digital security to a physical location."

In the experiment, the team used a technique called ranging, which is similar to the principles behind echolocation, radar and the lidar sensors found in some smartphones. It sends a signal and measures how long it takes for the response to return.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"You can send a signal at the speed of light and measure how long it takes to get back," Shalm told Live Science. "But the problem is, that's the thing that can always be spoofed classically."

In the experiment, two trusted stations called "verifiers" sat 640 feet (195 meters) apart, linked by cables and optical fibers running through the hallways of a NIST research building. A "prover," whose location the verifiers wanted to confirm, sat in between.

One verifier created pairs of entangled photons — particles so deeply linked that measuring one reveals something about the other, even when they're separated at great distances. The verifier kept one photon from each pair and sent its twin to the prover. At the same time, both verifiers sent random bits of information that were timed to reach the prover at the same moment.

The prover combined the two inputs with a simple math operation and used the result to decide how to measure the photon's polarization ‪—‬ the direction in which its electric field oscillates. The measuring device works much like the filter in polarized sunglasses. A detector then recorded whether the photon made it through the filter, and the prover sent that yes-or-no result back to both verifiers.

Because nothing travels faster than light, the round-trip time told the verifiers how far away the prover could be. And because the photon can't be copied, the measurement had to be made in that exact spot.

To confirm that no one cheated, the team ran a loophole-free Bell test, which checks whether particles are more strongly correlated than classical physics allows. If anyone tampers with the photons or the equipment, the test fails. Shalm led one of the first such tests in 2015.

NIST physicist Krister Shalm performing a Bell test in 2015. Shalm was part of the team that demonstrated the new location verification method.

Scientists first proposed position verification in the late 2000s, but the experiments are extremely demanding, Shalm said. Many earlier designs could tolerate losing only a few percent of the photons along the way, which is "just not practical or reasonable" with today's technology. The NIST team relied on superconducting detectors that catch nearly every photon.

The surprise, Shalm said, was that the Bell test approach worked at all on the first try. It offers the strongest security of any quantum protocol because it makes very few assumptions about how the equipment works, but it is usually the hardest to pull off. "The sort of gold-plated deluxe version — you were able to do that on the first demonstration of a full protocol," he said.

The system ran about 250,000 trials per second. Each verification required 30 million to 60 million rounds of signals sent back and forth ‪—‬ roughly two to four minutes of data. Over two days in fall 2024, the team ran 335 verifications, and nearly all of them passed. The prover's location was confirmed within a region about 4.5 times smaller in volume than what a comparable classical method could guarantee, the team said.

The experiment proved secure against attackers who shared little or no entanglement of their own. Protecting against attackers with more powerful quantum resources will require longer strings of random bits, the researchers wrote.

The initial users of this technology are expected to be data centers, financial backend systems and critical infrastructure like power plants, Shalm said. However, incorporating this technology into cellphones will take significantly longer, as the components are currently too large and expensive.

"In terms of a computer analogy, we are much closer to the building-sized computers of the 1950s and 1960s than today's smartphones," he said in an email. "However, with consistent improvement it might be possible in several decades to come up with a compact handheld version of the devices needed for quantum position verification."

Real-world use may be more than a decade away, Scott Glancy, a NIST physicist and study co-author, said in the statement. To verify that a customer is truly communicating with someone from their bank, high-quality quantum networks must be utilized to share entangled photons between the two parties.

The team already knows how to speed things up. Faster measurement devices could cut each verification from minutes to about a second, according to the study, and low-latency communication links could shrink the verified zone to a single building, even with stations miles apart.

"It may not be this year, but I think it's something that we're building towards, and we know the steps that are needed to get there," Shalm said.

Kavuri, G. A., Zhang, Y., Gookin, A. R., Patra, S., Bienfang, J. C., Fu, H., Alnawakhtha, Y., Reddy, D., V., Mazurek, M. D., Abellán, C., Amaya, W., Mitchell, M. W., Miller, C. A., Mirin, R. P., Stevens, M. J., Glancy, S., Knill, E., & Shalm, L. K. (2026). Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

#6518. This Is the Number One Cheese You Need on Your Holiday Cheese Board (No, It’s Not Cheddar)

I chatted with two cheesemongers to find out exactly what I should be putting on my cheese spreads this holiday season. Surprisingly, a classic cheddar isn't at the top!

After playing Tetris in my oven an hour before a holiday party, I’m always relieved I decided to serve a cheese board as the appetizer. Cheese boards don’t require much time to put together (and take up zero oven space), but I seem to linger on the cheese selection, always asking myself the same question: Which cheeses would everyone like to eat?

So, I sat down with the experts: Molly Browne, dean of mongers at Cheese State University and education director at Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin, and Emilia D’Albero, the first American ever crowned World’s Best Cheesemonger. They gave me the scoop on putting together the perfect holiday cheese board. Molly and Emilia recommend three to five cheeses per board, representing a variety of milk types, styles and flavors.

But which cheese should I buy that everyone would like? More specifically, what feels indulgent but won’t alienate picky eaters? I expected Molly and Emilia to recommend some extremely specific, hard-to-find cheeses, but both suggested varieties I could pick up at the grocery store.

According to Molly, the best cheese for a holiday cheese board that appeals to all ages is butterkase. This semi-firm cow’s milk cheese is creamy, smooth, relatively mild and exceptionally buttery—hence its German name, which translates to “butter cheese.” (If you’re as chronically online as I am, you may have heard of butterkase from @courtneycookinsta, who famously stuffs butterkase in a warm sweet potato and eats it for lunch.)

Butterkase is typically aged for only about a month, so it doesn’t have much funk, making it approachable for the under-10 and over-60 crowd. “I’ve seen my own child pick up a piece of it and eat it like an apple on multiple occasions,” says Molly. But because of butterkase’s slight complexity, Molly explained that it won’t leave those in the middle feeling devoid of flavor or a good eating experience, so it’s a safe bet for a charcuterie board.

Butterkase is made in Wisconsin and sold nationwide, but if you’re having trouble finding it, Gouda is a good alternative, especially Emilia’s recommendation: aged Gouda.

Aged Gouda is a Dutch-style hard cheese that matures anywhere from nine months to five years. As Gouda matures, the soft paste turns firm and speckles with those irresistible crunchy crystals. It takes on an indulgent butterscotch flavor, with subtle tropical notes, so it’s on the sweeter side. The longer the Gouda ages, the more intense those characteristics become. “In my experience, nobody’s ever turned down an aged Gouda,” says Emilia.

Because it’s especially buttery and mild, butterkase pairs well with tangy, acidic foods, like olives, the foods on a relish tray and all kinds of pickles: classic pickles, pickled vegetables and pickled fruit. Their acidity cuts through the richness of the cheese. Butterkase would also be a fantastic addition to a supper club board. Its soft texture is great on crisp crackers studded with nuts and fruits, with a German mustard nearby.

For wine and cheese pairings, opt for something light and refreshing, like Prosecco or an unoaked chardonnay, to balance the richness of the cheese. Even a bottle of inexpensive champagne makes the cheese board feel a little fancier.

Slice butterkase while it’s still cold from the fridge. If it sits for a while, butterkase can become soft enough to spread, making it difficult to slice. As a general rule, Molly and Emilia recommend slicing harder cheeses in advance to get ahead of cheese board prep. Keep backup portions in the fridge to quickly replenish the board as the night goes on.

Aged Gouda pairs well with sweeter fruit jams, chocolate, candied pecans and even tropical fruits like mango. Fruit-and-nut studded crackers work just as well with aged Gouda as they do with butterkase. For dessert, try pairing the cheese with brownies or caramelly stroopwafels. Drink pairings range from red wine to spiced rum.

While there are guidelines for pairing, Emilia encourages people to step out of their comfort zone and explore out-of-the-box options. “There’s no wrong answer to pairing,” she says. “People tend to think that they have to only pair fancy things with cheese, and honestly, some of the best pairings I’ve had have just been snacks or things I love that are lying around the house.” Take a cue from Emilia’s cheese competition days: Try the cheese with whatever you have in the kitchen; you may discover an unexpected favorite. “Get weird with it,” says Emilia.

#6514. Is It Safe to Eat from a Charcuterie Board That’s Been Out All Afternoon?

Charcuterie boards are a party favorite, but how long can they safely sit out? Here's what to know before you grab another bite of that wilted cheese.

I totally understand the excitement that comes from spying a gorgeous charcuterie board at a gathering. Between the cheeses, the cured meats and all the little finger foods, there are too many potential combinations to wonder how long everything has been sitting out. But as a registered dietitian, I can’t help thinking about it!

Food safety was a big deal in my studies, and all those lessons about safe cooking temperatures, proper food handling and food storage have stuck with me. After all, cut a few corners here or let food sit out a little too long there, and you could find yourself in a real pickle—one where you risking spoiling all that delicious food you took time to prepare.

So, how long can a charcuterie board safely sit out before it’s time to show it the bin? With the holidays in full swing and cheese boards popping up at just about every gathering, these food safety tips will keep you snacking happily and safely all season long.

Yes, but you’ll want to keep an eye on the clock! Most perishable items on a charcuterie board—including soft cheeses, deli meats, chilled dips and cut fruit—shouldn’t sit at room temperature for more than two hours. If the temperature is above 90°F (like at an outdoor summer party), that window shrinks to just one hour.

Harmful bacteria can multiply quickly when perishable foods spend too much time in the temperature danger zone, which is between 40°F and 140°F. And unfortunately food doesn’t have to look or smell spoiled to be unsafe to eat.

Some charcuterie boards are designed to keep food chilled, with built-in compartments for ice packs or trays that sit over ice. If the perishable foods are kept at 40°F or below, they can stay out a little longer without entering the temperature danger zone.

One thing to keep in mind: The clock starts when the perishable foods come out of the refrigerator, not when guests start digging in. If a charcuterie board has been sitting out for more than two hours, it’s safest to toss the perishable items rather than save them for later.

And if you’re a guest and aren’t sure how long the board has been sitting out, you have a couple options. You can either casually ask the host, or you can skip the perishable items altogether and stick with shelf-stable munchies like crackers, seasoned nuts and pretzels.

Sort of! Hard cheeses like Parmesan, Manchego and aged Gouda handle room temperature better than soft cheeses like Brie, fresh goat cheese, fresh mozzarella and cream cheese.

That’s because hard cheeses contain less moisture, so they’re a little less hospitable to the harmful bacteria that can make you sick. Soft cheeses have more moisture, so they’re more perishable and should follow the same strict two-hour rule as other refrigerated foods.

While hard cheeses are a safer bet than soft varieties, that doesn’t mean they can sit out indefinitely! They’re still subject to food safety concerns, so if you’re not sure how long the board has been sitting out, it’s safest to skip the perishable items regardless of the cheese type.

You can’t always tell if food is safe to eat just by looking at it, but there are a few visible signs that a charcuterie board may have been sitting out for a while. You might notice cheeses sweating or getting extra soft or oily, or you might see sliced meats starting to look dried out around the edges. Cut fruit may also turn mushy or discolored as it sits.

Not everything on a cheese board carries the same food safety risk. When in doubt, don’t take a chance on foods that need refrigeration. You can always fill your plate with the shelf-stable nuts, crackers and whole fruit instead.

If you’re hosting, put out smaller portions of cheeses and meats and replenish the board as needed. That way, you can keep the extra food refrigerated until it’s time to serve more, rather than letting everything sit out for hours.

During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo, an Anglo-Saxon cemetery in the U.K. that's famous for an enormous seventh-century ship burial of an early medieval king. The unusual grave does not have any bones but rather ghost-like shapes where a body was once buried.

Sand bodies were "burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person, not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii," Angus Wainwright, an archaeologist at the U.K.'s National Trust, said in a statement. These burials have been found at Sutton Hoo in the past, as well as at other Anglo-Saxon sites in the Suffolk area of the U.K.

The new sand burial, which was uncovered at a burial ground called Garden Field at the end of a 2025 dig, features in a four-part documentary created by the television series "Time Team" and archaeological experts with the National Trust and FAS Heritage. Whereas a 2024 excavation unearthed pieces of a bronze bucket used in a cremation ritual, the 2025 excavation was aimed at discovering evidence for the extent of the cemetery, when it was used and whether the people buried there were connected with the occupant of the famous ship burial.

"Until now, archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds," Wainwright said. In particular, experts have tried to work out who was buried in the "great ship burial" at Sutton Hoo. That person may have been King Rædwald, who ruled a kingdom in East Anglia and died around A.D. 627. The ship burial also contained an intricate and striking helmet. But the archaeologists are trying to learn more about the everyday East Anglians with the 2025 dig, which "moves the focus to these people and their ancestors and descendants," Wainwright said.

During the last week of the month-long excavation, the team unearthed the unusual sand body burial. Accompanying the deceased were grave goods, including beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch, according to the statement. But directly underneath the sand body, the team found evidence that a second person may have been buried in the same grave.

"It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery," Wainwright said. Experts think the sand bodies and cremations discovered in the burial ground may predate the famous ship burial.

In the first episode of a four-part Time Team series on Sutton Hoo, which launched on YouTube on Nov. 14, experts found new evidence that the people buried in the Garden Field cemetery were acquiring wealth and increasing their social status — so much so that they buried at least one person with a gold ingot.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also investigated the possible remains of a dock that was used to build and launch ships into the River Deben and found an unusual fragment of a cremation urn that surprised the archaeologists because it was decorated rather than plain.

"Well, it's at Sutton Hoo. Anything can happen," Justin Garner-Lahire, managing director at FAS Heritage, said in the video.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6511. These 3-Ingredient Salt Dough Ornaments Are a Christmas Tradition Worth Starting

Some of the most treasured ornaments on my Christmas tree started with a bag of flour.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Of all the ornaments I’ve collected over the years, my two favorites were made in my kitchen about nine Christmases ago. One is my son’s little handprint, cut from a simple salt dough and painted to resemble Santa Claus, with his fingers forming Santa’s white beard. The other is my daughter’s impossibly tiny footprint, turned into a Christmas tree. Neither is a particularly impressive work of art, but I handle them with more care than any of the antique glass ornaments I’ve acquired over the years.

Those two ornaments marked the beginning of what has become an annual Christmas tradition in our house, and our collection of homemade salt dough ornaments has grown quite a bit since. And while the opportunities to capture tiny hands and feet are rather fleeting, the appeal of making our own Christmas ornaments hasn’t diminished much as my children have grown. Our designs have just become more ambitious.

Salt dough is a simple modeling dough made from flour, salt and water. When dried, it hardens into a sturdy material that can be painted, embellished and hung on the tree. When properly dried and stored in a cool, dry place, the ornaments can last for years.

Mix the flour and salt in a bowl, adding the water gradually until you have a soft dough that’s easy to work with. Turn it out onto a floured countertop and knead it for a minute or two until it’s smooth.

I use a chopstick to poke a hole at the top of each ornament for the ribbon. A word of advice from someone who learned this the hard way: Do this before baking. Salt dough is remarkably unforgiving once it’s hardened.

With plain dough, you have the freedom to paint your ornaments to match your Christmas decor, whether that means traditional reds and greens or the colors of your favorite vintage glass baubles.

If you’d like to give your ornaments some extra protection, finish them with a clear craft sealer. Once everything has dried, string them with velvet ribbon, baker’s twine or whatever you have in your craft drawer. Store them somewhere dry after Christmas, and you can add to your collection year after year.

AI has upended the math community with a flood of results. We have to rethink how we assess which questions and answers matter — putting humans back at the center.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Anthropic mathematician using Claude claims to have proven the most famous problem in math — the Riemann hypothesis — in the latest, but potentially most consequential, example of artificial intelligence (AI) producing stunning math results.

AI has steamrolled its way into the math community. Anthropic's proof will certainly and rightly be scrutinized, but rather than picking apart every single result these models produce, we should respond by changing how we evaluate and reward expertise — placing less weight on the volume of results and more on the human judgment required to decide which questions and answers matter.

Without this shift, we risk drowning genuine insight in a flood of plausible but poorly understood mathematics.

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're putting out for free. If you liked this story, please consider subscribing.

Mathematical judgment is the ability to distinguish a result that is correct, but boring, from one that might fundamentally change how we think about the problem or even the whole area of mathematics surrounding the problem.

AI could generate hundreds of thousands of complex variations on a theorem, but these variations might add very little to mathematical knowledge, each one ultimately proving a dead end. A truly consequential result might settle a long-standing unsolved problem or connect to apparently unrelated areas. It is mathematical judgment that allows us to tell the difference between the two.

Earlier this year, an OpenAI system produced a counterexample to the long-standing planar unit distance problem, overturning a conjecture of Paul Erdős that had resisted mathematicians for decades. More recently, OpenAI announced an apparent solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a celebrated question about whether equations describing fluid flow can develop singularities, or infinite values. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems — a set of seven well-known and complex math problems, each with a $1 million prize attached.

Whether OpenAI's result ultimately stands up to scrutiny remains to be seen. But what is clear is that AI systems are now operating at a level that many mathematicians did not expect to witness for years, if not decades. OpenAI has since released hundreds of further mathematical results, leaving mathematicians scrambling to assess their correctness and significance.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This does not mean that mathematicians are about to become obsolete. But it does mean we need to carefully reconsider what their precise purpose is.

Traditionally, expertise has been closely associated with production: Experts solve difficult problems, prove theorems, construct models and write papers. If AI can generate proofs, conjectures and probe research areas at unprecedented speed and scale, mathematical production is no longer necessarily the bottleneck. Instead, many pure mathematicians would argue that it is mathematical judgment that will become the scarcer resource.

Human judgment remains necessary because proofs generated by AI are not necessarily illuminating, comprehensible or even reliable. Some proofs may be so long or opaque that checking them requires substantial work by specialists and even more work to reinterpret them in a way that is meaningful to human mathematicians.

A proof can be valid without offering insight into why it is true or how its ideas might be employed elsewhere. The job of human mathematicians will be to become arbiters of the correctness of proofs, but also to scrutinize the reasoning and to extract the underlying ideas, determining whether the result says anything that meaningfully advances the field.

Mathematics, as a research community, needs to react rapidly to this change. Mathematicians and journals must prioritize significance over output. Mathematics involves deciding which results are important as well as generating them. A proof can be correct without being insightful. To give a simplified example, AI might "prove" that the square of a number divisible by two is divisible by four and then prove that the square of a number divisible by three is divisible by nine, and so on with ever larger integers. However, each new "proof" isn't an example of insightful mathematics, just a variation on the same elementary idea.

AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

In contrast, a significant proof might settle a long-standing question, reveal an unexpected connection between disparate fields or develop a technique which is useful in the solution of many other problems.

Journals should therefore require authors to explain clearly what is genuinely new, why it matters — and what role AI played. Reviewers should judge whether a result deepens understanding, rather than merely verifying that the argument works. That does not mean rejecting work whose eventual importance is uncertain. The history of mathematics is full of ideas whose significance became apparent only decades later, so journals must continue to make room for foundational, exploratory and curiosity-driven research.

But there is a difference between a result with as-yet unknown implications and one that is unlikely ever to be insightful. Mathematical judgement cannot guarantee that nothing valuable is ever overlooked. It can, however, distinguish work that contains genuinely new ideas or possibilities from the automated production of uninteresting dead ends.

Universities and funders should also stop treating publication counts as a convenient proxy for quality. Careers are built around papers, citations, grants and prizes, but these measures were developed when producing sophisticated mathematics demanded substantial human time and effort. In the age of AI, work that might previously have taken years of careful thought could now be produced in weeks or even days.

Consequently, as the cost of generating mathematical results falls dramatically, those measures of quality become less useful. A decreased reliance on traditional metrics may be no bad thing, but institutions need credible alternatives: assessments of a researcher's most important contributions, evidence of intellectual leadership and explanations of how their work has changed understanding. This is urgent because mathematicians are already struggling to evaluate the sheer volume of material being produced.

Finally, mathematical training must continue to reward understanding. Written work alone will become a less reliable guide to individual capability when papers, reports and applications can be written mostly using AI. Seminars, discussions and collaborations can reveal whether someone understands an argument, can defend it and can connect it to other ideas. Demonstrating understanding has always been a more important quality in university students than simply presenting the answer; education and recruitment should now reflect that principle more explicitly.

Critics might argue that this is an overreaction. Mathematical claims still require proof, peer review already evaluates significance, and AI is simply another tool, like a calculator or computer algebra system. There is a degree of truth to each objection. Yet the explosion in the number of published papers changes the nature of the game. A calculator does not generate hundreds of research claims that specialists must spend precious time checking. AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

Recent advances have understandably generated both excitement and anxiety. The right response is neither to reject AI nor to unguardedly celebrate every finding it produces. Journals, universities and funders should adapt their incentives now, before quantity overwhelms judgment completely.

In an environment increasingly capable of automatically generating research-level mathematics, the most valuable experts will be those who know which questions are worth asking, which results deserve trust and which ideas are worth our attention.

#6505. Green Beans Almondine

Green beans are a must-have on Thanksgiving, but maybe you aren't particularly craving the classic green bean casserole. If that's the case, this is the recipe for you! This French-inspired green bean dish is much easier to make than it sounds and a great way to switch things up this holiday season. Sautéed with shallots and garlic, tossed with buttery, toasted almonds, and finished with lemon, these green beans are quick enough to serve for a weeknight dinner while also being fancy enough to have a spot at your holiday dinner.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Meanwhile, prep an ice bath by filling a large bowl with ice and water. Cook the green beans until crisp-tender, 2 to 3 minutes (you want them to be slightly undercooked as they will continue to cook later).

Using a slotted spoon, immediately transfer beans to ice bath then drain.

In large skillet over medium-low heat, melt butter until its lightly bubbling. Add in the almonds and cook, stirring frequently, until they are golden brown, which should take about 3 to 4 minutes. Reduce heat to low and add shallots and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the whole mixture is fragrant, another 2 to 3 minutes. Add in the green beans and toss until combined and beans are tender.

Stir in lemon zest and juice, tossing to coat. Season with salt and pepper and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover green beans almondine in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

You can’t go wrong with a meal kit like Blue Apron, one of the OGs in the space. The promise is similar to HelloFresh: pre-portioned ingredients and straightforward instructions that'll have you making healthy and delicious meals at home with ease.

Purple Carrot is a fully plant-based meal kit delivery service that offers both premade meals and meal kits for you to prep. Multiple BA staffers and contributors have tried it many times throughout the years, and it's consistently fared well in our product tests. Proof? This review from contributor Carina Finn: “I never missed the meat in a Purple Carrot meal. I even found myself getting legitimately excited about my “healthy dinner at home” nights—especially since I didn’t have to grocery shop.”

For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, they’re offering new customers 50% off their order plus free shipping. Use code 50FORME to redeem the discount, which is valid on all orders over $65.

If you love cooking but don't have time for all of the planning, prep, and shopping required to put together satisfying home-cooked meals, try Marley Spoon. The service uses recipes from Martha Stewart herself and still requires you to do at least some of the chopping and dicing to making your meal. The recipes even recommend a few cooking tricks to use in your everyday life.

Parents and caregivers who want to skimp on shopping and prep without skimping on nutrition will love Little Spoon—a meal kit specifically for feeding babies, toddlers, and little kids. The service will ship ready-to-heat-and-eat meals (and snacks!) that are chef- and dietician-approved. For Black Friday, save 60% on your first order with the code EARLYBIRD60 through 11/26, and 65% on your first order with code SAVEBIG65 from 11/27–12/01.

#6502. The Great British Baking Show Crowns Moyin Its 2026 Winner After An Unforgettable Season

Even Paul Hollywood couldn’t help getting a little emotional.

Moyin Odeniran is officially the winner of season 17 of The Great British Baking Show, and after everything the 22-year-old went through in the tent, he’s got plenty to celebrate. The political economy student from Essex beat fellow finalists Mo Mahir and Tom Whittaker after 10 weeks of elaborate desserts, demanding technical challenges, and a finale that put their baking skills to the ultimate test.

Even Paul Hollywood seemed a little swept up in the emotion of it all.

“The reaction from his family, I have never seen anything like it. It was pure magic!” Hollywood said in the official winner announcement. “He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers, he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better. That cake in the Signature was one of the best cakes I have had for a long, long time.”

Nigella Lawson agreed, while making sure the runners-up got their flowers, too. “He is such a worthy winner, but having said that, Tom and Mo are sensational. They have created cakes that I will never forget.”

Somewhere in the middle of all that celebrating was a 22-year-old still trying to wrap his head around what he'd just accomplished.

“I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can’t believe it, I am in shock,” Moyin said. “I have made friends for life, and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more.”

It’s quite the achievement for someone who started baking alongside his mother at just five years old and had mastered macarons by 14. His Nigerian heritage has influenced many of his creations, but even with years of experience under his belt, Moyin quickly discovered how much he still had to learn.

“Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by Week 2 you question whether you know anything about baking,” he recalled.

By Week 8, however, he’d found his stride. During Caramel Week, Moyin made a sticky-toffee treacle tart, finished second in the millionaire's shortbread technical, and constructed an elaborate Omo Oba nougatine sculpture for his showstopper. Those incredible efforts earned him his first (and only) Star Baker title of the season.

The episode also delivered some serious emotional whiplash and a goodbye Moyin—and likely most viewers—probably would’ve preferred to skip. Just as he was celebrating his biggest achievement of the competition, Elizabeth “Connie” Lewis, one of his closest friends in the tent, was eliminated the same week. Their bond had also become a favorite among viewers, making the timing of her departure that much harder to take.

“I think the worst moment for me was when Connie left, and I cried for about an hour,” he admitted. “That surprised me as I am not really a crier, but I found it very emotional as I knew I was going to miss her.”

For fans who’d watched their friendship blossom week after week, that goodbye was a particularly heartbreaking moment to watch. Despite their 41-year age gap, Moyin and Connie clearly adored each other, and Baking Show fans would probably be more than happy to watch an entire episode of the two of them baking up a storm together.

When it came time for the finale, the bakers faced citrus celebration cakes, crème brûlée doughnuts, and ambitious showstoppers inspired by British landscapes. Moyin admitted his final creation became “a bit messy... well, a lot messy” toward the end, although he still managed to enjoy his last two days in the tent.

"I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward and I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it,” he said.

Moyin also credited the show with helping him open up to people in ways he hadn’t before, something that made his experience all the more meaningful.

“What was important to me was that you were appreciated as the person you are and allowed to be free,” he said. “I will never forget my time there and the friendships made, which will always continue.”

For someone who started the season doubting his own abilities, he isn’t exactly dreaming small anymore.

“My baking dream ideally would be to be one of the best bakers in the world, but in the meantime I would like to continue baking, look forward to new openings, and just see what happens for me out there," he said.

After this season, that doesn’t sound like such a far-fetched goal at all.

#6501. Khanom Tom (Coconut Balls)

The first time writer Ali Domrongchai went to Thailand with her grandmother, they had a mission: eat as many khanom (the Thai word for desserts and small snacks) as possible. They wandered from market to market, weaving through the stalls and sharing everything that caught their eye. Their hands-down favorite was the khanom tom, which her grandmother grew up buying from a street vendor in Bangkok as an after-school treat. Traditionally made with both fresh coconut and coconut milk, the bite-size sweets are chewy, fragrant, and irresistible.

Thankfully, khanom tom are easy to pull together at home and require no special equipment or technique. Glutinous rice flour gives the dough a pleasantly bouncy texture, and a palm sugar and coconut filling imparts a rich, caramel-like sweetness. After a quick boil, each ball is rolled in shredded fresh coconut for a soft, snowy finish.

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope followed up on years-old observations to confirm the first recorded act of a giant star swallowing its companion. The stellar cannibalism occurred just next door, in the Andromeda galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, astronomers have caught two stars — a supergiant and a star slightly smaller than the sun — in the act of merging. After orbiting each other for thousands of years, the pair came together in just under seven years — a span short enough that researchers could watch the drama play out from start to finish. The discovery was described in a study published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, said in a NASA statement. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do."

The stars' imminent merger was originally picked up by NASA's now-retired Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer — a spacecraft that was designed to spot asteroids but also discovered many other interesting changes in the night sky.

Researchers noticed that a previously stable binary star system in the Andromeda galaxy, the closest major galaxy to ours, had begun to brighten. Follow-up observations from the Wide-Field Infrared Transient Explorer ‪—‬ a near-infrared instrument at the Palomar Observatory in California — revealed that the galaxy had also started spewing dust. Karambelkar’s team backed up these observations with data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in December 2025.

The researchers dubbed the binary pair "Bao" (after its formal name, AT 2025abao) and started keeping tabs. They found that sometime in 2018, the smaller component of Bao bumped into the surface of the supergiant Bao. From there, things escalated quickly. The stars started exchanging gas in a process known as common envelope evolution. The larger Bao dragged its smaller companion closer and closer, until it was finally sucked into the supergiant's core, releasing a gigantic burst of energy.

Views of the stellar merger in Andromeda (left) captured by the NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and James Webb space telescopes (right).

This dramatic culmination was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," study co-author Kishalay De, an astronomer at Columbia University, said in the statement.

The researchers were surprised by not only the speed of this interaction but also its outcome. Bao could have easily exploded into a supernova, transformed into a neutron star or collapsed into a black hole. Instead, it seems to have settled back into a single massive star. Future observations will give scientists a sense of how the new, rejuvenated Bao is holding up after its act of cosmic cannibalism.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team's analysis could also help inform future studies of supergiant stars and binary systems. Getting a clearer picture of how common envelope evolution works could allow astronomers to reconstruct how previous mergers went down. Thanks to NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, Karambelkar predicts Bao will be far from the last merging stars scientists spot.

Joanna Thompson is a science journalist and runner based in New York. She holds a B.S. in Zoology and a B.A. in Creative Writing from North Carolina State University, as well as a Master's in Science Journalism from NYU's Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program. #6498. Dijon Balsamic Chicken Thighs

This dish is built for those nights when it’s chilly outside, and you want something that tastes like it’s been simmering for hours but actually comes together extremely easily. It's a simple one-pan dinner, but the sauce is the star. It’s a mix of tangy balsamic, sharp Dijon mustard, and hot honey. The hot honey adds a glossy, spicy sweetness that makes this perfect for colder weather and coats every bite of the tender, juicy chicken perfectly.

Cooking the chicken:The real secret to this dish is all in the sear. We’re starting the chicken skin-side down to fully render out the fat. This step is important as it keeps the skin from being chewy and lets all that rendered chicken fat melt into the sauce, giving it a nice boost of savory flavor. Serve it with white rice or a fluffy rice pilaf to soak up every drop of that sauce. Tip: If you don't have a bottle of hot honey on hand, regular honey plus a teaspoon of your favorite hot sauce is a great backup.

Make ahead & storage:To make ahead, you can whisk the sauce ingredients 2 days ahead and keep it in a jar in the fridge. When you're ready to cook, just sear the chicken and pour it in. For storage, you can keep leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

#6497. Why Is Everyone So Obsessed With Protein?

Welcome to Gut Check, our column dedicated to the complex, ever-evolving relationship between food and our bodies. Whether you’re curious about mindful eating or want to understand what makes picky eaters picky, read on and let award-winning journalist Betsy Andrews answer all your burning questions.

I recently shed 20 pounds for my health, and I’m keeping it off by avoiding simple carbohydrates—pasta, pastries, white rice, most breads—and exercising with weights and resistance bands. Carbs make you feel full, at least temporarily, and without them, especially when I’m hungry after a workout, I’m turning to an even more filling macronutrient: protein. I’m 63, and my wife is 60. We’ve heard that dietary protein is key to wellness in aging. But, after recent blood work, she is worrying about “bad,” or LDL, cholesterol. All this leaves me pondering the types and amounts of proteins I should be cooking that won’t increase her cholesterol levels or my waistline but will make for satisfying, healthy meals.

In my current obsession with protein, I’m not alone. Americans are bingeing on the stuff: Social media is glutted with influencers promoting protein powders and heavy meat consumption; supermarket shelves have filled with packaged snacks advertising excess protein; and restaurants are overhauling menus to feed the needs of protein-hungry diners. Even the new USDA dietary guidelines encourage protein uptake. At its extreme, it’s a trend known as protein-maxxing, and everyone from the Kardashians to the American Medical Association is talking about it.

Our bodies need protein to function. “Protein is made of amino acids. When we digest protein, we release those amino acids and use them to build and maintain our own proteins: muscle, liver, heart, lungs, and even some bone,” explains kinesiology professor Stuart Phillips, director of the Physical Activity Centre of Excellence (PACE) at Ontario’s McMaster University in Canada. “Protein supplies materials for enzymes, antibodies, transport proteins, some hormones, and the repair of tissues and organs.”

Of the 20 amino acids in our bodies, nine are essential, meaning we can’t create them ourselves. We must get them from eating protein, and we need to keep up protein consumption, because our bodies deplete it as we digest it. “The simple takeaway is that protein builds you from the inside out. It is foundational,” says dietitian Daphene Altema-Johnson, senior program officer at the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future. “But unlike fat, your body doesn’t have a dedicated storage system for protein, so you need a steady supply from food.”

In a culture built on body image, protein is also touted for its body-sculpting and weight-loss benefits. “You use protein to help build and maintain muscle mass and also recover from a workout,” explains Zach Rocheleau, the creator of the protein-rich recipes that comprise The Flexible Dieting Lifestyle. “It’s also the most satiating macronutrient. Getting the satiety effects of protein and thus feeling full, so eating less calories, is the driver that goes into losing weight.”

When influencers like Rocheleau claim that the protein they’re eating has helped them shape their physique, they aren’t wrong. Research does show that if you eat more protein it assists (to a point) in building lean muscle mass during resistance training. And studies have established the relationship between protein consumption, satiation, and weight loss. “The hype has come from real physiological needs,” says Dr. Megan Rossi, founder of The Gut Health Doctor, “but it’s more of an aesthetic effect, where people associate protein with big muscles and think the more protein they eat, the bulkier they’ll get.”

Scarfing down cheeseburgers and looking great doing it sounds good, but eating too much protein can put stress on your body, especially the kidneys. When you eat protein, Altema-Johnson explains, “The nitrogen part of it is stripped off and converted to urea, which is filtered out by your kidneys. Lots of nitrogen waste leads to a chronically higher kidney workload.”

For most people, this shouldn’t be much to worry about: Though he notes that this isn’t an endorsement of long-term protein bingeing, Phillips’ meta-analysis found no negative effect of higher protein consumption on kidney function in healthy adults. But if your kidneys aren’t in tip-top shape, stressing them can contribute to high blood pressure and other heart conditions. And studies show that consume excess animal-based proteins, in particular, can increase the risk of kidney stones.

There’s another potential problem: Your small intestine can only digest so much protein, so in high amounts, some of it ends up in your colon, where it can produce potentially harmful by-products. “Excess protein, like poorly absorbed egg whites and red meat, can ferment and produce toxic metabolites, which are associated with heart disease,” says Rossi. The solution is to eat fiber as well. But when you’re protein-maxxing, other nutrients, including fiber, can fall to the wayside.

Finally, though protein-maxxing is often touted as a way to slim down, the opposite can be true, too. “Your body has a ceiling for how much protein you can use,” says Altema-Johnson. Excess protein gets converted into glucose or fat for energy. Calories are energy units. You only need so many of them, and if you’re “chasing a protein number instead of eating until full,” as Altema-Johnson puts it, studies show that the extra calories can lead to weight gain.

Some protein-enriched packaged foods harbor sneaky calories. According to Rocheleau—who, by the way, eschews the phrase “protein-maxxing” in his work—“You would think that somebody putting out a high-protein product would take calories from carbs and fats and replace them with protein, but generally they keep the product the same but add protein, so you’re getting a lot more calories.” Plus, the marketing of protein-added snacks actually creates an insidious halo effect. “If you slap ‘high protein’ on a package, there’s the perception that it is automatically healthy, which can lead to overconsumption,” says Altema-Johnson. And while dairy- or plant-based protein products, including powdered supplements, can be a convenient way to support higher training needs to fill a genuine gap in the diet, Phillips’ research shows that they’re not a substitute for exercise itself and that protein intake had diminishing gains over a certain amount.

So what is the optimum amount of protein we should consume? Guidelines differ. Like the USDA previously, Canadian guidelines suggest a daily protein intake of .8 grams per kilogram of body weight. (To convert your body weight from pounds to kilograms, just divide it by 2.2.) For me, at 77 kilograms, 62 grams of protein per day is a good target, according to these guidelines, which comes out to a little over 8 ounces of roast chicken to meet my goals for the day. U.K. guidelines recommend slightly less, at .75 grams per kilogram, while the new USDA guidelines have been cranked up to 1.2 to 1.6 grams. At that serving goal, I can scarf down more than a pound of roast bird a day, and in theory, that’s what experts want me to do. For active and older adults, Phillips likes the new USDA targets, because we lose muscle mass as we age, and we start to need more protein to help retain it.

But not all protein is created equal. With my partner’s concern over cholesterol, maybe a skin-on bird dripping fat or a well-marbled steak seared in butter, both high in saturated fat, isn’t optimal for us. “This is where individualization matters,” says Altema-Johnson. “The goal is not zero red meat, but smaller proportions, moderation, and smarter cuts.” Experts like her, and plenty of studies, will warn you away from fattier and, especially, processed meats. “Unprocessed steak, ground beef, even pork chops have a modest health-associated risk,” Altema-Johnson says. “But bacon, sausage, deli meat, hot dogs—if you’re eating those constantly, you’re at higher risk for heart disease, colorectal cancer, and other health issues.”

Unlike animal proteins, not all plants contain every amino acid that our bodies need. But you can combine various vegetable proteins to meet those goals. Phillips and his colleagues found that young vegan and omnivorous men eating around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day achieved similar muscle and strength gains with resistance training. “Grains tend to be relatively low in lysine. Legumes help address that limitation, while grains complement legumes’ amino acid profiles,” he says. “Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, edamame, eggs, milk, yogurt, nuts, and seeds can all contribute. Soy is a particularly useful plant protein.” You don’t have to mix and match them at every meal, but a diverse plant-based diet can bring the protein you need.

The biggest takeaway is that you can’t just protein-max in the absence of overall healthy lifestyle choices. One of those is a balanced diet. According to Altema-Johnson, we should “individualize, moderate and balance. It’s important to have a diverse plate. If you’re focusing on one type of protein, especially meat, you’re missing out on all the good yummies a body needs.”

Chief among those yummies is fiber. Rossi says that recent studies support the idea that increasing protein can have benefits for weight-lifting and even aging, “but you need to increase fiber to balance it so your microbiome has more to eat than just excess protein. We need to swing the fiber flag.” Another recent study showed that 93 percent of Americans get enough protein, but other research reveals the opposite for fiber: Just 7 percent of us eat an adequate amount. That’s not good. A review of more than 5,000 studies found that a diet low in red meat but high in fiber-rich whole grains, vegetables, and nuts lowered our risk of death due to heart disease. “For gut health,” Phillips says, we should “ask what your protein habit is pushing off the plate.”

The other important lifestyle choice is exercise. “You can’t just expect to be sitting on the couch and eating protein and having these huge gains. Physical activity and resistance training bring far bigger results,” Rossi notes. That’s why I’ve ultimately been committed to moving more: Preventing muscle loss is insurance for my future. “Without enough protein and—most importantly, in my opinion—resistance exercise, this loss speeds up significantly,” says Altema-Johnson. “It affects strength, ability, balance, and fall risk. Muscle loss is directly tied to independence. It’s the difference between carrying your own groceries at 80 or needing help.”

Of course, I’m getting a late start. “You do not wake up at 65 with a new protein requirement. Start paying attention in midlife (over 40), and pair the protein with strength training, as that is the big lever to promote health, not protein,” notes Phillips. Well, I’m not 65 yet, but I did almost hit that age without addressing these health needs. Now I know that I need to exercise, and to support the training, I need a bit more protein, but not piles of it, and it has to come from a variety of sources. Perhaps most importantly, I’ll continue to take whatever the trend-setters are pushing on the socials with a grain of salt. As Phillips puts it, “Protein is a nutrient, not an identity. The goal is enough to support health, not as much as you can eat.”

Hungry for even more stories to sink your teeth into?

And studies show that consume excess animal-based proteins, in particular, can increase the risk of kidney stones.

There’s another potential problem: Your small intestine can only digest so much protein, so in high amounts, some of it ends up in your colon, where it can produce potentially harmful by-products. “Excess protein, like poorly absorbed egg whites and red meat, can ferment and produce toxic metabolites, which are associated with heart disease,” says Rossi. The solution is to eat fiber as well. But when you’re protein-maxxing, other nutrients, including fiber, can fall to the wayside.

Finally, though protein-maxxing is often touted as a way to slim down, the opposite can be true, too. “Your body has a ceiling for how much protein you can use,” says Altema-Johnson. Excess protein gets converted into glucose or fat for energy. Calories are energy units. You only need so many of them, and if you’re “chasing a protein number instead of eating until full,” as Altema-Johnson puts it, studies show that the extra calories can lead to weight gain.

Some protein-enriched packaged foods harbor sneaky calories. According to Rocheleau—who, by the way, eschews the phrase “protein-maxxing” in his work—“You would think that somebody putting out a high-protein product would take calories from carbs and fats and replace them with protein, but generally they keep the product the same but add protein, so you’re getting a lot more calories.” Plus, the marketing of protein-added snacks actually creates an insidious halo effect. “If you slap ‘high protein’ on a package, there’s the perception that it is automatically healthy, which can lead to overconsumption,” says Altema-Johnson. And while dairy- or plant-based protein products, including powdered supplements, can be a convenient way to support higher training needs to fill a genuine gap in the diet, Phillips’ research shows that they’re not a substitute for exercise itself and that protein intake had diminishing gains over a certain amount.

So what is the optimum amount of protein we should consume? Guidelines differ. Like the USDA previously, Canadian guidelines suggest a daily protein intake of .8 grams per kilogram of body weight. (To convert your body weight from pounds to kilograms, just divide it by 2.2.) For me, at 77 kilograms, 62 grams of protein per day is a good target, according to these guidelines, which comes out to a little over 8 ounces of roast chicken to meet my goals for the day. U.K. guidelines recommend slightly less, at .75 grams per kilogram, while the new USDA guidelines have been cranked up to 1.2 to 1.6 grams. At that serving goal, I can scarf down more than a pound of roast bird a day, and in theory, that’s what experts want me to do. For active and older adults, Phillips likes the new USDA targets, because we lose muscle mass as we age, and we start to need more protein to help retain it.

But not all protein is created equal. With my partner’s concern over cholesterol, maybe a skin-on bird dripping fat or a well-marbled steak seared in butter, both high in saturated fat, isn’t optimal for us. “This is where individualization matters,” says Altema-Johnson. “The goal is not zero red meat, but smaller proportions, moderation, and smarter cuts.” Experts like her, and plenty of studies, will warn you away from fattier and, especially, processed meats. “Unprocessed steak, ground beef, even pork chops have a modest health-associated risk,” Altema-Johnson says. “But bacon, sausage, deli meat, hot dogs—if you’re eating those constantly, you’re at higher risk for heart disease, colorectal cancer, and other health issues.”

Unlike animal proteins, not all plants contain every amino acid that our bodies need. But you can combine various vegetable proteins to meet those goals. Phillips and his colleagues found that young vegan and omnivorous men eating around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day achieved similar muscle and strength gains with resistance training. “Grains tend to be relatively low in lysine. Legumes help address that limitation, while grains complement legumes’ amino acid profiles,” he says. “Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, edamame, eggs, milk, yogurt, nuts, and seeds can all contribute. Soy is a particularly useful plant protein.” You don’t have to mix and match them at every meal, but a diverse plant-based diet can bring the protein you need.

The biggest takeaway is that you can’t just protein-max in the absence of overall healthy lifestyle choices. One of those is a balanced diet. According to Altema-Johnson, we should “individualize, moderate and balance. It’s important to have a diverse plate. If you’re focusing on one type of protein, especially meat, you’re missing out on all the good yummies a body needs.”

Chief among those yummies is fiber. Rossi says that recent studies support the idea that increasing protein can have benefits for weight-lifting and even aging, “but you need to increase fiber to balance it so your microbiome has more to eat than just excess protein. We need to swing the fiber flag.” Another recent study showed that 93 percent of Americans get enough protein, but other research reveals the opposite for fiber: Just 7 percent of us eat an adequate amount. That’s not good. A review of more than 5,000 studies found that a diet low in red meat but high in fiber-rich whole grains, vegetables, and nuts lowered our risk of death due to heart disease. “For gut health,” Phillips says, we should “ask what your protein habit is pushing off the plate.”

The other important lifestyle choice is exercise. “You can’t just expect to be sitting on the couch and eating protein and having these huge gains. Physical activity and resistance training bring far bigger results,” Rossi notes. That’s why I’ve ultimately been committed to moving more: Preventing muscle loss is insurance for my future. “Without enough protein and—most importantly, in my opinion—resistance exercise, this loss speeds up significantly,” says Altema-Johnson. “It affects strength, ability, balance, and fall risk. Muscle loss is directly tied to independence. It’s the difference between carrying your own groceries at 80 or needing help.”

Of course, I’m getting a late start. “You do not wake up at 65 with a new protein requirement. Start paying attention in midlife (over 40), and pair the protein with strength training, as that is the big lever to promote health, not protein,” notes Phillips. Well, I’m not 65 yet, but I did almost hit that age without addressing these health needs. Now I know that I need to exercise, and to support the training, I need a bit more protein, but not piles of it, and it has to come from a variety of sources. Perhaps most importantly, I’ll continue to take whatever the trend-setters are pushing on the socials with a grain of salt. As Phillips puts it, “Protein is a nutrient, not an identity. The goal is enough to support health, not as much as you can eat.”

#6496. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s big meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

A spectacular sea of fog, a perfectly formed rainbow and dramatic lightning strikes feature among this year's winning photographs for Weather Photographer of the Year 2026.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first light of dawn illuminates a sea of fog spilling over the rugged cliffs of Mallorca, Spain, in this year's winning Weather Photographer of the Year 2026 image. Photographer Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the scene from the Albercutz Watchtower, looking toward the Formentor Peninsula, after several days of high pressure and humid nights created the perfect conditions for fog to blanket the landscape.

On Nov. 17, the photograph, titled "Mares de Niebla (Seas of Fog)," was named overall winner of the Royal Meteorological Society's competition, which attracted more than 5,500 entries from photographers around the world.

The competition celebrates the ephemeral scenes created by weather, which can for brief moments transform landscapes into something extraordinary. Take a look at this year's winning photographs below and let us know your favorites in the comments.

Photographer Weilu Chen took second place in the main category with this spectacular image of golden light shining over the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge that runs for 34 miles (55 kilometers) across the Pearl River estuary in southern China.

A striking bolt of lightning illuminates a horizontal cloud during a thunderstorm, earning third place in the main category. These clouds are called arcus clouds that have a distinct shelf-like shape. "Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night," photographer Laura Hedien said in a statement.

Photographer Mahmudul Hasan won first place in the public vote category for this image of the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.

Watching from Bayonne, New Jersey, photographer Dan Martland captured this triple lightning strike above New York City, earning second place in the public vote category.

Photographer Aung Soe Min captured the Kuthodaw Pagoda emerging through the morning mist in Myanmar, as the sunrise light filters through the trees in this winning mobile category image.

Photographer Anthony Bird took second place in the mobile category with this spectacular rainbow stretching across Loch Duck in the Scottish Highlands.

Climate-award winning photographer Erfan Samanfar shot this haunting image of a farmer trying to protect his farmland from a raging fire in Marvdasht, Iran, in 2025.

Earning second place in the climate award category, photographer Andres Miraglia captured the moment a floating iceberg was seen in the sunset off Antarctica's Paradise Harbor.

#6492. The New Werwulf Popcorn Bucket Is Dividing Fans—And Christmas Might Be To Blame

Santa definitely didn’t sign off on this one.

Cinemark has revealed a new popcorn bucket inspired by Werwulf, and it’s probably safe to say Santa won’t be adding this one to his present delivery. The aptly named Claw Bucket resembles an enormous gray, furry werewolf paw, complete with long, menacing claws and some particularly blood-soaked fingers. The opening where the wrist would normally be is where your popcorn goes.

The collectible is tied to Robert Eggers’ upcoming horror film Werwulf, which arrives in theaters on December 25. Starring Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp, and Willem Dafoe, it’s set in medieval England and follows a farmer dealing with a rather unfortunate supernatural curse.

Cinemark shared the first look on Instagram, captioning its post with, “Do not dread the darkness. Our Werwulf claw popcorn bucket is COMING SOON to theaters!” And judging by the comments, some people are already prepared to make this horrifying little accessory part of their holiday plans.

“That's so ugly LMAOOO I want it,” one person wrote, capturing a sentiment I suspect plenty of popcorn bucket collectors can relate to.

“I’ll be on the hunt for this 🔥," someone else declared, while another commenter wondered what the gruesome design might reveal about the movie itself, calling it a “nice hint to what kinda werewolf we’ll be seeing.”

Of course, there’s also the small matter of the calendar. Christmas is hardly the first holiday that comes to mind when you see a furry, blood-covered monster hand, and some people aren’t thrilled about the timing.

“Ngl that’s creepy , should of came out for like Halloween or something,” one person commented. Another took considerably greater issue with the movie’s release date, writing, “Christmas is about Christ and gifts and Santa and all above not scary evil movie that belongs on December of Christmas. It should’ve been October they should’ve released it.”

I can understand expecting a little less bloodshed from your Christmas Day entertainment. Then again, for anyone who doesn’t celebrate Christmas—or whose ideal holiday involves escaping the family gathering for a horror movie—this sounds like a perfectly reasonable way to spend December 25.

The whole thing is another memorable entry in the increasingly bizarre popcorn bucket competition we’ve been following. Between the Hunger Games collectibles and AMC's Dune: Part Three sandworm buckets, movie theaters have been getting pretty creative with how they serve their snacks. A giant severed werewolf paw was the logical next step, of course.

The Claw Bucket will be available at participating Cinemark theaters while supplies last, complete with an extra-large popcorn and a free same-day refill. There’s no confirmed price or exact on-sale date yet, so anyone planning a particularly bloody holiday outing might want to keep an eye on their local concession stand.

#6491. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.
