He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6412. Mathematicians Find a Brilliant Shortcut to a 174-Year-Old Math Puzzle

A faster way to color maps using only four colors has revealed hidden mathematical patterns that could help solve puzzles involving far more complex shapes.

In 1852, English mathematician Francis Guthrie noticed something curious while drawing a map of England’s counties. He needed only four colors to ensure that no two neighboring counties shared the same color. Could the same be true of every flat map, regardless of how complicated its borders were?

What seemed like a simple observation became one of the most famous problems in mathematics. It took 124 years to prove Guthrie right and another half century to discover the most efficient way to assign those four colors. In solving the latter problem, an international team of mathematicians has uncovered something previously unknown about the mathematical structures underlying maps.

The history of the Four Color Problem is filled with frustrated attempts. A proof presented in 1879 stood for 11 years before an error was discovered. When mathematicians finally succeeded in 1976, their proof was controversial because it relied heavily on computer calculations that were difficult for others to verify. A more accessible proof followed in 1997, although finding a suitable coloring for large maps remained computationally demanding.

“The previous proofs showed that it is always possible to color a map using four colors. But they are not very good at actually finding the colors for each individual region on a map. The new algorithm is efficient and provides a much faster way of coloring,” says Professor Mikkel Thorup from the Department of Computer Science at the University of Copenhagen.

The achievement marks the first major breakthrough on the problem in nearly 30 years. The first part of the research paper was presented at FOCS’26, one of the world’s leading conferences in theoretical computer science, where it received the Best Paper Award.

Mathematicians can represent a flat map using what is known as a planar graph. Imagine replacing each country or county with a dot and drawing lines between those that share a border. The challenge then becomes assigning colors to the dots so that no two connected dots have the same color.

Within these graphs are small arrangements called reducible configurations, which allow mathematicians to simplify the coloring problem. The researchers discovered that graphs contain far more of these useful arrangements than anyone previously realized.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four coloring. We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before,” says Professor and co-author Carsten Thomassen from DTU.

Where earlier methods could often identify only one suitable starting point, the researchers can now work from many different parts of a graph. The advantage becomes particularly pronounced as maps grow larger.

“We have gone from what mathematicians call quadratic time to linear time. This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” explains Carsten Thomassen.

Finding this solution occupied Thorup and his colleagues, including Thomassen, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Bojan Mohar, for around a decade. Thorup has a name for the peculiar fascination that has kept mathematicians returning to the problem for 174 years: “the four-color disease.”

“The disease is believing that there must be a simple proof for such a simple statement. I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding. It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”

Thorup is equally candid about the appeal of devoting years to an apparently modest mathematical puzzle.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions. We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles,” says Mikkel Thorup.

That possibility is already emerging from the team’s work. The abundance of reducible configurations could help mathematicians investigate more complex graphs and surfaces whose geometry differs considerably from that of an ordinary map.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map. For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of Emmental cheese. That is why we believe the result could have significance far beyond the Four Color Theorem,” says Mikkel Thorup.

Reference: “The Four Color Theorem with Linearly Many Reducible Configurations and Near-Linear Time Coloring” by Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, Carsten Thomassen and Mikkel Thorup, September 30, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2603.24880

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

#6410. Should Space Data Centers Run on Solar Panels, Nuclear Reactors, or Both?

The last few days weâve been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently â maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? According to another paper from Dr. Turyshev, released as a preprint on arXiv, it all depends on the mission requirements.

One major problem with using solar panels for orbital data centers is the Sun doesnât always shine in their orbit. During some seasons, each orbital pass will result in the satellite crossing over the Earthâs shadow for up to 21 minutes. And given that the orbits these data centers are on happen around 15 times each day, that means in a 24-hour day, the satellite spends around 5 hours and 13 minutes in the Earth's shadow.

To combat this problem, engineers turn to an obvious solution â batteries. But they are notorious for being heavy, and according to Dr. Turyshevâs calculations, providing enough storage capacity to combat a 21-minute stretch with no power, would require a 1 MW data center cluster to haul 6.46 metric tons of batteries into orbit. Combine that with the needed solar panels and radiators to get rid of waste heat as infrared light, and you end up with a total mass of 43 metric tons for a 1 MW cluster, even before counting any actual computing hardware.

Fraser talks about the potential of a nuclear reactor in space.

A fission reactor would eliminate the need for solar wings, as well as batteries. However, it doesnât really deal well with the other physical constraint on these systems â waste heat. While it eliminates the heat generated by the solar panels themselves, it introduces another engineering problem â getting rid of the heat at two different temperatures.

Running a nuclear fission reactor at 25% efficiency (which is pretty standard for thermal electrical conversion) would produce about 3 megawatts of conversion waste heat for every one megawatt of energy generated, meaning a one-megawatt computing cluster creates nearly four megawatts of ultra-hot waste heat from its power conversion machinery alone. This waste heat would be at around 700 Kelvin â more than double the maximum temperature that processors on the data centers need to be kept below in order not to fry themselves. While this higher-temperature heat can be radiated away with a relatively compact radiator, it would have to be separate from the thermal sinks cooling the processors below their 320 Kelvin ideal temperature. Ultimately, a nuclear-powered cluster would only need around 6% less low temperature radiator area than a fully solar-powered version.

Despite that, after adding all the mass of the reactor, radiation shielding, power converters, and all the other necessary equipment to run a nuclear reactor, fission originally looks like a winner. Compared to todayâs standard solar panels, a compact fission reactor is around ten metric tons lighter per megawatt. And since weight is money in space, that sounds like a win.

Fraser talks about the new nuclear reactor NASA will use for future Mars missions.

However, there are several caveats to that. First, lighter, next-generation solar arrays are coming along quickly, whose increased efficiency could eliminate nuclearâs advantage entirely. Or the engineers could boost the satelliteâs orbit up to 1,450 kilometers, where the Earthâs shadow problem completely goes away and the satellite can consistently bathe in sunlight â admittedly ignoring the potential space debris and trapped radiation problems this causes, as well as the need for higher power communications equipment.

Nuclear suffers from another disadvantage - radiation. Data centers in space already suffer from stray cosmic rays flipping bits unexpectedly. Putting one next to an active nuclear reactor subjects them to random gamma rays and neutrons as well. While this could be lessened a bit by putting the reactor on a long boom â physically separating it from the server racks and placing a dense âshadow shieldâ near the reactor to block radiation from reaching the computers, that would require extra weight in the form of cabling and the boom itself, eliminating more of nuclearâs original weight advantage.

Despite all these trade-offs, there does appear to be a situation where running a hybrid of both solar and nuclear is the best option. If a mission requires a data center to survive a 24-hour failure of its main power system while keeping 20% emergency power active for safe-mode operation, an 80/20 nuclear/solar split weighs in at around 36 metric tons, around a third of the weight of either as a standalone option due to the weight of batteries needed to meet those mission requirements. But to be clear, without that power maintenance constraint, either system in a standalone configuration wins out on weight.

Fraser talks aobut the advantages and disadvantages of orbital data centers.

Ultimately, Dr. Turyshev thinks the financial picture is dependent on the lifespan of the nuclear reactor. Another disadvantage of a nuclear-powered satellite is it canât just burn up in the atmosphere at the end of its life â it has to be boosted to a âgraveyardâ orbit at around 2,000 km, where a spent reactor would stay indefinitely. But, if a reactor lasts ten years, Dr. Turyshev calculates that it would save around $190 per kilowatt-year in launch costs, whereas if it lasts for only two years (as many experimental space-based reactors are designed to), then that flips to a $783 per kilowatt-year deficit.

What the paper doesnât tackle is the social aspect of whether the general public would support putting potentially tens of thousands of small nuclear reactors into orbit. Just this week, NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy locked in the mission architecture for a nuclear-powered reactor known as Space Reactor-1 Freedom to power the propulsion system of a future Mars mission, so thereâs at least some support for it (or at least the government thinks there is). But as more and more data centers are launched, how to power them with the best trade-off of weight vs cost vs safety vs capability will remain an ongoing debate.

S.G. Turyshev - Power-Architecture Crossovers in Orbital Computing: Thermal, Radiation, and Lifetime Constraints

#6409. Why Some Farts Can Clear a Room While Others Barely Smell

A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.

A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen, and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

Your farts’ aroma depends on what your microbiome gets to eat.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves, and volcanic vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

Written by Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.

#6408. Scientists Discover Strange Dinosaur That Evolved To Eat Fruit

A dinosaur’s resemblance to modern fruit-eating parrots offers clues to how prehistoric animals adapted as flowering plants transformed life on land.

As flowering plants spread across the Cretaceous landscape, fruits became larger and more abundant, offering dinosaurs an entirely different source of food. Paleontologists have long struggled to understand how this transformation influenced dinosaur evolution. Now, the discovery of a turkey-sized dinosaur that lived alongside T. rex suggests that some dinosaurs developed remarkably sophisticated ways of eating fruit, much like parrots do today.

The newly identified species, Infernogallus jamesi, is the first known dinosaur with anatomical adaptations specifically linked to fruit consumption. The discovery was made by researchers from Stony Brook University, the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM), and the North Dakota Geological Survey. Led by Dr. Gregory Funston, assistant professor in the Department of Anatomical Sciences at Stony Brook University, the study was published in Nature Communications.

“We knew dinosaurs evolved to fill so many different roles in ecosystems in the Cretaceous, but we never expected to discover fruit-eating dinosaurs,” says Dr. Gregory Funston. “For more than 100 years, we didn’t know what the skulls of these animals looked like. Now, we know they were even weirder than we could have predicted.”

The dinosaur’s name, Infernogallus, means “hell chicken,” a reference to the Hell Creek Formation where its fossils were discovered. The formation stretches across Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Wyoming and preserves remains of familiar dinosaurs such as T. rex and Triceratops, which lived alongside Infernogallus. Its nearly complete skull, with the bones still connected, and partial skeleton are currently on display at the Royal Ontario Museum.

Despite descending from meat-eating dinosaurs, Infernogallus belonged to a group of toothless, feathered oviraptorosaurs known as caenagnathids. Weighing approximately 25 pounds (12 kilograms) as a fully grown adult, it was one of the smallest members of its group.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” says Dr. Thomas Dudgeon, Rebanks Postdoctoral Research Fellow at ROM and a co-author of the study. “The anatomy of Infernogallus is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we quickly realized that we were dealing with something special.”

Using CT scans to reconstruct the skull, the researchers noticed something unusual about the bones forming the roof of the mouth. These bones curved downward into the mouth, positioning certain chewing muscles horizontally rather than vertically. Instead of relying on the rigid, up-and-down bite characteristic of dinosaurs such as T. rex, Infernogallus could have moved its beak back and forth in a chewing motion similar to our own.

Forward-facing chewing muscles are uncommon in the animal kingdom, although they occur in mammals capable of complex chewing and in certain fruit-eating birds. The particular muscle arrangement identified in Infernogallus resembles that of the modern vulturine parrot (Psittrichas), suggesting that the dinosaur was adapted to processing soft food in its mouth rather than its gut. Its chewing motion appears to have been especially suited to separating the flesh of stone fruits from their hard central pits.

The finding also reveals an intriguing parallel in evolutionary history. As fruits became larger and more common, caenagnathids developed increasingly specialized chewing capabilities.

Fossilized fruits document how flowering plants gradually replaced cone-bearing plants as the dominant vegetation on land during the Cretaceous. By eating fruit, dinosaurs may have helped disperse seeds and influenced the evolution of flowering plants, fulfilling an ecological role that birds, reptiles, and small mammals play today.

“Complete remains of small dinosaurs like Infernogallus are very rare in the fossil record. The strange skull of Infernogallus is an exciting find because it reveals surprising insights into dinosaur evolution and feeding specialization,” says Dr. David Evans, chief curator of natural history and Temerty Chair in Vertebrate Paleontology at ROM and senior author of the paper. “This discovery shows that we still have a lot to learn about the world of T. rex, and about dinosaurs more generally.”

The discovery also contributes to an ongoing debate over whether dinosaurs were already in decline before their extinction. The specialized feeding behavior of Infernogallus suggests that the diversity of dinosaurs, and the ecological roles they occupied near the end of the Cretaceous, may have been greater than the fossil record has so far revealed.

Reference: “Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)” by Gregory F. Funston, Thomas W. Dudgeon, D. Jade Simon, Danielle M. Dufault, Clint Boyd, Denver Fowler, Philip J. Currie and David C. Evans, 10 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w

#6406. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

Our editor-tested and researched portable and whole-home options keep appliances and other essentials running during an emergency—no matter what.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

The generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s important to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review

Battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review

Pulsar is a relatively new brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.)

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, plan on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

When you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

My generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. #6405. Ancient Bison Hunting Site in Texas Challenges Decades of Archaeological Assumptions

Evidence of communal bison hunts spanning 3,000 years in Texas offers a fascinating glimpse into the enduring knowledge and ingenuity of ancient Indigenous hunter-gatherers.

For Indigenous hunter-gatherers in the Southern Plains, a successful large-scale bison hunt likely depended on people performing different jobs across the landscape. Some hunters located herds and guided them toward grazing areas near a cliff, while others waited in hiding to drive the animals over the edge, where the fall would kill or incapacitate them. Additional teams would have killed injured bison and processed the meat, hides, and other materials.

Archaeologists have now uncovered evidence that generations of Indigenous communities carried out such hunts at the same location in the Texas Panhandle over approximately 3,000 years. Known as Nighthawk, the site lies within Caprock Canyons State Park and is only the second scientifically verified example of a bison jump in Texas. For decades, archaeologists had questioned whether this sophisticated hunting technique, widely documented in the northern Great Plains, was also practiced farther south.

The findings, published in the journal American Antiquity, come from a collaborative investigation involving the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, Texas Tech University, Plains Archeological Research, and other research partners. Rice University adjunct lecturer August “Gus” Costa served as a principal investigator and is the study’s lead author.

“Bison jumping is exciting because it’s a community activity,” Costa said. “Large-scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful.”

These gatherings likely fulfilled needs beyond securing food and other resources. Costa believes the hunts provided opportunities for communities to trade, hold ceremonies, celebrate, and strengthen social relationships.

Initially, stone spear and arrow points recovered at Nighthawk suggested that at least two hunts had taken place there. Radiocarbon dating of bison bones revealed a much longer history, identifying evidence of at least seven separate hunting events spanning approximately three millennia.

During that time, hunting technology shifted from stone-tipped spears to bows and arrows, pottery was introduced, and the surrounding landscape underwent substantial changes. Erosion alone moved the cliff’s jump-off point roughly the length of a football field.

“Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility,” Costa said.

The shape of the landscape also presents an intriguing problem. At many northern Plains bison jumps, the terrain may have concealed the cliff edge from approaching animals. Nighthawk, however, sits on a projecting cliff, meaning the bison could likely see the danger ahead. How hunters adapted their methods to overcome this difficulty remains unknown.

“We don’t know exactly how they managed herding the bison, but the setting is different from the typical northern Plains jump,” Costa said.

Before Nighthawk was documented, Bonfire Shelter, identified more than 60 years ago, was the only scientifically verified bison jump in Texas. Costa and his colleagues have since identified eight additional potential sites in and around Caprock Canyons, suggesting that the practice may have been considerably more widespread.

Part of the difficulty in finding these sites lies in where archaeologists traditionally look. Investigations often concentrate on former living areas, where people left tools and other traces of daily life. Steep slopes beneath cliffs would have made poor campsites and consequently received less attention. Erosion and limited access to private property have further complicated the search.

“The jump was hidden in plain sight,” Costa said.

With fieldwork at Nighthawk complete, the researchers are searching for additional sites across the Southern Plains. They are also examining ancient bison DNA and the chemical composition of bones and teeth to reconstruct herd migrations, understand past environmental conditions, and investigate possible connections to the bison living in Caprock Canyons State Park today.

“For a long time when it comes to Indigenous bison hunting culture, the Southern Plains hasn’t received much respect, at least when compared to the north,” Costa said.

For Costa, the discovery illustrates the danger of judging ancient societies solely by the evidence that happens to survive. Gaps in the archaeological record can obscure generations of accumulated knowledge, ingenuity, and cultural practices.

“It’s about respect,” Costa said. “Bison jumping is a complicated community effort, and getting that incorporated into the story of Southern Plains people is important.”

Reference: “The Nighthawk Bison Jump: New Evidence for Recurrent Late Holocene Bison Jumping in the Southern Plains” by August G. Costa, Brett A. Houk, Anthony S. Lyle, Leland Bement, Christopher Lintz, Ken L. Lawrence, Charles D. Frederick and Brendan J. Culleton, 9 November 2026, American Antiquity. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

First the wolves skirt around edges of the bison herd, building tension, restricting movement, fomenting internal strife, preventing herd coalescence. Then, when the wolves sense the moment is right, they launch a series of targeted attacks, skirmishes if you will, to provoke the herd to panic. Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6402. Alzheimer’s Breakthrough? Experimental Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory in Mice

Experimental nose drops helped mice with signs of Alzheimer’s hold on to their memory, even though the treatment left the brain’s telltale protein clumps in place.

What if some of the memory loss associated with aging could be reversed with something as simple as nose drops?

Scientists at the University of Sydney have taken a promising step toward that possibility, developing an experimental treatment that restored learning and memory performance in older mice to levels comparable to those of younger animals. The same approach also protected mice genetically predisposed to Alzheimer’s-like disease from cognitive decline.

Both experiments centered on brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that helps nerve cells survive and adjust their connections as memories form. Lower levels of BDNF are associated with aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Supplying the brain with more of the protein poses a familiar problem. The blood-brain barrier keeps many medicines in the bloodstream from reaching brain tissue. Connections between the nasal cavity and the brain offer another way in, without surgery or injections into the brain or spinal cord.

“If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer’s that bypasses the blood-brain barrier,” said Professor Greg Neely, whose lab at the university’s Charles Perkins Centre led the study.

The researchers adapted the clinically validated design of the messenger RNA (mRNA) used in BioNTech’s COVID-19 vaccine, where it carries instructions that prompt an immune response. For the nose drops, the team packaged mRNA carrying instructions for BDNF in tiny particles made of fats, called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). As the researchers reported in Advanced Science, cells in the nose read those instructions and made the protein, which could then reach the brain.

“The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells,” said first author Dr. Maria Bergamasco of the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences. “We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way.”

To compare older and younger mice, the researchers used standardized behavioral tests that measured how well the animals could hold information in mind briefly, remember places, and recognize objects.

“In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime,” Neely said. “What’s exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic.”

For the Alzheimer’s experiment, the team used 5XFAD mice, a “humanized” model in which genetic mutations cause signs of the disease to appear rapidly. The researchers gave the mice nose drops twice a week starting at two months of age, when the first changes in the brain are usually detectable. At four months, when these mice typically begin to lose cognitive abilities, the treated animals showed no further decline.

The researchers also saw more new neurons forming in the hippocampus, a brain region critical for learning and memory. In the Alzheimer’s model, the drops preserved brain function without reducing amyloid plaques, the clumps of protein that are a hallmark of the disease.

“Current Alzheimer’s treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques,” Neely said. “However just under a third of Alzheimer’s patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it’s possible to live with Alzheimer’s disease pathology.”

“Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other.”

The researchers think the nasal delivery system could eventually carry medicines for stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental diseases. “This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose,” Neely said.

The mice appeared to tolerate the drops well, with no major side effects detected during the study. “Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals,” Neely said. “It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans to before we know whether it will work.

“We believe our new drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people.”

The team plans to refine the delivery system and assess its long-term safety and effectiveness. “Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans,” Neely said. “We hope we can move quickly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years.”

Reference: “Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer’s Disease Mouse Models” by Maria Bergamasco, Hannah Scarborough, Anna Ponta, Teleri Clark, Scott B. Cohen, Lipin Loo, Kazuma Fujikake, Rebecca Carr, R.M. Damian Holsinger and G.Gregory. Neely, 18 November 2026, Advanced Science. DOI: 10.1002/advs.78225

Funding was received from the National Health and Medical Research Council, the NSW Ministry of Health and an ongoing philanthropic donation from Dr John and Anne Chong to support the work of the Neely Lab.

Disclosure: Greg Neely and Maria Bergamasco are inventors on a provisional patent application related to this work.
