#6400. The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

These tested and researched models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and other trusted brands are the ones we stand behind and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

The EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

To get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

We got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

The Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

#6399. Scientists Discover a Unique Gut Microbe Signature in People Who Live to 100

People who lived to 100 carried a distinctive chemical fingerprint in their guts, and boosting the bacterial enzyme linked to it helped older mice respond better to insulin.

A single dose of engineered gut bacteria made older mice more sensitive to insulin about five months later. The UC San Diego team also analyzed data from young adults, older adults, and centenarians to see how the same gut bacterial activity varies with age in people.

The study focused on bile acids, which the liver makes to help digest fats. Bile acids also carry signals that help regulate metabolism, inflammation, and the body’s internal clock. Gut bacteria make enzymes called bile salt hydrolases (BSH) that change the chemical makeup of bile acids and can alter the signals they send.

Older mice showed more microbial activity linked to BSH and more extensive changes to their bile acids than younger mice. The researchers then looked for a similar pattern in existing data from 48 young adults, 107 older adults, and 125 centenarians.

Centenarians had higher ratios of certain modified bile acids than either of the younger groups. Their gut microbiomes also contained more copies of a gene linked to BSH activity than those of older adults.

“Many studies of aging focus on what goes wrong as we get older, but our findings suggest that some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body’s attempt to preserve metabolic health,” said senior author Amir Zarrinpar, MD, PhD, Stuart and Barbara L. Brody Endowed Chair in Circadian Biology and Medicine and professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine. “If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging.”

To test whether boosting BSH activity could change metabolism, the team gave 82-week-old mice a strain of gut bacteria engineered to keep making the enzyme. The bacteria took hold after one treatment and continued producing BSH over time.

About 20 weeks later, the mice responded significantly better to insulin and were modestly better at clearing glucose from their blood than mice given a matched control bacterium. By week 32, the treated mice also showed changes consistent with lower body weight, less body fat, and more lean mass.

Other measurements suggested that the mice used more fat for energy and that their mitochondria worked better. The researchers also saw shifts in the activity of genes involved in inflammation and the body’s internal clock.

Centenarians and aged mice represent different stages of life, and the mouse experiment did not establish whether the treatment extends lifespan. Studies in people will need to determine whether higher BSH activity helps preserve health with age, reflects healthier aging, or both.

The researchers plan to test how different forms of the enzyme affect bile acid metabolism, inflammation, and energy use. They also want to see whether female mice respond similarly, given known differences in how males and females age.

“The goal isn’t simply to live longer—it’s to understand the biology that allows some people to remain resilient as they age,” said Zarrinpar. “The microbiome gives us an intriguing opportunity because, unlike many aspects of aging, it may be something we can modify. This study gives us a starting point for asking whether beneficial microbial functions can be amplified to help preserve metabolic health later in life.”

Reference: “Microbial bile acid deconjugation counters metabolic decline in aging” by Ana Carolina Dantas Machado, Wuling Zhong, Anand R. Saran, Baylee J. Russell, Erica Maissy, Stephany Flores Ramos, Antonio F.M. Pinto, Juan Pablo Zuniga-Hertz, R. Alexander Richter, Max W. Chang, April L. Lukowski, Koji Atarashi, Alan R. Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6397. Scientists Develop a Powerful Two-in-One Treatment for Gum Disease

Gum disease can eat away at the bone that holds teeth in place, and a tiny cage made of DNA helped slow that damage in rats.

Researchers at Sichuan University built a DNA carrier that delivers two compounds together to treat periodontitis, a chronic form of gum disease and a leading cause of tooth loss in adults. The team, led by Geru Zhang, Yunfeng Lin, and Xiaoxiao Cai, published its findings in the International Journal of Oral Science.

Periodontitis starts when bacterial plaque builds up beneath the gums. The resulting immune response can gradually destroy the tissue and bone that anchor teeth. Deep cleaning and antibiotics can reduce the number of bacteria, but they may leave existing damage unrepaired and do not always stop the disease from progressing.

“We aimed to create a multifunctional DNA nanoplatform capable of delivering both curcumin and the antimicrobial peptide defensin directly to periodontal tissues, with the goal of overcoming the limitations of existing therapies,” Zhang said.

The team loaded both compounds into tiny, four-sided DNA structures called tetrahedral framework nucleic acids (tFNAs). The researchers tested the resulting complex, called Cur-de-tFNA, against bacteria linked to periodontitis and used a bacterial molecule to trigger inflammation in human periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs) in the lab.

“The DNA carrier enhanced the stability and cellular uptake of curcumin while protecting defensin from degradation, allowing both therapeutic agents to function more effectively,” Lin said.

In lab tests, the combined treatment outperformed its individual components across several experiments. It acted against bacteria linked to gum disease, reduced oxidative stress, and dampened an inflammatory signaling pathway called TLR4/NF-κB. It also increased levels of proteins involved in bone formation.

In rats with periodontitis, the treatment reduced bone loss and inflammatory damage around the teeth. The researchers observed less activity from cells that break down bone, along with more collagen deposition and new bone formation. “As a result, the nanoplatform delivered stronger antimicrobial activity, better control of inflammation, and improved preservation of periodontal tissues in preclinical models,” Cai said.

The biodegradable DNA carrier was well tolerated in preclinical tests. Human trials are needed to determine whether the treatment is safe and can help preserve or rebuild the tissues that support teeth.

Reference: “DNA framework-based nanomedicine platform: a triple-function strategy for treating periodontitis via antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and osteogenesis-promoting activities” by Geru Zhang, Weitong Cui, Haoyan Wu, Xiaowei Liu, Liwei Huang, Yunfeng Lin and Xiaoxiao Cai, 29 April 2026, International Journal of Oral Science. DOI: 10.1038/s41368-026-00439-2

#6396. The 7 Best Garage Heaters for Your Workshop

These editor-approved electric and gas models turn chilly spaces warm fast—so you can pull off your gloves and get your projects done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you plan to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

Garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

Heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most important things to know before buying.

Although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

The garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

Thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

The garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

For a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

The fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

Designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

The heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

For a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

The heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

It runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

Note that the Big Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

There’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, New Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

Both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you plan to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

Aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

Using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

As we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

Infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat quickly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

For most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

“A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio says. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very quickly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”

Before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

Whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

Second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

#6395. A Black Hole Smaller Than an Atom Could Trigger One of the Universe’s Most Violent Explosions

An ancient black hole no larger than an atom could consume a star from within and eventually trigger a spectacular explosion. New simulations by physicists at MIT and collaborating institutions suggest that these events could produce detectable bursts of radiation, offering a possible way to discover black holes formed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, could also help scientists investigate dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Primordial black holes may have formed when exceptionally dense regions collapsed under gravity during the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang. The smallest would have evaporated through Hawking radiation, but heavier examples could survive today. Some might be as small as an atom yet contain the mass of an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

The researchers investigated what would happen if one of these black holes encountered a Sun-like star. Although a star’s gravity alone would not capture a passing black hole, interactions involving a companion star or planet could trap it. Repeated passages through the star would gradually reduce its orbital energy, allowing it to settle into the stellar core over thousands to millions of years.

“Then, this is where the action begins,” says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

The team’s three-dimensional simulations suggest that a captured black hole could grow by consuming stellar material. Within several million years, it might absorb approximately 1 percent of the star’s mass. If the star rotates fast enough, the remaining gas would form a spinning disk around the black hole.

“Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,” Gottlieb says. “The black hole is also spinning, and it’s twisting space and time.”

As material spirals inward, the black hole would twist magnetic fields in the surrounding disk, generating powerful jets capable of tearing through the star.

“Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,” Gottlieb says.

“This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,” Gottlieb explains. “And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It’s very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.”

The resulting explosion could produce a brilliant flash of blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays. As the event evolves, its emissions would shift across the electromagnetic spectrum.

“We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,” Gottlieb says. “This is something we could potentially detect, if it’s not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.”

Other cosmic explosions can produce similar signals, so astronomers would need additional evidence to identify a primordial black hole. One possible clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not normally be expected to explode.

“For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside,” Gottlieb says.

No primordial black hole has yet been confirmed through this mechanism, but the predicted signals could guide future observations.

“There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,” Gottlieb says. “We expect this to be visible, and it’s something we should look into.”

“The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.”

Reference: “The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes” by Ore Gottlieb, Matteo Cantiello, Cameron Norton, Ken Van Tilburg and Matthew Kleban, 19 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb7e1

This work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program, and by the National Science Foundation.

#6394. In a 1996 study, researchers reviewed 22,793 poinsettia cases reported to U.S. poison centers and found no deaths, but the plant can still upset pets

Poison Control says the deadly reputation rests on a child's death over 100 years ago. Tests of about 500 to 600 leaves found no poisonous dose.

Every holiday season, poinsettias go up on tables and windowsills, and so does an old warning: keep them away from children, because they are deadly.

Researchers led by the Pittsburgh Poison Center checked that idea against hard numbers. In a study published in 1996 in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine, they analyzed 849,575 plant exposures reported to the American Association of Poison Control Centers (HRSA).

Poinsettias accounted for 22,793 of those cases. There were no deaths among them.

The researchers wrote that the poinsettia “is a much-maligned plant which is thought by the public and some health professionals to be extremely toxic.”

Their data told a different story. Almost all of the poinsettia exposures, 98.9%, were accidental, and 93.3% involved children.

Most of the people involved, 96.1%, were not treated in a health care facility. And 92.4% did not develop any toxicity related to the poinsettia at all.

“Most patients do not require any type of therapy and can be treated without referral to a health care facility,” the authors concluded.

The study is 30 years old, but the current advice from Poison Control, run by the National Capital Poison Center, says the same thing.

“The poinsettia plant is often considered deadly. That’s wrong,” its guidance states. “Poinsettia can be irritating but it is not fatal if eaten.”

Poison Control says some stories “just won’t go away.” “Over a hundred years ago, a child was found next to a wild poinsettia plant. He died and people blamed the plant. This hasn’t happened since,” it says.

Researchers have even tried to find a poisonous dose. They “just couldn’t, even after reaching experimental doses of about 1.25 pounds (500-600 leaves),” according to Poison Control.

That does not mean the plant is a snack. If children or pets eat it, Poison Control says, they can develop mouth irritation and stomach upset, such as nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.

The sap can cause a skin rash, and Poison Control notes reports of gardeners who work with the plant frequently developing one.

Poison Control describes one real case. On Christmas Day, a 10-month-old put a small piece of a poinsettia leaf in his mouth, and his mother called a poison center.

The specialist told her no problems were expected and advised her to wipe the child’s mouth and give him something to drink.

The plant can also be a choking hazard, so Poison Control recommends placing poinsettias, and other houseplants, where children and pets cannot reach them.

The ASPCA lists the poinsettia as toxic to dogs, cats and horses, and it names the plant’s irritant sap as the toxic principle.

Under clinical signs, the ASPCA describes the plant as “irritating to the mouth and stomach, sometimes causing vomiting, but generally over-rated in toxicity.”

Poinsettias are only one of the season’s concerns for pet owners. Earth.com has looked at how to keep cats safe at Christmas, from toxic trees to dangling decorations, and at festive plants that may be less safe than they look.

The poinsettia is the most popular flowering plant sold in the United States, with more than 70 million sold each year, according to a Clemson Cooperative Extension factsheet last revised in 2015.

It is named after Joel R. Poinsett, the first U.S. ambassador to Mexico. He brought the plant to the Bartram Botanical Garden in Philadelphia in 1828, and a Philadelphia nurseryman, Robert Buist, named it after him, the factsheet says.

The wild plants in Mexico grew 12 to 15 feet tall. The red parts that people think of as flowers are actually bracts, a kind of modified leaf. The true flowers are the small yellow clusters in the center.

If someone does swallow part of a poinsettia, Poison Control’s advice is to call a poison center at 1-800-222-1222, which is free, confidential and available 24 hours a day.

The information was obtained from the study Poinsettia exposures have good outcomes…just as we thought (American Journal of Emergency Medicine, 1996), Poison Control’s page Are poinsettias poisonous?, the ASPCA’s poinsettia entry, and Clemson Cooperative Extension’s poinsettia factsheet.

This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6392. Astronomers Discover the Sun Contains 55% More Silver Than Previously Thought

Some of the oldest rocks in the solar system hinted that astronomers were undercounting the Sun’s silver. A fresh look at sunlight suggests they were right.

Researchers at Uppsala University estimate that silver is 55 percent more abundant in the Sun than previous calculations indicated.

The revised estimate brings the Sun much closer to the silver abundance found in primitive meteorites. Both preserve material from the same cloud of gas and dust that gave rise to the solar system 4.6 billion years ago.

Silver atoms in the Sun’s atmosphere absorb light at specific wavelengths, leaving dark lines in the spectrum. The pattern identifies silver, but estimating how much is there requires a model that predicts how strongly those atoms absorb light.

The team modeled the motion of the Sun’s outer layers and used more detailed calculations of how silver atoms interact with light and other particles. The model accounts for how radiation changes the energy states of silver atoms, which affects the strength of the lines astronomers use to measure the element’s abundance.

“With our new model, we were able to interpret the spectral lines used to determine the solar silver abundance more accurately,” says Sema Caliskan, who conducted the research during her PhD studies at Uppsala University.

Hydrogen and helium make up nearly all of the Sun. Heavier elements such as carbon, iron, and silver account for just 1.5 percent of its mass. Many of these elements form inside stars or during stellar explosions, then become part of later generations of stars and planets. Measuring their abundance helps astronomers reconstruct how the Milky Way’s chemistry changed over time.

“The new knowledge about the Sun’s composition is important for the understanding of other stars, planets, and cosmic material, because the Sun is one of astronomy’s key reference points,” says Caliskan.

The team plans to apply the same method to other stars. “By studying the light of stars of different types and ages, we hope to understand where silver is formed in the universe, and how it has been distributed throughout the Milky Way over time,” says Caliskan.

Reference: “Ag I model atom and the 3D non-LTE solar silver abundance” by S. Caliskan, A. M. Amarsi, P. Jönsson, N. Grevesse and B. K. Sahoo, 17 July 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202659578

This study was funded by the Swedish Research Counsil, KVA Kungliga vetenskapsakademien, and ANRF India.

#6391. An mRNA shot made hearts pump about 10% more blood after a heart attack, with the effect lasting 12 weeks

An experimental mRNA treatment helped mouse heart cells divide after a heart attack, improving pumping function, but human trials are still needed.

An experimental treatment pushed adult heart muscle cells in mice to divide again after a heart attack, something those cells normally cannot do.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge delivered a modified messenger RNA that briefly switches on two proteins inside heart cells, Myc and Cyclin T1.

Treated mice pumped around 10 percent more blood with each heartbeat than mice given a mock treatment, the university reported.

The gain held when the animals were reassessed at 12 weeks. The work was done in mice, and the treatment has not been tested in people.

An adult human heart can lose up to one billion heart muscle cells in a heart attack. Those cells are never replaced, which weakens the pump and leaves scar tissue behind.

An estimated 920,000 people in the U.K. are living with heart failure, and a transplant is the only cure, according to the British Heart Foundation (BHF).

“Getting the human heart to repair itself is the holy grail for cardiologists,” said Professor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the BHF.

Myc is better known as a cancer gene. Switching it on makes liver cells multiply within days, yet in the heart it does almost nothing.

A 2020 mouse study explained why. Myc protein binds DNA in heart muscle cells but cannot turn genes on, because the heart is short of a partner protein, Cyclin T1.

“When the Ccnt1 and Myc genes were expressed together, the heart switched into a regenerative state,” said Dr. Megan Bywater, a senior research officer at QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute and first author of that work.

The new experiment turns that finding into something closer to a therapy. Instead of altering genes, it uses mRNA, the kind of instruction a cell reads and then breaks down.

The team injected 100 micrograms of modified mRNA straight into the heart muscle during surgery. Injections guided by ultrasound did not work efficiently.

Myc and Cyclin T1 protein showed up in heart tissue one hour and four hours after the injection, and had gone by 24 hours.

A fluorescent version of the molecule, used to track where it travelled, was still visible around damaged heart cells 24 hours after the injection.

The university says the brief, localized signal is not expected to cause any permanent modification, which is meant to limit the risk of overgrowth.

Ultrasound scans tracked each animal on days three, six and 28 after treatment.

Ejection fraction, the share of blood the left ventricle pushes out with each beat, dropped by 26 percent in treated mice by day 28. In untreated animals it fell by 37 percent.

At 12 weeks the decline was 7.1 percent in the treated group, against 16.1 percent in controls.

Markers of cell division rose in the treated hearts, and the number of heart muscle cells had climbed by day five.

Tagging cells and their descendants showed 41.5 percent of labeled heart muscle cells sitting in adjacent pairs after treatment, compared with 5.5 percent in control hearts.

A genetically engineered version of the same approach did even better, holding the day-28 decline to 9 percent against 23 percent in controls.

Scar tissue told a different story. By day 28 the scar was no smaller in treated mice, although the volume of working muscle in the left ventricle had grown.

Waiting did not ruin the effect. In the transgenic model, switching the two proteins on seven to eight days later held the ejection fraction drop to 14 percent by day 36, against 30 percent in untreated animals.

No tumors were found in the treated animals at either checkpoint, and laboratory tests found no added capacity to transform cells.

Switching Myc on across the whole heart, by contrast, killed seven of eight mice in the transgenic version of the experiment, which is why the team confined the signal to the injured area.

Among the animals that received the mRNA, survival across 12 weeks did not differ significantly from controls.

Human heart muscle cells grown from stem cells in a dish also showed more signs of division after treatment.

The Cambridge group is now refining the treatment with BHF funding.

Larger animal studies, and then human trials, are needed to establish safety and effectiveness before the approach could help a human heart heal after a heart attack.

“These are really exciting results,” said Dr. Catherine Wilson, an associate professor of pharmacology at the University of Cambridge and co-senior author of the study.

“We’re not just treating the symptoms of heart failure – this approach could help the heart to repair itself,” Wilson added.

“That makes it exciting when studies like this are able to reignite regeneration in heart muscle cells,” Williams said.

The study was published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research.

#6390. The 6 Best Wood Stoves for Warmth, Ambiance, and More

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These simple appliances can generate an impressive amount of heat safely, and without increasing your energy bill.

The crackle of a fire on a cold winter night can add charm to any home. However, fireplaces aren’t particularly efficient heat sources, especially in chilly temperatures. And electric fireplaces, space heaters, and other supplementary heat sources can leave you in the dark (and out in the cold) during a power outage.

Instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source. Modern wood stoves can be safe, affordable, and efficient if you clean and maintain them regularly.

More than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S. are older, uncertified models that put out far more particulate pollution than newer ones, according to the EPA, and some states prohibit or restrict these wood-burning devices. All of the wood stoves recommended here are EPA-certified, and they still crank out enough BTUs to make your home or cabin cozy.

Before you buy, think carefully about where you’ll install your stove. You’ll need proper clearance from combustible materials in walls and floors, and the stove’s weight has to work for your house.

The Expert (Alex Rennie): I'm a freelance writer who specializes in the Home Improvement, DIY, and Tool space. As a former residential and commercial carpenter, I use my hands-on experience to write practical buying guides, how-to articles, and product reviews. Based in Los Angeles, I spend my free time exploring the beaches and mountains with my fiancé and our dog Louie.

To choose my wood stove recommendations, I selected non-catalytic models that are affordable while still meeting EPA emissions standards. Among the wood stoves that made the cut, you’ll find a wide variety to meet your space limitations and style preferences while maintaining efficient BTU output.

One of the best things about having a huge fire in the middle of your home is that it lets you make the most of those rustic vibes. Many of the stoves I picked have a cooktop (very convenient) or a large window, so you can put your feet up and enjoy watching the flames. I also relied on prior research conducted by writer Alex Rennie, who also contributed to this article.

This pedestal stove from Ashley Hearth hits the sweet spot between size, heat output, and price. Its 2,500-square-foot heating range fits the average home with room to spare, and the brick-lined, 2.7-cubic-foot firebox accepts logs up to 21 inches long. That means fewer trips to the woodpile on cold nights.

One of the best features is the cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass, which helps keep soot off the window so you can enjoy the view of the fire. A non-catalytic secondary burn extracts more heat from every load and keeps emissions within EPA standards. It’s mobile-home approved when paired with the optional fresh air kit. The stove runs fine without electricity, but an optional blower will help push warm air into the rest of your house.

If you don’t need to heat your entire home, this compact Ashley Hearth model delivers plenty of warmth for the money. Its 68,000 BTU output covers up to 1,200 square feet. That makes it a smart fit for a cabin or an open living area, or as a supplemental heat source that takes some pressure off your furnace.

It shares many features with our Best Overall pick, including a firebrick-lined firebox and a non-catalytic secondary burn that keeps emissions within EPA standards. It also has a heavy cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass. It ships with both legs and a pedestal, so you can choose the look that suits your space. At 258 pounds, it’s relatively easy to move into place, and it’s mobile-home approved with the optional fresh air kit. The trade-off is a smaller 1.3-cubic-foot firebox, so you’ll load logs more often than with a larger stove.

If watching the fire matters more to you than heating every corner of the house, this Superior stove is built around the view. A large rectangular ceramic-glass door gives you a wide view of the flames, and the built-in air-wash system sweeps air across the glass to keep soot off.

The high-density firebrick holds heat longer for a more efficient burn. It puts out just 2.1 grams of particulate per hour, well under EPA limits. It fits logs up to 18 inches long, and one control handles the airflow. A black pedestal base comes standard, and an optional variable-speed blower can push warm air into nearby rooms.

The trade-off is a heating range of up to 1,400 square feet, so it’s best suited to a living room, a cabin, or a smaller home.

The WoodPro 300 is the largest model in the WoodPro line, built for anyone heating a large open floor plan, a farmhouse, or a drafty workshop. Its 2.26-cubic-foot firebox takes 18-inch logs and can burn for up to 12 hours on a single load, so you won’t have to refill it every couple of hours.

The stove is made of heavy-gauge steel with a cast-iron door. The Smart Air Control uses two levers, so the lighting procedure is simple: get the fire going, set the air, and leave it alone. It meets EPA 2020 standards at 1.6 grams of smoke per hour with 74.2 percent efficiency, and it’s approved for mobile homes with the outside air kit. Its peak output of 61,700 BTU is modest for a stove rated for 3,000 square feet, so treat that number as a best case in a well-insulated home, not something to count on in a cold climate.

This rustic model from Ashley Hearth—under the US Stove Company umbrella—the US1269E, is a natural fit for log cabin homes that want a rugged addition to their living space, or for anyone looking to add woodsy charm to their home.

My favorite feature is the oversized safety handle, which is comfortable to grab when opening or closing the door and stays cool to the touch, even when the stove is in operation.

Tested and certified to U.L.1482 by Warnock Hersey International, this stove’s 900-square-foot heating range isn’t the largest of my selections, but it's still impressive for its size. The integrated cooking surface on top is also a valuable feature.

If you’re looking for a pint-sized stove for a small space, including a mobile home, US Stove's Tiny Wood Stove may provide the perfect fit. The slim profile doesn’t mean it’s short on efficiency or on meeting emissions standards, and it still qualifies for the 30-percent Biomass federal tax credit.

A compact design, however, comes with a few caveats, including a rather small log size and a relatively low BTU output. Still, the US Stove Tiny Stove is a great trade-off for a single-room cabin or a more compact space in your home.

Wood stoves come in all shapes, sizes, and designs. Choose one that suits your space in terms of style and efficiency. Here’s how to decide what you need in a wood stove and what you don't.

There are two types of modern wood stoves: catalytic and non-catalytic. Both reduce air pollution by reburning exhaust to limit emissions, but catalytic stoves use a different process that is slightly more efficient at this second burn. Non-catalytic stoves are popular because they’re less expensive and slightly more efficient at producing heat.

Because the cost of a wood stove with a catalytic converter is currently prohibitive for the average homeowner, the wood stove models we’ve recommended below are all non-catalytic.

More Hot Stuff: Smokeless Fire Pits • Fire Pit Tables • Portable Fire Pits • Heated Blankets

The size of your wood stove matters not just for the space it can heat, but also for safety. Before you install a wood stove, check your state requirements for clearance. Federal guidelines stipulate that the stove should be installed at least 3 feet from any combustibles in the wall, ceiling, or floors.

If you have children, also consider how much clearance you might need around the stove for a child safety gate and where you plan to stack and store firewood.

British Thermal Units (BTUs) might sound fancy, but it's just a measurement of how much heat is being generated. This differs from the heating area of a wood stove because it refers to the energy the stove produces in an hour. A rule of thumb: You need 20 BTUs for every foot of space you want to heat. Use this online BTU calculator to dial in exactly how many thermal units your home needs.

Decide whether you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source or for supplemental heat in the winter. In general, a small wood stove can heat about 500 square feet, while a medium wood stove warms up to 1,000 square feet. A large model will heat a room of 1,500 square feet or more.

More isn’t always better. To keep costs in check and your wood stove efficient, consider if you really need to heat every space in your home or just the living areas your family frequents.

Modern wood stoves are lighter than ever, but many large models can still tip the scales at several hundred pounds. Depending on the stove's weight, you may not be able to install it in a mobile home or in certain structurally vulnerable spots in your house. Instead, look for a wood stove approved for mobile homes by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

If your goal is an outdoor wood stove portable enough for camping or backpacking, choose a lightweight model with components that collapse into a compact package.

The size of the logs and the kind of wood you put into your wood stove is about more than convenience or cost. It can also affect burn time and efficiency, which is especially important if you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source.

Generally, most wood stoves fit logs about 16 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. As you can imagine, wood stoves designed for smaller logs may leave you rolling up your sleeves and grabbing the axe more often than you might like.

Since 2020, nearly all new wood stoves sold in the United States must be certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to meet its 2020 emissions standards, which limit fine particle pollution to 2.0 grams per hour (2.5 g/h when tested with cordwood). All of the wood stoves we’ve recommended below meet this standard, and you can look up any model in the EPA’s database of certified wood-burning heaters.

A wood stove’s effectiveness in converting wood into heat is expressed as a percentage of combustion efficiency. Efficiency matters because it directly translates into how much wood you’ll burn to keep your home warm. Most modern EPA-certified stoves fall between 70 and 80 percent efficiency, and every few points add up over a full heating season in fewer logs split, stacked, and hauled inside.

From insulating the chimney to adhering to proper stovepipe clearance, to wall shields and floor pads, there’s quite a bit to do when you install a wood stove, and much of it is mandated by building codes and state or federal laws. To protect your safety, it's critical that you don't miss a step, which is why I recommend leaving the installation of the wood stove to a professional.

Clean your wood stove (and chimney) thoroughly and often to avoid creosote buildup, a highly flammable byproduct of burning wood.

While cleaning your chimney, tidying up your wood stove is pretty straightforward. When the stove is cool, lay down a cloth or newspaper, then empty the ashtray and any ashes from the firebox into an ash bucket. Then wait at least 24 to 48 hours before you dump the ash bucket so any slightly warm embers don’t catch fire.

You can wipe down the interior with a soft, wet cloth and use a chimney brush to scrub out the stovepipe and loosen any residue. If the exterior has rust, you can use a wire brush or sandpaper to remove it.

Yes, you can leave a wood stove unattended for a few hours or overnight, but with some caveats. You should tamp down or mostly close some vents to ensure the fire stays under control. Also, shut and lock the door, and clear any objects from around the stove.

Just be aware that if you plan to leave the fire unattended and it goes out overnight, you’ll have to restart it, which is harder than simply feeding a live fire.

Most new wood stoves you can buy in the U.S. will be EPA-certified, but you should still check the packaging to verify.

EPA certification means the wood stove has been independently tested to meet a particulate emissions limit of no more than 4.5 grams per hour. If you have an old model that is not EPA-certified, check whether your state has a program that provides tax deductions for replacing your wood stove.

#6389. New Technology Could Help Astronauts Make Their Own Oxygen on the Moon

Astronauts on the Moon could one day breathe oxygen pulled from lunar soil using a technique borrowed from chipmaking.

Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

Using technology widely employed in semiconductor manufacturing, we have shown that it is possible to extract oxygen and products containing oxygen from material designed to mimic lunar soil.

This matters because oxygen is one of the most valuable resources for future space exploration. Astronauts need it to breathe, and it is also a major component of rocket propellant.

But transporting large quantities from Earth would be enormously expensive, so space agencies are investigating ways to obtain it directly on the Moon instead.

The challenge is that lunar oxygen does not exist as a readily available gas. Instead, it is chemically bound within minerals that make up the Moon’s surface layer. And although that layer contains a large amount of oxygen by weight, extracting it requires breaking strong chemical bonds within lunar minerals.

Many of the complex techniques that could potentially achieve this extraction would require large amounts of energy.

So our team decided to explore an alternative, lower-temperature approach inspired by a well-established industrial technology called “plasma-processing.”

Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter (after solid, liquid, and gas). It forms when sufficient energy is supplied to a gas, creating a mixture of charged particles, electrons, and highly reactive chemical species.

In semiconductor fabrication, plasma interacts with silicon dioxide in a process that underpins the production of billions of electronic devices every year.

We asked a simple question: if plasmas are highly effective at reacting with compounds containing oxygen in semiconductor processing, could a similar approach be applied to the oxygen-based compounds in lunar soil?

To investigate, we exposed artificial moon soil (known as lunar regolith simulants) to plasmas generated using gases that are commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing.

The results were encouraging. During plasma treatment of the lunar regolith simulants, we detected oxygen and oxygen-containing gaseous products being released.

Further analyses confirmed that the plasma was chemically modifying oxygen-bearing minerals within the material, with some lunar minerals reacting more readily than others.

Understanding these underlying mechanisms is important for enhancing the efficiency of the process and identifying opportunities to improve future systems. But oxygen yields would need to increase substantially before any practical lunar system becomes possible.

One reason this approach is attractive is that it builds on decades of experience developed by the semiconductor industry. Space engineering often requires entirely new technologies, but there are advantages in adapting systems that already exist, are well-understood, and have been refined for years on Earth.

The semiconductor industry has spent decades studying how fluorine plasmas interact with materials containing oxygen. Rather than starting from scratch, future researchers can draw on that extensive knowledge base.

There are practical benefits too. Plasma processing is a dry process, avoiding some of the challenges associated with transporting and handling liquid reagents (chemicals added to the process to make a reaction occur) in space. The operating temperatures of plasma processing can also be significantly lower than those required by some conventional oxygen extraction methods.

The implications may extend beyond using oxygen for life support on lunar bases. Lunar soil contains useful elements, including silicon, aluminum, and iron. While our current work focused on oxygen-bearing reactions, future studies may explore whether plasma-based processes could contribute more broadly to the use of other lunar resources.

Much more research is needed to understand the chemistry, to improve yields, and to determine whether the process can be scaled economically.

But the plasma technology that enables the manufacture of billions of transistors may also help humanity tackle one of the biggest challenges of space exploration: learning how to live off the land on another world.

Reference: “Impact of oxygen extraction from lunar regolith simulant using fluorinated plasma processes” by Aneeta Jaggernauth, Sean Kelly, Brian K. Tanner, Robert O’Connor, Aidan Cowley and Rajani K. Vijayaraghavan, 2 September 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-67891-2

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.
