#6388. Extreme weather in India and China shared a hidden atmospheric connection

A new analysis reveals how atmospheric circulation connected extreme heat in India with a rapid shift from flooding to humid heat in southern China.

India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.

A new analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.

Meng Gao from Hong Kong Baptist University led the analysis, with collaborators from the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences and Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

For much of early May, temperatures across the Indian region studied had been below normal.

Starting on May 17, that changed sharply, with temperatures staying over 1°C above the recent May average.

The researchers combined weather observations, atmospheric reanalysis, and climate simulations to trace the change.

Their maps showed daily average temperatures exceeding 40°C in some locations.

May 20 stood out. Across the region studied, it was the hottest May 20 in the record stretching back to 1979.

Humidity added to the strain. The wet-bulb temperature, which reflects the combined effects of heat and moisture, ranked third-highest for that date.

For people working outside, particularly in northern India, the combination made an already difficult season more dangerous.

The developing El Niño offered part of the explanation. By May, the central and eastern equatorial Pacific had entered El Niño conditions.

Atmospheric circulation shifted far beyond its shores.

The researchers linked this developing El Niño to a stronger western Pacific subtropical high. This broad area of high pressure also stretched farther west than usual.

Meanwhile, a persistent wave pattern in the upper atmosphere strengthened another high-pressure system over the Iranian Plateau. That system moved eastward.

Over India, the two highs joined, creating a stable “heat dome.” Air sank beneath it, warming as it descended and helping keep skies clear.

With more sunshine reaching the ground, temperatures continued rising. Warm waters in the northern Indian Ocean also helped strengthen the Pacific high, further supporting the persistent heat.

In southern China, the same Pacific high helped produce a different sequence of hazards.

Guangdong had endured repeated downpours since early May.

Particularly heavy rain between May 19 and 23 brought widespread flooding, followed almost immediately by humid heat from May 24–29.

The abrupt switch followed the high-pressure system’s movement northwestward. Rain eased, sunshine increased, and descending air warmed the region.

The atmosphere, however, remained laden with moisture after the downpours. The result was a “rainfall-to-deadly humid heat” sequence, with little time between the two emergencies.

The paper reports dozens of heatstroke ambulance calls in Shenzhen and thousands of livestock deaths in Maoming.

Such dangerous combinations of heat and humidity arrived one to two months earlier than usual.

Air temperatures alone did not explain what happened in Guangdong. Readings were near the top of the historical range, but comparable heat had occurred before.

The difference was the moisture accompanying them. Relative humidity during the dangerous hours averaged about 60%, compared with roughly 50% during similarly hot hours in earlier years.

Humid air makes it harder for sweat to evaporate, limiting the body’s ability to shed heat. That means familiar thermometer readings can conceal much greater physical strain.

For several hours, conditions exceeded a modeled threshold for safe, sustained activity among healthy adults aged 65 or older. That applied even to sitting quietly or standing with minimal movement.

That threshold describes a particular group under specified conditions. Heat tolerance varies with age, activity, and exposure to sunlight.

The timing was exceptional too: these conditions appeared earlier than in any year of the available 2011–2025 comparison record.

The team also asked how human influence had changed the likelihood of India’s heat.

Using 11 climate models, the researchers compared simulations including human influences with a preindustrial climate.

Their central estimate suggested human influences had made a similarly intense Indian heatwave roughly 27 times more likely.

The estimated range was wide: about 16 to 52 times, at a 90% confidence level. The authors caution that differences between models and limitations in correcting their biases affect the result.

The authors describe the finding as evidence of a likely human contribution, with the precise scale still uncertain. The estimate applies to the Indian event, not to the entire sequence across both countries.

A common atmospheric influence helps explain why distant places suffered heat at nearly the same time. Whether those heatwaves also reinforced each other remains unresolved.

For southern China, the order of events matters. Flooding can damage electricity supplies and other infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable cooling when the heat follows.

Warnings therefore need to account for what happened in the preceding days.

A heat forecast issued during flood recovery may reach people whose homes, workplaces, and access to electricity are already disrupted.

The researchers call for stronger infrastructure and better preparation in vulnerable regions.

In places facing rapid weather reversals, flood response and heat preparation may need to happen at the same time.

The study is published in the journal Advances in Atmospheric Sciences.

#6385. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

M. Martin et al. Ubiquitously efficient solo navigation in group-living meerkats. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252200

#6384. Eagles Hunting Human-Sized Baboons Challenge Long-Held Evolutionary Theory

Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.

In the middle of the Sahara, researchers have found evidence that eagles are killing primates as large as some of our early ancestors. One of the apparent victims, an adult male baboon, was estimated to have weighed more than 26 kilograms (57 pounds), challenging a long-held assumption about the dangers early humans faced.

Eagles have hunted primates for millions of years, yet no primate weighing more than 13 kilograms (29 pounds) had previously been confirmed to have been killed by a bird of prey. Scientists believed that humans and their ancestors had escaped this threat for roughly the past 2.5 million years because they were too heavy for even the giant eagles of the past to lift.

The discovery comes from the Ennedi Plateau in northern Chad, where an isolated population of baboons lives in the Sahara Desert. Researchers from the University of St Andrews traveled to the region with colleagues from Dartmouth College, the University of Konstanz, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

Lead author Professor Catherine Hobaiter, from the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews, said, “This was such an extraordinary expedition, any primatologists dream! Some of the baboons there are so remote they rarely, if ever, see people, and so after a couple of days they ended up following us around—we were probably the most interesting thing they’d seen for a while!”

She added: “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them. Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”

In a new study published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, the researchers describe finding the remains of adult male baboons with telltale signs of eagle predation, including talon punctures in their skulls and distinctive scrapes and rake marks on their shoulder bones.

Senior author Professor Nathaniel Dominy from Dartmouth College said, “At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t. Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”

The behavior of the living baboons offered another clue.

Professor Hobaiter explained, “One of the most exciting observations was seeing the baboons respond when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles swept overhead—primates are very specific about only responding to eagles that are a genuine threat. We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety.”

For scientists studying human evolution, the possibility of attacks from above is particularly interesting. Primates defend themselves differently against eagles than they do against predators such as big cats and crocodiles. One strategy, known as mobbing, involves primates, particularly larger adult males, charging an attacker to drive it away. If our ancestors faced similar threats, eagles may have helped shape the evolution of communication and group cooperation.

Many primates living in areas where eagles hunt also travel in large groups alongside other primate species. For much of our evolutionary history, our ancestors shared their surroundings with other early human species and primates. Although these relationships are often viewed in terms of competition, protection from predators may have given them a reason to stay together.

Dr. Gisela Kopp, from the University of Konstanz and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, said, “Primatology often focuses on regions with a high diversity of primates, but shifting our attention to a place where no primatological data has ever been collected before, proved to be extremely rewarding.”

Dr. Jean Didier Akpona, from African Parks, said, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence. This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”

The researchers are eager to continue studying the isolated baboon population, whose unusual lifestyle is already challenging several assumptions about the species.

Professor Hobaiter added, “Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!”

Reference: “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate” by Catherine Hobaiter, Tewogbade J. D. Akpona, Gisela H. Kopp and Nathaniel J. Dominy, 18 November 2026, American Journal of Biological Anthropology. DOI: 10.1002/ajpa.70377

This work was supported by the University of St Andrews (Global Partnerships Travel Grant), the Scottish Funding Council (International Science Partnership Fund), the Dartmouth College (Harris Distinguished Visiting Professorship program), the Marion and Jasper Whiting Foundation (Fellowship for Higher Education), the Rust Family Foundation; the Hector Stiftung II (Hector Pioneer Fellowship), and the Zukunftskolleg, University of Konstanz (ZENiT Fellowship, through the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of Science as part of the Excellence Strategy of the German Federal and State Governments).

#6383. On November 26, 1922, Howard Carter first looked inside Tutankhamun’s tomb

In his journal entry for that day, Carter recorded his reply to Lord Carnarvon as 'Yes, it is wonderful.' The famous line comes from his 1923 book.

On November 26, 1922, in Egypt’s Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter held a candle up to a small hole in a sealed doorway and looked into the tomb of Tutankhamun for the first time.

What he said next is one of the most quoted lines in archaeology. In his published account, Carter, asked whether he could see anything, answered, “Yes, wonderful things.”

But in the journal he kept during the excavation, Carter wrote down a different reply.

Carter’s handwritten journal for the first season of work on the tomb is held by the Griffith Institute at the University of Oxford, which has published a transcript online. Its entry for November 26, 1922, describes the moment step by step.

That afternoon, after clearing 9 meters (about 30 feet) of a descending passage, the team reached a second sealed doorway.

Carter made “a tiny breach in the top left hand corner to see what was beyond.” Candles were brought, he wrote, as a test for foul gases.

Carter’s patron, Lord Carnarvon, his daughter Lady Evelyn Herbert and Carter’s colleague Arthur Callender waited “in anxious expectation,” Carter wrote. “It was sometime before one could see, the hot air escaping caused the candle to flicker,” he added.

Then the room appeared, “with its strange and wonderful medley of extraordinary and beautiful objects heaped upon one another.”

“There was naturally short suspense for those present who could not see, when Lord Carnarvon said to me ‘Can you see anything’. I replied to him Yes, it is wonderful,” the entry reads.

The more famous version appeared in 1923 in the first volume of “The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen,” credited to Carter and A. C. Mace, an associate curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

In the book, Carter describes seeing “strange animals, statues, and gold” and “everywhere the glint of gold.”

He writes that he was “struck dumb with amazement,” and that when Carnarvon asked, “Can you see anything?” it was all he could do “to get out the words, ‘Yes, wonderful things.'”

The journal does not settle exactly what Carter said out loud in that passageway. But it shows that the line most people know comes from the book, not from the words Carter wrote in his journal.

The journal entry goes on to list what the light revealed. Carter wrote of “two strange ebony-black effigies of a King, gold sandalled, bearing staff and mace,” gilded couches, painted caskets, alabaster vases, “a golden inlaid throne” and “a confusion of overturned parts of chariots glinting with gold.”

His first impression, he wrote, was of “the property-room of an opera-house of a vanished civilization.”

The team was not even sure it had found a royal burial. Even that afternoon, Carter wrote, the passage had seemed to support “our first conjecture that we had found a cache.”

Then they saw a sealed doorway between two guardian statues and the name of Tutankhamun on most of the objects.

“Was it a tomb or merely a cache?” Carter asked in the journal. With the evidence in front of them, he concluded, “there was little doubt that there behind was the grave of that Pharaoh.”

The next day, Callender set up electric lights, and the group made a careful inspection of the room, which came to be called the Antechamber.

The look inside came 22 days after the first sign of the tomb. According to the Griffith Institute, Carter’s journal covers the discovery of the tomb’s stairway on November 4, 1922, and the uncovering of the first sealed doorway on November 5.

On November 4, Carter wrote, “At about 10am I discovered beneath almost the first hut attacked the first traces of the entrance of the tomb.” By sunset the next day, the workers had cleared down to the 12th step and exposed the top of a plastered, sealed doorway.

Carter then sent a cable to Carnarvon, who was in England. “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley a magnificent tomb with seals intact recovered same for your arrival congratulations,” it read, as copied into the journal.

More than a century later, the tomb still needs protecting. Earth.com has reported on cracks from water damage that threaten King Tut’s painted tomb and on another long-lost royal tomb that has emerged in Egypt.

The information was obtained from Howard Carter’s journal for the 1922-23 excavation season, as transcribed by the Griffith Institute, University of Oxford, and from the first volume of The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen by Howard Carter and A. C. Mace (1923).

#6382. The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

From wood pellets to charcoal, these cookers use a little heat and a lot of time to make incredible barbecue.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty. Whether pulled pork, brisket, ribs, or chicken is on the menu, this type of specialized home grill brings a new dimension to your backyard barbecues all year long.

There isn’t just one type of smoker. Purists prefer the iconic offset or “barrel” smoker, which reflects an array of regional barbecue traditions found in Texas, Memphis, Kansas City, and the Carolinas. In the last decade or so, increased interest in the art of barbecue has led to an expanded range of more beginner-friendly alternatives, including hardwood charcoal smokers and low-maintenance wood pellet smokers.

Some models have made the cooking process even easier with WiFi-enabled smart features for monitoring and adjusting internal temperature via an app on your phone. That way, you don’t have to stand by for hours as you cook.

If you’re in the market for a new smoker, we have one for every setup and skill level. Continue reading for our choices of the best smokers and tips on what to consider before you buy.

We’ve tested dozens of grills and smokers of all different shapes and sizes over the years. Tony Carrick, coauthor of this article, currently uses a Masterbuilt charcoal-fed gravity smoker and a Weber Smokey Joe at home. David Dritsas is a reviews editor at Popular Mechanics and is an amateur cook who has tested a variety of grills. Both drew on their combined experience with smokers, along with external research, to inform our recommendations.

We supplemented our own experience and criteria for smokers with extensive research into the various types that are available. We compared specifications of dozens of smokers and consulted user reviews to find trends or qualities that stand out (both positively and negatively) and might impact your ultimate choice. Our final recommendations span a range of designs and price points, and each offers solid performance, durable build quality, and great value.

One of the first things you notice about the Pit Boss Navigator 1600M is how well-constructed it is. The metal frame is sturdy, the hardware is strong, and the main section is well-insulated, including a heavy hood that is lined all the way around the edges by a fireproof, padded seal that keeps the heat in. (The Navigator performed very well in that regard.)

It has a large hopper that holds up to 30 pounds of pellets, and the controls are easy to understand. There’s WiFi on board, and we experienced a one-time issue where the app disconnected and would not reconnect, but it otherwise worked well, and navigation was intuitive. The Navigator also has two wired thermometer probes, for which you can set temperature alerts, so you know when your meats are ready.

For our main cooking test, we smoked a flat iron steak, as well as a mix of garlic-marinated zucchini, onions, and red peppers (that was enclosed in aluminum foil, open at the top). We were impressed with how quickly the grill heated up and how efficiently it maintained the temperature (even as we grilled in cold weather).

The only feature we did not find exceptional was the flame broil setting, which allows you to expose food to the flames of the burner cup directly. While it technically works, the cooking area of this feature is only roughly 3 inches in diameter, so it’s not very effective for large pieces of meat or more than one burger. But that complaint is a minor one.

You don’t have to spend a lot of money to get proficient at smoking food, and Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe proves that point. It’s a very basic charcoal barrel-shaped model that requires you to stay near and mind the coals to maintain the temperature, but it offers a few nice extra features to help you do it.

The biggest is the three-position charcoal tray. Set it high to sear meat while grilling or set it low to help keep temperatures down around 250 degrees Fahrenheit when smoking low and slow. Of course, airflow is integral to smoking, and there are three control options here, including a side vent, a chimney, and a large front door that you can also open to gain access to the coals for adjustment without having to remove the cooking grates. We used it several times to spread out the charcoal when things were getting a bit too hot.

There’s also a built-in thermometer that’s easy to read, even from a short distance, two side tables, and a lower shelf. All said and done, even if you don’t use it as a smoker, we think this makes for a fantastic charcoal grill with plenty of cooking area (940 square inches) to make a ton of burgers for your next barbecue party.

The Laredo Deluxe is not as solidly constructed as some of the other selections on our list, but that’s to be expected for a grill that’s usually on sale for under $300. We smoked a delicious brisket with ease during our tests, and we’d happily do so again.

Full Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe Grill and Smoker Review

Masterbuilt’s Gravity Series 800 gives you unique flavor from hardwood charcoal smoke in your barbecue without dealing with all the fuss of micromanaging your smoker. It pairs a large gravity-fed hopper for hardwood charcoal with a digital thermostat that controls the internal temperature. The hopper keeps your cooking fire fed, while an internal fan system regulates temperature to maintain consistency. Just load it up, light it, and let it cook for hours with minimal maintenance.

As with our top pick, the Gravity Series 800 features wireless-enabled smart controls, which allow you to monitor the temperature from your phone. It also includes a digital meat probe.

With 800 square inches of cooking surface, you’re getting a lot of space here. There’s plenty of room for ribs, whole chickens, and pork butts. But at nearly five feet wide, the Masterbuilt 800 is a big boy—possibly too big for some decks and patios. That said, it also functions as a standard charcoal grill and a flat-top griddle, so you could ditch your standard grill to make space for it.

This Woodridge Pro is a midrange model in Traeger’s line of pellet smokers, featuring some of the technology found in its higher-end models but at a lower price. When we unboxed the grill, we were impressed by how easy it was to put together, despite the large number of loose parts. Traeger’s assembly guide was one of the best we’ve seen, with clear directions and marked boxes with icons that corresponded to the instructions.

Some construction elements, such as light plastic wheels and thin grill grates, seemed lacking, and there’s no seal around the interior of the hood (which helps with heat retention). Once together, however, this grill is sturdy and not at all difficult to move around. We really appreciate that the top of the pellet hopper serves as an extra shelf, which is handy and something you don’t always get with other grills. There’s also a special pellet sensor that lets you know if pellets are running low.

The Woodridge Pro is extremely straightforward to operate. The rather retro display with large block numbers is readable from a distance, and basic temperature control is quick to adjust and set with a large push-button dial. You can also set a timer, check probe temperature, and with the press of a button, add extra smoky flavor for slow cooks under 225 degrees Fahrenheit. One thing we really liked was a motion graphic that shows whether the grill is heating up or lowering the temperature. During our tests, it was helpful to have that feature as a reminder as we multitasked. Wireless control is available with WiFi and Bluetooth, and the app, named WiFire, is easy to use.

The food we made turned out delicious, whether slow-cooked for a deeper smoky flavor or grilled at a higher temperature for just a hint. We used both the included wired probe to monitor temperature, as well as a Meater thermometer, and found some slight discrepancies between the grill’s temperature setting and the ambient temperature on the Meater. We found ourselves pushing the temperature up a few degrees to get it where we wanted it to be. This didn’t mar the experience too greatly, however. The Woodridge Pro is a reliable pellet grill that’s fun to use and a worthy addition to any back patio.

In many ways, the 18-Inch Smokey Mountain from Weber is a standard water smoker (a 14-inch model is also available). Like similar models, it has a bottom rack and retaining ring for the charcoal, a large bowl for water, and two racks for smoking food. But it stands out because it’s made from heavier porcelain-enameled steel, which helps retain heat and maintain a consistent temperature, as well as a heat shield on the bottom to protect your deck or lawn. It also comes with a cover.

When we first fired it up to season the smoker, we took the opportunity to get familiar with how to use the three air vents around the bottom, as well as the top vent, to help hold a desired temperature. To help you gauge this, there’s a thermometer in the lid that shows a highlighted smoking zone from 200 to 275 degrees Fahrenheit, and we found it was relatively easy to keep it in that range.

We put this to the real-world test when smoking some beef jerky. To do this, we wanted to keep the temperature on the lower side at around 200 degrees Fahrenheit. This proved a little challenging; the temperature kept creeping up, so we watched it closely and adjusted the vents as needed. In the end, the jerky smoked a bit faster than we intended. In hindsight, we used a little too much charcoal, which generated more heat than we needed. While this was our mistake, it shows just how well this smoker can retain heat.

When smoking a smaller-sized brisket, we more successfully managed the temperature and were able to hold close to 225 degrees Fahrenheit for the 5 hours it took to smoke it. One thing we really appreciated during longer smoking sessions was the large door, which made it easy to add fuel and wood chips. The Smokey Mountain is a basic smoker that will require a little experience to use effectively, but will ultimately be worth the time and produce great results. — tested by Bradley Ford

Though they are frowned upon by traditionalists, electric smokers like this one from East Oak are the quickest way for new barbecuers to enter the world of smoking. Its digital controls make it easy to maintain specific temperatures, and the combination of a side wood chip loader and glass door means you can check on your cook without opening the door, which could impact your cooking temperature.

The 725-square-inch cooking surface gives you plenty of room to experiment with various types of food in a single session, but the smoker itself is quite slim, measuring nearly 19 inches wide and 18 inches deep, so it won’t take up a lot of space on your deck or patio. Bottom line: This is a straightforward and, above all, convenient way to try smoking barbecue at home.

If a grill could be a pop-culture icon, the Big Green Egg is it. The brand has a whole group of fans—known as Eggheads—who gather at grilling events called EGGfests held all across the country. And it’s not just home enthusiasts. According to the company, nearly 1,800 restaurants use this extremely popular kamado grill. Its excellent heat retention and temperature range, enabled by its shape and porcelain-coated ceramic enclosures, make them an instant upgrade over your average gas or charcoal grill.

That thick ceramic body is also very effective at retaining heat, making it very effective for cooking low and slow. Just add some smoking wood, and you can smoke a brisket overnight. This grill can get as hot as 750 degrees Fahrenheit when you’re grilling, but smokers will want to maintain a stable 225 to 300 degrees using the air vents at the top and the bottom of the egg. And it’s large enough to feed a crowd—we’re talking about smoking a 20-pound turkey for Thanksgiving.

This small electric smoker from GE lets you take your smoking indoors. It uses two heat sources—one to cook food and the other to burn pellets—along with a filtration device to prevent the smoke from filling your kitchen. Its modest 293 square inches of cooking surface is enough to smoke three half racks of ribs or a small pork butt.

There’s a bevy of controls for setting smoke levels and adjusting temperatures. There are also preset food settings, including brisket, ribs, pork butt, and chicken wings. Built-in probes and WiFi connectivity let you monitor meat temperatures remotely, and this smoker is compatible with voice controls via Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Traditional offset or “barrel” smokers feature two parts: A large main cooking chamber for your food and a smaller cook box for the fuel. The wood or charcoal burns, heating the main chamber and filling it with smoke, which slowly cooks the meat with indirect heat and infuses it with smoky flavor. Offset smokers, like the Royal Gourmet model we recommend as our Best Value pick, are beloved by barbecue aficionados, but are also the most challenging to use. Learning how to control the temperature in an offset smoker takes practice.

Vertical or “cabinet” smokers have a tall, closet-like design with a single door on the front and three to five racks for food inside. The heat source sits in the base, allowing the heat and smoke to waft upward and fill the space. Going high instead of wide makes a vertical smoker more compact, so it’s a good option if you don’t have much room on your patio. That said, the narrow profile may limit your ability to cook large pieces of meat, such as a full rack of ribs.

Like vertical smokers, the pill-shaped bullet smoker has a fuel area at the bottom with the main cooking chamber above. Vents on the bottom and top of the smoker allow you to control the temperature inside the chamber, and a water pan sits just below the cook area to keep food moist. Bullet smokers are compact, however, and some models are stacked so tightly that you may have trouble accessing the food on the middle racks mid-cook.

Most pellet smokers, including the Traeger Ironwood 885, look more like a grill than a smoker, with a wide cook box and a clamshell lid that opens up to reveal a broad cooking surface. To generate smoke and heat, an electric auger feeds small hardwood pellets from a hopper on the back or side into a fire inside the cook box. The auger automatically adds fuel to the fire based on the temperature you dial in on the smoker’s digital thermostat, so you don’t need to babysit the smoker to maintain the proper temperature. However, they require a power source and tend to be the most expensive.

Kamado grills, like the famous Big Green Egg, are hybrid grill-smokers. These large, acorn-shaped ceramic cook boxes can maintain low temperatures for many hours or build up scorching heat with temperatures that eclipse 800 degrees. It’s an incredibly versatile option, which has made it a gateway device for new barbecuers.

Smokers can use a variety of fuel types, including hardwood, charcoal, gas, electricity, or wood pellets. Hardwood and charcoal are the fuels of choice for smoking purists. This combination creates a lot of smoke, maximizing that flavor. Maintaining a consistent low temperature takes time to learn, though, and it makes more of a mess with leftover ash.

Electric and gas smokers are convenient because they require little to no maintenance, but they don’t inherently produce smoke. Instead, they rely on wood chip trays that aren’t as effective as wood, charcoal, or pellets at instilling flavor into food. However, they still can produce decent results.

Pellet smokers use compressed wood pellets that generate real smoke for instilling flavor into food, while minimizing maintenance with automatic temperature regulation. Pellet grills offer excellent heat retention and temperature control, but don’t need as much constant attention as charcoal or wood grills.

Smoking meat can take eight hours or more, depending on the cut, so you’ll probably want to cook as much as you can in one session. It’s important to look for a smoker with an efficient interior design that has space for everything you want to cook. The average cooking surface size for a smoker is around 550 square inches, which is enough to fit five full racks of ribs, four whole chickens, or five pork butts. That said, I’ve seen cooking surfaces range in size from 250 square inches to more than 800.

Some modern smokers can connect to your smartphone via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, allowing you to track their internal temperature, change temperature settings, and monitor meat probes remotely through an app. They can also send you alerts if the smoker’s internal temperature rises or falls, the food reaches a target temperature, or if it’s low on fuel, allowing you to keep tabs on your smoker without having to hover over it.

What’s the best temperature for smoking meat?

With a smoker, you want to keep the temperature low and cook for a long time. Depending on what you’re cooking, I’d recommend maintaining your heat between 190 and 225 degrees. In that range, you will cook your meat slowly enough to make it incredibly tender and infuse it with smoky flavor.

It depends on what you’re cooking. Smoking a rack of ribs typically takes between four and five hours, but a pork butt may need 8 to 10 hours. Brisket is well-known for needing an especially long smoke—around 12 to 18 hours.

Technically, yes. You can add a smoker box to a gas grill, which holds wood chips to generate smoke. So long as you keep the top of the grill closed, that’s a smoker. Make sure to set up the grill so that the food is not sitting directly above the heat source, and set the burners so that the grill only heats to a maximum of 225 degrees with the lid closed.

That said, it’s far from ideal. It’s more difficult to maintain the consistently low temperatures needed for smoking with a gas grill than it is with a dedicated smoker. On top of that, flames from a gas grill will not impart the same distinctive taste as a proper smoker burning charcoal or hardwood. (Purists don’t even like gas as a fuel for dedicated smokers.)

Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins, some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought, governed and died thousands of years ago.

Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide invaluable clues about long-lost languages and civilizations. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script, one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

Each type of discovery offers a new window to the ancient world. But which of these archaeological treasures would you most want to uncover? Vote in the poll below and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6380. Cougars battle deep snow and freezing weather every winter, but nature is not what kills most of them

People, not weather, caused most deaths among tracked cougars. The hunting season, roads, and human houses each play a role.

You might expect deep snow and bitter cold to be the biggest threat to a wild animal in winter. Yet when researchers tracked cougars across five winters in the foothills of Alberta’s Rocky Mountains, they found the weather was not what killed them. People were.

Of 80 cougars fitted with tracking collars, 37 died, and people caused 29 of those deaths. Nearly all of them came between November and March, and Alberta’s cougar hunting season falls inside those months.

Where a cougar spent its time mattered too. Cats that stayed close to houses and unpaved roads died at higher rates than cats that kept away from them.

Carter Littlefair and Andrew Derocher of the University of Alberta’s Department of Biological Sciences led the study. Their co-authors, Paul Frame and Mark Edwards, work at Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, the province’s environment ministry.

Between 2016 and 2021, the team used hounds to tree cougars in the country south of Whitecourt and north of Sundre. They then darted each cat and fitted a GPS collar. The collars reported a location every seven hours.

The 80 cats were followed for a little over a year each, on average. When a collar signaled a death, crew reached the site within three days to work out what had happened.

Hunters killed 16 of the 37 that died. Another eight died in traps set for other animals, and two were hit by vehicles. Three more were killed as problem animals or by landowners with permission.

Wolves killed three adult females, two of them with kittens still depending on them. Seven deaths in all were natural, and one could not be explained. The cats share this country with wolves, black bears, and grizzlies, and their main prey is white-tailed deer.

In an average year, a collared cougar had a 60 percent chance of living through the next 12 months. That figure hides a split between the seasons.

From April through October, 96 percent of the cats survived. From November through March, only 62 percent did.

Cougar hunting in the study area opens on December 1 and closes at the end of February, or earlier once an area’s quota is filled. Hunters there use hounds to follow a track and tree the cat. Of the 37 cougars that died, 33 died in the cold months.

Since 2019, the province has set each area’s hunting quota at roughly 14 to 16 percent of the cougars it estimates live there.

In an interview with Earth.com, Littlefair said that lowering harvest limits would have the greatest direct effect on survival, since hunting caused the majority of the deaths the team documented.

Alberta’s system lets each management area’s limits be adjusted every year, separately for males and females, and the findings can help inform how they are set, Littlefair said.

The team then asked which parts of the landscape went with dying. Rugged terrain and forest edges, which the team expected to make a cat easier to spot or reach, made no difference to survival.

What mattered was access. A cougar within about 490 feet (150 meters) of a house faced a much higher risk of death than one farther away. So did a cougar within about 165 feet (50 meters) of an unpaved road.

The authors suggested a reason: a hound hunt begins with a track rather than a sighting, and hunters find those tracks along roads and cutlines before the chase starts.

“Mortality risk increased with proximity to residences and secondary roads, indicating that cougars occupying accessible areas were more vulnerable to harvest,” they wrote.

Cats that crossed cutlines, pipelines, power lines, and seismic lines more often as they traveled were also more likely to die. Logging and oil and gas work have left this part of Alberta with a dense network of unpaved roads.

Littlefair said that reducing the density of roads and other human-made disturbances across the landscape could also help lower that risk.

Familiar ground did not seem to protect them either. Of 15 cougars whose previous year’s range could be mapped, 12 died inside it.

Alberta’s rules are built to steer hunters toward males. Quotas allow more males than females, and a female with kittens is off limits. Hunters using hounds also tend to select large males.

So the team expected males to die more frequently, as they do in hunted populations elsewhere. They didn’t find that and Littlefair told Earth.com it was one of the more surprising results.

Other studies with similarly female-heavy samples have still found hunters taking more males. In this study, however, hunters killed nine females and seven males, and the team could not detect any difference in survival between the sexes.

Hunting did make up a bigger share of male deaths, with 64 percent in comparison to 35 percent for females. But with only 24 males in the study, that difference could have come up by chance.

Mothers were at no extra risk the team could detect: it found 18 litters, and females with kittens survived at the same rate as females without them.

Hunting’s 43 percent share of the deaths is smaller than the 62 to 75 percent reported in some other hunted cougar populations. Provincial records also show human-caused cougar deaths have fallen since a peak in 2015.

“One important distinction is that high mortality does not necessarily indicate an unsustainable population,” Littlefair said.

Judging that would require counts that the study did not make, of the cougars there, their kittens, and the young that reach adulthood.

The study did not measure how many hunters were out or how hard they hunted, so it can’t separate a road from the people driving on it.

The authors treat a cat’s use of roads and houses as a stand-in for its chances of meeting a hunter, not as a danger in itself.

A second gap is the number of males. With 56 females and 24 males collared, the study can say less about males.

“It would certainly be interesting to repeat the study with a more balanced sample of males and females to see whether this pattern persists,” Littlefair said.

For now, the finding covers one stretch of Alberta, where a cougar’s odds of surviving the winter depend on how close it lives to a house or an unpaved road.

Littlefair and his team believe that managers should weigh that pattern of access when they judge how much hunting a population can absorb, and where it falls.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

#6379. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”

#6378. Komodo dragons have a thin layer of iron on their teeth that keeps them razor-sharp for tearing apart prey

Researchers discovered that Komodo dragons coat the serrated edges of their teeth in iron, staining them orange and keeping them razor-sharp for ripping apart prey.

Look closely at a Komodo dragon’s teeth, and you will notice an orange tint along the cutting edges. It is not a stain from feeding. Even teeth that have not yet pushed through the gums are just as orange.

The color actually comes from iron. In a 2024 study, researchers found a thin, iron-rich coating along the tips and serrated edges, concluding that it helps keep the teeth sharp.

Scientists had never seen anything like it in a meat-eating reptile before.

“Komodo dragons have curved, serrated teeth to rip and tear their prey just like those of meat-eating dinosaurs,” said Aaron LeBlanc of King’s College London, the study’s lead author.

LeBlanc’s team looked for the same coating on fossil dinosaur teeth and saw no evidence of it. But fossilization may be the reason.

Komodo dragons are the largest predatory lizards alive, and scientists have studied their teeth before. One detail had still been overlooked.

LeBlanc’s team examined teeth from skeletons and from specimens preserved in fluid. Every unworn tooth tip and serration was orange.

Serrations are the small points along a cutting edge, like the ones on a steak knife.

The rest of each tooth looked white. The enamel there is transparent, so the white comes from the layer underneath, called dentin.

The enamel on a Komodo dragon’s serrations and tooth tips is about 0.0008 inches (20 micrometers) thick. That’s roughly one-fifth the thickness of a sheet of printer paper.

The team found iron in the outermost layer of that enamel with every method it used. At its thickest, the iron-rich layer makes up about a tenth of the enamel’s thickness.

One of those methods was X-ray mapping at a type of particle accelerator called a synchrotron. Those maps showed the iron concentrated along the serrations.

With another method, the team found more oxygen where the iron was concentrated. The authors took that as a sign the coating is an iron oxide. Rust is made of iron oxides too.

How hard is the coating? On a Komodo dragon tooth, LeBlanc’s team found that difficult to test reliably, because the coating is so thin.

So the team turned to a tooth shed by an American alligator at a British zoo. That tooth had iron-rich enamel thick enough to test.

To test it, the team pressed a fine tip into the enamel of that one tooth 74 times. The iron-rich enamel was slightly harder than the enamel beneath it, by about 9%.

Like the team’s electron microscope and X-ray experiments, the hardness tests were each run once, on individual teeth.

Iron may make the outer enamel along a cutting edge more resistant to wear. For the Komodo dragon, that’s less certain. Its iron-rich layer is much thinner than the alligator’s.

Still, worn Komodo dragon teeth hint that the coating protects the serrations. Enamel can flake off most of a worn tooth and expose the dentin. On the serrations, the enamel appears to wear down gradually instead.

Komodo dragons replace their teeth quickly. So the thin coating must be enough to keep each tooth sharp until a new one takes its place, the authors wrote.

Meat-eating dinosaurs had serrated teeth with thin enamel, just as Komodo dragons do.

The team also tested teeth shed by crocodiles and their relatives living in zoos. All four species, the American alligator among them, had an iron-rich outer layer of enamel.

So the team looked for iron in fossil teeth from tyrannosaurs and from the family that includes Velociraptor. Every technique gave the same result. The team saw no consistent sign of extra iron in the enamel on the serrations.

LeBlanc’s team gave two possible explanations. Either fossilization masks the iron, or these dinosaurs didn’t normally concentrate it along their serrations. For now, the fossils can’t show which explanation is right.

“With further analysis of the Komodo teeth we may be able to find other markers in the iron coating that aren’t changed during fossilization,” LeBlanc said.

“With markers like that we would know with certainty whether dinosaurs also had iron-coated teeth and have a greater understanding of these ferocious predators.”

The full study was published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

#6377. The 8 Best Portable Refrigerators If You’re Tired of Buying Bags of Ice

This convenient appliance works better than your average cooler and offers versatile power options. Here are the ones we recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Even the best coolers we’ve tested from names like Yeti, Coleman, and RTIC with superior insulation eventually get too warm for ice to stay frozen. That’s where portable refrigerators shine, offering cooling capability that you just can’t get from a regular cooler. They’re great for long camping trips where you need to keep meat and other food at safe temperatures and come in plenty of sizes to suit hardcore camper rigs and RVs or fit in a standard sedan.

Portable refrigerators—often called car refrigerators—plug into your car’s 12-volt outlet, an AC outlet, or a portable power station. They’re pricier and heavier than the standard cooler, but they're more efficient at cooling. And you get to skip the expense and hassle of dealing with bags of ice. They can also be helpful around the house if your fridge breaks or there’s a power outage.

We used our expertise on coolers, power stations, and camping gear to find the best portable refrigerators. We checked camping and overlanding gear reviews and forums to find models that hold up on long treks in remote areas and are viable alternatives for people who don't want to deal with bags of ice for a cooler.

We chose options in different capacities and across a range of prices and prioritized models that offer convenient features like USB chargers, wheels, and LED lights. If you want some extra cooling power on-the-go, consider one of the portable refrigerators for your next trek.

This portable fridge from Bodega has great build quality, convenient features for easy portability, and cools down fast. The compressor can cool the interior down to 32 degrees Fahrenheit in about 30 minutes.

It has two separate compartments to keep things organized. They can’t be individually controlled but the smaller section typically gets cooler than the larger side. It also has a user-friendly app for setting the temperature and a USB port to charge other devices. Some customers report minor differences between the temperature they see on the app versus the actual internal temperature, but say it’s only off by a couple degrees.

The portable refrigerator has sturdy handles and a built-in LED light so you can quickly find what you need in the dark. Standout features include wheels and a drain plug—two things that are standard on most larger coolers but something a lot of portable fridges lack. The lid can be opened from either side or popped off entirely for fast loading.

This portable refrigerator is a great value for efficient cooling, a low power draw, and large capacity. The 59-quart space is split into two zones for easy organizing and the unit comes with a removable wire basket.

Its tall, slender shape fits easily behind a row of seats in the car. The handles are also removable to make for easy stowing. The app lets you set and monitor temps, though you can’t do much else. Some users report the app is user-friendly but wish it had more features.

The Alpicool is a budget portable refrigerator that cools down fast to roughly zero degrees Fahrenheit and operates quietly in comparison to most other models.

It has an automatic shutoff to ensure it doesn’t drain your car or portable battery and eco mode that pulls less energy. An external LCD display and control panel shows you the interior temperature. This budget option also has an LED light inside and a drain plug.

Setup is rather easy but the included manual doesn’t show you how to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The brand’s website has a detailed owner’s manual that's more helpful.

Thinking of Igloo might still conjure the image of the old-school Playmate cooler you had as a kid. But the ICF electric cooler is anything but that. The portable refrigerator has a sturdy plastic build that can handle the bumps and bruises that come with transporting it to sporting events, grocery stores, and campgrounds.

Its spacious interior works as one large storage space or, with the help of the included removable divider, two separate areas. This helps separate dry items like canned drinks from wet items like fruit and sandwiches. The ICF is also remarkably simple. All the controls are built right onto the body, so all you have to do is turn it on and set the temperature.

Like other portable refrigerators, the ICF has a three-stage battery protection system to prevent it from draining your car battery.

The Bouge comes in a compact package that can serve as a personal cooler for a remote overnight, or extra storage on long treks. It has a single compartment that works as a fridge or freezer.

Set the temperature from the external control panel and monitor through the LCD thermometer. There’s no app to keep tabs on the temperature while driving but customers report it stays consistent even in hotter ambient temps. Recessed handles add to its space-saving design.

Some reviews mention the external thermometer can be off as much as seven degrees—a bit higher than most other models.

The Travoca Rigel eCooler has a number of small, but notable, features that intrigued us right away. For one, it’s somewhat modular. You can unscrew the wood paneling on the front and replace it with attachments such as a small shelf for placing drinks or snacks.

The lid is fully detachable and reversible, so you can pop the whole thing off and get a full look at everything inside. Beyond this, dual-zone cooling is powerful. Each section can work as either a fridge or freezer.

And if you don’t need separate sections, the internal divider comes out, converting the entire interior to one large space at the same temperature. Travoca also sells internal baskets separately for easier organization.

Dometic is the best-known brand of portable refrigerators, with a reputation for turning out models that are durable and reliable With that comes the higher price tag, but overlanders and outdoor enthusiasts are still fans—I see this one touted most in forums as the main fridge people use while traveling on long remote treks.

It’s on the heavier side at 60 pounds when empty, but its compressor is more powerful than other models on this list—and it operates quietly.

The portable refrigerator has a sleek display and an intuitive app to set and keep tabs on the interior temperature, plus a USB port for charging for mobile devices.

With a wheeled base and telescopic handles, this portable fridge from BougeRV is a well-built mix between portability and size. The interior comes with two separate sections. You can tune each to different temperatures, allowing you to have both a functional fridge and freezer at the same time.

One of the more user-friendly features the CRD2 has is an opening for a standalone battery. While sold separately, the battery allows the cooler to operate without any large power source, like a wall outlet or car, nearby. With the attached battery, the portable fridge can run for up to 20 hours with no other power source, making it an ideal way to escape to the beach or sleep overnight in the woods away from your car and still wake up to fresh produce and unspoiled milk.

Portable refrigerators run on a compressor just like your kitchen fridge and freezer and keep food fresher a lot longer than a cooler and ice. Most reach an average minimum temperature of -4 to -7 degrees Fahrenheit to freeze and refrigerate food, though some are refrigerators only, reaching a minimum temperature of 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Although portable refrigerators don't rely solely on insulation for cooling power, they're still well insulated enough to take some of the load off the compressor when it comes to temperature regulation.

Don’t confuse portable refrigerators with electric coolers, as that’s another product category entirely. Electric coolers rely on thermoelectric cooling, which isn’t as efficient because it's impacted by ambient temperatures. As such, they can only cool to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Unlike portable refrigerators, electric coolers don’t have a compressor and don’t have the power to achieve freezing temperatures.

Portable refrigerators typically draw an average of about 45 watts of power, which is less than a standard mini fridge. This won’t blow out any car fuses or drain a car battery unless the unit is kept on for days without the car running. We chose portable refrigerators that have features like eco modes and automatic shutoff so there are precautions in place to prevent it from draining a car or portable battery.

While portable refrigerators offer more storage than coolers because they don’t need ice, their built-in compressor makes them relatively heavy at about 30 pounds or more. Still, some are more portable than others thanks to built-in handles and wheels. They don’t have shoulder straps and aren’t meant to be carried over a far distance. Also, most don't have drain plugs like standard coolers because condensation is minimal and can easily be wiped out with a small towel.

#6376. Hunters are allowed inside Grand Teton National Park until December 6 under a 1950 law, but only 40 permits were issued this year

Grand Teton hunters must use non-lead ammunition, carry bear spray and turn in every elk head for chronic wasting disease testing. Visitors should wear bright colors.

In Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, a small number of licensed hunters are allowed to take elk inside the park until December 6.

The annual elk reduction program runs from November 14 through December 6, according to the National Park Service.

It is authorized under the park’s 1950 enabling legislation and managed jointly by the Park Service and the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.

This year, only 40 permits are authorized, and hunters may take only cows and calves.

After reviewing available biological data, the Park Service and Wyoming Game and Fish determined that the program is necessary “to maintain the herd at its population objective and achieve desired elk distribution,” according to the Park Service.

The program uses Wyoming-licensed hunters with limited-quota permits to harvest elk in designated areas. The Park Service calls it “an important management tool with requirements that distinguish it from traditional elk hunting programs.”

Participants must carry a state license for Elk Hunt Area 75, a conservation stamp, an elk special management permit, a 2026 park elk reduction program permit and a hunter education card, regardless of age.

They must use non-lead ammunition and wear fluorescent orange or pink clothing. They also have to carry bear spray that is immediately accessible, in a non-expired can of at least 7.9 ounces.

Archery equipment, handguns, non-centerfire rifles and artificial elk calls are prohibited, the Park Service says.

Only Area 75 is open for the program this year. It lies mostly east of U.S. Highway 89, according to the park.

Within Area 75, the Antelope Flats portion and the Snake River bottom between Deadman’s Bar and Ditch Creek are closed throughout the season.

Area 79 is closed to the program this season “to limit harvest pressure on northern migratory and resident elk,” the park says.

To support surveillance for chronic wasting disease, known as CWD, participants must turn in the head of every elk harvested in the park at the designated drop-off location in Moose.

Park staff collect lymph nodes and send them to the Wyoming Game and Fish Wildlife Health Lab for testing, and hunters can check their results online.

Elk face other health threats too. Earth.com has reported on an emerging hoof disease that may change how elk bodies work.

The areas remain open to park visitors during the program, the Park Service says, and visitors are “strongly encouraged to wear bright colors.”

Park Service and Wyoming Game and Fish staff patrol the area to check that hunters follow the rules and to share information about bear safety.

Hunters are not the only pressure on elk in the region. In nearby Yellowstone, research suggests cougars pose an even bigger threat to elk than wolves.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news release 2026 Elk Reduction Program begins November 14 in Grand Teton National Park (November 6, 2026) and Grand Teton National Park’s Elk Reduction Area 75 page.

The BepiColombo spacecraft has overcome a last-minute computer glitch to enter orbit around Mercury — the 2nd craft in history to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update: On Tuesday (Nov. 24) ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on X that the BepiColombo team has isolated the computer glitch, and tweaked the mission accordingly. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24).

After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team.

However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury.

ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft should be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now.

An illustration of BepiColombo approaching Mercury for orbital insertion.

Built jointly by ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), BepiColombo is actually two separate probes, which are currently stacked one atop the other in orbit. The ESA-built orbiter, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and the JAXA-built orbiter, the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), carry separate science instruments, and they will soon diverge into separate orbital paths around the mysterious inner planet, operating as two probes gathering different streams of data.

A selfie of BepiColombo during a flyby of Mercury's north pole in 2025.

The pair of probes launched together aboard an Ariane 5 rocket in October 2018, and spent the following eight years on an interplanetary journey that took them past Earth, the moon and Venus. It even passed by Mercury itself six times. (During one of these flybys, in January 2025, Bepi snapped an incredible closeup photo of Mercury's north pole.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This complicated cosmic choreography was necessary to prevent BepiColombo from picking up too much speed and overshooting Mercury's orbit, according to ESA. Mercury sits about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers) from our star, or roughly one third of the distance between Earth and the sun. That makes it very difficult for a spacecraft to reach Mercury without being captured by the sun's considerable gravitational pull and dragged off course.

Only one other spacecraft — NASA's MESSENGER probe — has succeeded in entering Mercury orbit before, circling the planet from 2011 to 2015 after its own seven-year journey through space.

BepiColombo will spend the next few months getting both probes in position to start mapping Mercury in the greatest detail ever.

MPO and Mio are expected to separate in early December, with Mio entering a highly elliptical orbit around Mercury's poles. MPO will then take a few more months to fine-tune its trajectory, reaching a lower and more circular polar orbit in March 2027, according to ESA. Its science operations are expected to begin in April.

The sibling probes will each orbit Mercury several times a day, with MPO completing an orbit every 2 hours or so. Observing the mysterious inner planet from several different vantage points, the probes will make the most comprehensive map of Mercury ever. The mission's suite of science instruments will study the planet across the electromagnetic spectrum, taking observations in X-rays, gamma-rays and ultraviolet light, as well as collecting detailed measurements of the planet's magnetic field.

With this information, scientists hope to unravel many mysteries of the least-explored planet in the solar system. The new data should enable scientists to tackle myriad long-standing questions: What is Mercury's interior made of, and where does its magnetic field come from? How was the planet formed, and to what extent is it still tectonically active today? By making precise measurements of the spacecraft's orbit and position, a radio experiment will also provide a new test of Einstein's theory of general relativity.

Stay tuned for more updates from ESA about humanity's first visit to Mercury in more than a decade.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99

Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. #6373. In 1958, the Hope Diamond went to the Smithsonian by mail for $2.44 in postage, and the museum says a jeweler likely embellished its curse to sell it

A jeweler's employee paid $145.29 to mail the 45.52-carat blue gem from New York, nearly all of it to insure it for $1 million.

On November 8, 1958, an employee of Harry Winston’s jewelry store in New York City mailed an ordinary-looking package. Inside was the Hope Diamond.

The employee paid $145.29 to send it to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., according to the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum. Only $2.44 of that was postage. The rest paid for $1 million in insurance.

The 45.52-carat blue diamond traveled by registered mail in a plain brown wrapper. It is still on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, and the museum has a short answer for anyone who asks whether it carries a curse.

“Is the Hope Diamond cursed? Of course not!” the museum says on its history of the gem.

In Washington, local letter carrier James G. Todd picked up the package at the city post office, a building that now houses the National Postal Museum.

Leonard Carmichael, the Secretary of the Smithsonian, brought Todd into the Gem Hall, where reporters and cameras watched him pull the package from his mail satchel and hand it over, the Postal Museum recounts.

The Natural History Museum dates the arrival to November 10, 1958. Harry Winston’s wife presented the diamond to Carmichael and to George S. Switzer, the museum’s curator of mineralogy. It “almost immediately became its premier attraction,” according to the museum.

The diamond’s history is far older. The Smithsonian traces it to a blue diamond of about 115 carats known as Tavernier’s Diamond, after the French merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, which King Louis XIV had recut.

It must have come from India, the museum says, since India was the only commercial source of diamonds in Tavernier’s time.

The curse is much younger. “The story of a curse is a recent part of the diamond’s history, apparently having its origins in the early 20th century,” the museum says.

One early account ran in the Washington Post in January 1908. According to the Smithsonian, it offered “a selective history” of the gem, listing the bad luck of earlier owners. Later versions of the curse followed the same pattern.

A November 1909 newspaper report that a former owner, the Turkish diamond merchant Selim Habib, had drowned with the gem when a steamer sank at Singapore added to the legend.

The museum calls that report “wildly inaccurate.” Neither Habib nor the diamond was on the ship, and he had already sold the stone in June 1909.

The Smithsonian says some of the people who spread the curse stories may have done so for their own gain.

The French jewelry house Cartier bought the Hope Diamond in 1910, and Pierre Cartier set out to sell it. Intriguing histories helped sell gems in those years.

“Cartier thus began to fabricate a fanciful story around the Hope Diamond that included a curse, which he would pitch to potential buyers,” the museum writes.

He pitched it to Ned and Evalyn Walsh McLean, and the sale took two years. In the Smithsonian’s words, Cartier “likely embellished the stories as a sales tactic.”

The tale did not scare Evalyn McLean off. She told Cartier she believed objects that brought bad luck to others would bring good luck to her.

After he had the stone reset and left it with the couple for a weekend, she agreed to buy it in 1912 for $180,000 plus the return of a pendant she no longer wanted.

May Yohé, who was once married to Lord Francis Hope, an earlier owner, helped make the curse a popular modern legend.

In a book and a film released in 1921, she blamed the diamond for her failed marriage and the loss of the Hope family fortune, according to the Smithsonian.

After Evalyn McLean died in 1947, Harry Winston bought her jewelry, including the Hope Diamond, in 1949. He showed it across the United States in a traveling exhibition called the Court of Jewels before giving it to the Smithsonian.

At the donation ceremony, Winston’s wife scoffed at the idea of a curse and noted that her family had held the gem without any ill effects.

Todd, the letter carrier, had a harder time. Within a year of the delivery, he was hurt in two separate car accidents, his wife died of a heart attack, his dog strangled on its leash and his home in Seat Pleasant, Maryland, was partly destroyed by fire, according to the Postal Museum.

He still did not blame the diamond. “I don’t believe any of that stuff,” he told a reporter.

“If the hex is supposed to affect the owners, then the public should be having the bad luck,” he added.

The diamond stayed at the Natural History Museum, and the brown paper wrapper it came in is now part of the National Postal Museum’s collection.

The Hope’s deep blue color has its own science story. Earth.com has reported that some blue diamonds formed hundreds of miles below Earth’s surface.

The Smithsonian has hidden history of its own, including a secret chamber from 1847 found beneath the Smithsonian Castle.

The information was obtained from the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History’s History of the Hope Diamond and the National Postal Museum’s Delivering the Hope Diamond.
