#6372. The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our New York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

Solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He says that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

Another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he says is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review

After trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”

Beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

Cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

This hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.)

The black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

Some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

Because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

If you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

The fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

It’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he said its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”

The substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

The ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.)

The whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

There is one important caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn quickly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

This one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer says it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

This one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

Before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

Then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an important consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

They could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

Ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

If you plan to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

If you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

Material affects how long your new pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite quickly, as some testing showed. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

Smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you plan to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. She’s reviewed everything from roller bags and cameras to hiking equipment and home decor for outlets such as The Montreal Gazette, Fodor's, AFAR, and US Park Pass. #6371. Why does sleep get worse with age? A common vitamin deficiency may offer a clue

A study of 460 adults found that people with vitamin D deficiency slept 23 minutes less each night than those with normal levels.

Sleep often becomes shorter and more fragmented as people age. A new study has examined whether the level of vitamin D in the blood is related to that change.

Among middle-aged and older adults, higher vitamin D concentrations were associated with longer sleep at night. Episodes of waking during the night were also found to be shorter.

The largest difference was observed in participants whose vitamin D was low enough to meet the definition of deficiency. These individuals slept about 23 minutes less per night than participants with normal levels.

The analysis was led by Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Department of Epidemiology. This department forms part of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Researchers from the National Institute on Aging were also involved in the work. Because the design was observational, an association could be identified but a causal effect could not be established.

Most vitamin D in the human body is synthesized in the skin following exposure to sunlight. Additional amounts are supplied through diet and through supplements.

Receptors for the vitamin are present in the brain. They are found in high numbers within a small region that regulates the body’s daily rhythm of sleep and waking.

Deficiency is also common among older adults in the United States. According to the estimates cited by the authors, roughly half of this population has low levels.

Disturbed sleep is reported by more than half of older Americans. Such sleep problems have been associated with greater risks of illness and death.

In a 2015 study of 3,048 older men, low vitamin D was linked to shorter and less efficient sleep. Whether the same relationship would hold in women had not been determined.

Participants were drawn from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, an ongoing project that follows healthy adults as they age.

Data collected between 2012 and 2019 were used. The final sample consisted of 460 adults aged 40 years or older with a mean age of about 71.

Women made up slightly more than half of the sample. Approximately one participant in five was Black.

Inclusion was limited to people whose memory and thinking were normal. Individuals with dementia or milder forms of cognitive impairment were excluded at the outset.

Such conditions can disturb sleep in their own right, and poor nutrition linked to them may lower vitamin levels.

A fasting blood sample was obtained from each participant and analyzed for vitamin D and vitamin B12.

Each participant was also asked to wear a small motion sensor on the non-dominant wrist for seven full days.

Over the same week, bedtimes, rising times and any daytime naps were logged by the participants in a sleep diary.

Sleep averaged approximately 6 hours and 40 minutes per night, with about 48 minutes awake after sleep onset.

For the main comparison, participants were sorted by vitamin D concentration into three groups of similar size.

Age, sex, race, education, body weight, depressive symptoms and other medical conditions were taken into account in the models.

Following these adjustments, the highest group was found to sleep about 19 minutes longer per night than the lowest group.

A slightly greater proportion of time in bed was spent asleep by this group. Their waking episodes during the night were also somewhat shorter.

Although 19 minutes may seem modest for one night, the difference amounts to more than two hours weekly.

The researchers then grouped participants using clinical thresholds. In this analysis, concentrations below 20 nanograms per milliliter were classified as deficient and those above 30 as normal.

Using these categories, deficient participants slept approximately 23 minutes less per night than those within the normal range.

Participants with concentrations between the two thresholds did not differ clearly from the normal group.

Vitamin D supplement use was reported by nearly half of the volunteers. Its inclusion in the analysis did not materially alter the results.

The association between vitamin D and sleep appeared stronger among Black participants than in the rest of the sample.

Black participants in the middle and highest vitamin D groups spent a greater proportion of their time in bed asleep. This proportion was about three percentage points higher than in the lowest group.

Among White participants and those of other races, the corresponding difference was smaller and may have arisen by chance.

This finding was described by the authors as exploratory. Confirmation in other populations will be required.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” Chen said.

Vitamin B12 was also assessed because of its role in the processes by which cells maintain DNA.

In the sample as a whole, no clear association was detected between B12 concentrations and any sleep measure.

A possible difference between the sexes was nevertheless noted. Women with higher B12 concentrations spent slightly less time awake during the night.

An opposite pattern was seen in men, although that estimate was too imprecise to be distinguished from chance.

Low B12 concentrations were identified in only 14 participants, so a modest effect may have gone undetected.

Most participants were assessed on a single occasion. Changes in sleep therefore could not be tracked as vitamin D concentrations rose or fell.

The direction of the association remains uncertain. Poor sleep could lead to lower vitamin D rather than the reverse.

Low vitamin D may also act as a general indicator of declining health. The sources of each participant’s vitamin D could not be distinguished.

The cohort was relatively healthy, and the results may not apply to less healthy populations.

Wrist sensors are also limited in what they record. The time spent in individual sleep stages cannot be measured with such devices.

Adam Spira, a professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School, served as senior author.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” Spira said.

Earlier trials have reported that vitamin D supplements improved self-rated sleep. Those assessments were based on questionnaires rather than on sensor recordings.

The next question is whether raising vitamin D would lengthen sleep as recorded by a sensor. Future studies in older adults could test this directly.

The full study was published in The Journals of Gerontology: Series A.

A recent satellite image captured a striking scene at the Shiveluch volcano, which has been erupting for nearly 30 years in Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Shiveluch volcano, Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia [56.66230841, 161.3449064]

What's in the photo? Snow melting around a growing lava dome at the volcano's summit

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This striking satellite snap shows a heavy blanket of snow surrounding a growing lava dome at the summit of one of Russia's most active and unstable volcanoes.

The snow-covered peak, called Shiveluch (also spelled Shivelyuch or Sheveluch), is a 10,771-foot-tall (3,283 meters) stratovolcano. The name Shiveluch loosely translates to "smoking mountain" in the language of the region's Indigenous Itelmen people. It is the northernmost active peak in the Kamchatka Peninsula, a highly volcanic region in eastern Russia that's famous for its unusually powerful and dramatically beautiful eruptions.

Shiveluch stands out even among its extremely active volcanic neighbors and is one of the planet's most active volcanoes, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. It has experienced at least 15 eruptions in the past 100 years, the most recent of which has been going on since 1999, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

On average, the volcano spews around 530 million cubic feet (15 million cubic meters) of lava every year — enough to fill 6,000 Olympic-size swimming pools, according to a 2007 study. As a result, its appearance constantly changes when viewed from above.

"On a near-daily basis, satellites detect new signs of activity within [Shiveluch's] horseshoe-shaped caldera, including thermal anomalies, hot avalanches and debris flows," Earth Observatory representatives wrote. The volcano is also constantly spitting out "ash deposits that darken the surrounding landscape," they added.

A massive lava dome was growing from Shiveluch's summit. It likely looked something like this dome, which grew from the same place in 1993.

In this image, you might be able to see a particularly dark circle at the top of the volcano's caldera. This is a lava dome — a steep-sided landform that emerges when lava piles up on top of a volcanic vent — that has been growing rapidly in recent months, according to the Earth Observatory.

The lava within this swelling blob is "extruded slowly and piles up into lobed, sloped, or spine-like shapes akin to those that form when toothpaste is squeezed from a tube," Earth Observatory representatives wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Eventually, lava domes grow so large that they give way under their own weight, often causing the caldera's walls to collapse. However, it doesn't take long for the volcano to rebuild itself after these events. (It is currently unclear if the photographed lava dome subsequently collapsed after the photo was taken.)

"Shivelyuch is an incredible volcano that has collapsed over and over again, on several scales, ranging from enormous flank collapses to more modest dome-collapse events," Janine Krippner, a volcanologist based in New Zealand, told the Earth Observatory. "It goes through cycles of collapse but then builds itself up again and again through constant volcanic activity."

Lava flows, visible as black lines snaking down the volcano's slopes and large patches of ash (at the bottom of the image) have retained so much heat that snow cannot settle on them, despite being months or even years old.

In a zoomed-out version of the satellite image (see above), black streaks are visible at various points along the volcano's flanks, including a thick dark line emanating from the summit caldera. These are lava flows from recent months or years that have retained enough heat that any snow that lands on them soon melts away, according to Live Science's sister site Space.com.

Krippner noted that when she previously visited Shiveluch for fieldwork, she could still feel heat coming from lava flows that were over 5 years old.

Further afield, you can also see larger black streaks that look as if they have been painted onto the satellite image with rough brushstrokes. These are patches of pyroclastic ash left over from a 2023 eruption that burned down large parts of a nearby forest, according to the Earth Observatory.

A 2022 astronaut photo shows a thick blanket of snow covering Yellowstone Lake, transforming the frozen body of water into a featureless white void. But below the ice lie some of Earth's hottest hydrothermal vents.

A 2025 satellite image shows a series of ghostly ice swirls sculpted on the surface of Lake Michigan by strong winds during an extreme cold snap that covered Chicago in a blanket of snow.

A 2017 astronaut photo shows an unusual checkered pattern surrounding a river, just south of the Canadian border. The unique sight is the result of a forest management initiative dating to the 1800s.

#6369. The 6 Best Flashlights for Everyday Use

Yes, they’re better than the one on your phone.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Smartphones may give us an easy access to a light source, but for seeing objects at a distance or brightening a workspace in places like the attic or under the sink, you need the power and range of a LED (light-emitting diode) flashlight. Flashlights are vital for navigating the outdoors at night and absolutely essential during a blackout or emergency, when you don’t want to drain your phone’s battery.

We’ve tested a variety of popular models to find the best flashlights, whether you’re looking for one to use in the midst of a blackout or simply want to put a decent one in the glove box of your car, just in case.

Perhaps the most important element of testing flashlights is to ensure they’re as bright as manufacturers claim. Brands typically list a lumen count, though they’re often inflated. Flashlights tend to dim slightly after you turn them on and your eyes adjust, and how quickly they do so is key. It’s not just about the peak brightness, but how long that brightness actually lasts and how bright the light is after it dims.

To measure lumen, you need an integrating sphere, which is an expensive piece of equipment. So for testing flashlights, we built our own. We consulted with product engineers at two different companies to go over our plans. We also used their commercial spheres to verify lumens on calibration lights to make sure that our own sphere sensors would be accurate.

After construction and calibration, we measured each flashlight individually at specific time intervals. We recorded our measurements immediately after turning on the light, every 30 seconds for the first 3 minutes, at 5 minutes, and then every 5 minutes for a full half an hour. Our official figure is based on our measurement at 30 seconds because most flashlights drop brightness quickly after that before eventually stabilizing at a dimmer level.

After completing the quantitative portion of our testing process, we used each flashlight in a variety of real-world applications, noting aspects including quality of build, ergonomics, weight, water-resistance, and other key specs.

Our best overall is an evolution on the classic hefty Maglite you remember in your parents junk drawer that could blind you if you looked directly at it. This model trades in the D batteries for a rechargeable and replaceable battery. Furthermore, the flashlight has an LED bulb that shines just as brightly as the old-school models you remember.

While Maglite lists that the flashlight shines with a brightness of 1,082 lumens, our own testing measured an even higher figure, not dropping below 1,082 lumens for more than three minutes.

Beyond this, I really love how it feels in my hand. It isn’t quite as clunky as the giant models of the past, but it still boasts a similar heft that feels solid and durable. The aluminum frame and IPX4 water resistance rating backs that feeling up.

If raw lumens and longevity are top of your priority list, it’s hard to find a better choice than the Streamlight Polytac X USB. The starting point of 554 lumens is already solid, but in testing, the flashlight settles between 334 and 324 lumens, which is a far higher than nearly all other options we tested.

The relatively compact design doesn’t detract from the overall performance, as the light beam extends for close to 300 feet. That said, the reflector is not adjustable, so you’ll have to look elsewhere for a floodlight.

Beyond this, we liked the nylon polymer body which was grippy and a lot more comfortable to hold in comparison to a fully metal exterior, which can be icy to the touch in cold temperatures.

There are three preprogrammed function sets we were able to access using Streamlight’s Ten-Tap selector switch. The selection process is a little awkward, but most people will likely only use it sparingly to set the preferred programs, which include low/medium/high, high/strobe/low, and high only. We recommend reading the instructions thoroughly to get this right.

From a fully charged state, the Polytac X ran for almost 5.5 hours during our runtime test before going dark.

No, Energizer isn’t just for batteries and Jeep isn’t just for cars. The collaboration between the two brands has led to an affordable, sturdy flashlight with enough brightness to cut through the darkness during late nights on the trails or on the roadside.

While Jeep’s involvement isn’t more than some design elements and a logo, this particular option is part of a larger lighting collection the brand did in collaboration with Energizer, featuring headlamps and other flashlights.

During our lumen testing, the flashlight measured a little less than 20 percent below the 1,000 lumens Energizer claims, which isn’t uncommon given nearly all flashlights fall a little short of their advertised number. It still offers tremendous light, especially in tandem with the reflector and lens, which do a nice job angling the light out in a steady, powerful beam.

Test Editor Bradley Ford noted: “The unique feature on this light is the Power Indicator screen for which it is named. When the light is turned on, or the mode changed, the screen displays estimated runtime for that mode—then it switches to battery capacity, listed as charge capacity remaining. Really a nice feature, and better than typical three or four battery-level indicators that are more common.”

We’ve tested other flashlights from ThruNite and were impressed by their durable, powerful lighting. That’s why we called in the Archer 2A V3 to test.

The flashlight is said to have more than 8 hours of consistent lumen output, higher than many flashlights we tested. Along with brightness, the Archer flashlight is compact and easy to carry around for everyday tasks. Need a quick light to check the back of your shed? Simply reach into your pocket and use the Archer.

The ThruNite won’t be top of the list in any one category but thrives on being pretty consistent across all of them. It’s bright, long-lasting, and durable, which is just about all you really need.

This ArkPro line of flashlights from Olight caught our eye not just for its slim, pocket-sized design, but also for the volume of additional features it offers. The ArkPro Ultra has four different lighting options: a long-range spotlight, a shallow floodlight, a UV light, and a laser pointer.

Furthermore, you can use those lights in combination with one another. For example, you can turn the laser pointer on and off while shining the flood.

During testing, the long-range spotlight and floodlight ended up being our favorite dual feature. We were able to illuminate small dark rooms easily with the shallow floodlight, while using the long-range spotlight for hallways and large empty spaces. Having both in one body is not a common feature. While we might have initially winced at the price tag, the Olight makes a solid case that it has the value of multiple flashlights.

That said, it’s worth noting that our measured lumens fell short of Olight’s claimed 1,700 figure. The flashlight is still much brighter than most other options but did degrade over the 30-minute test.

Another promising feature: the physical display lights on the body that indicate battery, brightness, and a lockout mode. That last one prevents kids from accidentally flashing the laser or other lights in their eyes by locking the device from shutting on and off.

The USB-C charging is also a plus. With nearly every smartphone charger already built in the same design, you’ve likely got dozens of compatible charging cords lying around.

This small, tactical flashlight from ThruNite does a number of key things well. The over 2400 lumens at its brightest setting rivals some of the most powerful options we recommend. At the same time the compact body and hip clip make it a great portable option that easily slips in a pocket or center console of your car.

What sets the TC15 apart from other options is the extraordinary runtime. On its Firefly mode (which is admittedly a very low setting), the flashlight can run for up to 30 days before needing to recharge.

The durable aluminum body is capable of handling a steep drop and the IPX8 rating means you can feel confident using it in the rain.

Traditional light bulbs, while nostalgic, are inefficient and waste a lot of energy. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, as much as 90 percent of the energy required to illuminate an incandescent light is given off—essentially lost—as heat. Halogen bulbs are an improvement on classic incandescent lights, but still generate a ton of heat. Beyond this, the bulbs themselves are also quite delicate. If dropped, they can easily shatter.

In contrast, LEDs are 70 to 75 percent more efficient than incandescent lights. That efficiency doesn’t lead to lower brightness either, with LEDs actually shining far stronger than most classic bulbs. The LED itself is a semiconductor that emits light when current passes through it. Furthermore, without a delicate filament inside, LEDs are far more durable.

While LEDs in flashlights are more efficient than traditional bulbs, they still generate a fair amount of heat. Especially as brands continue to push to create brighter and brighter flashlights, the heat generated grows too. That said, most LED flashlights have circuitry designed to manage power consumption and prevent your light from burning up.

For the most part, as long as you use common sense and don’t max out your light for hours on end, your LED flashlight should be fine. Take care of it responsibly and you’ll never deal with heat issues.

The actual brightness of your flashlight is measured in lumens. Lumens are essentially measuring the total light created by flashlight, with the higher the figure, the brighter the flashlight should shine.

Even accurate figures reported by a company can often refer to the absolute highest possible lumen output, which is not realistically what you end up using most of the time. Being able to measure them ourselves provides a lot of much needed reassurance.

That said, lumens aren’t the end all, be all. A lot of the perceived brightness and clarity of the beam is due to the reflector shape and lens. So, the width and length of the light beam from your flashlight will likely be a better determination of whether it works for you or not.

IP is short for ingress protection, meaning protection from stuff getting inside the flashlight. Those letters will be followed by two numbers: The first digit indicates protection from solids like dust or grit. The second digit indicates protection from moisture, in this case the concern is usually water. Sometimes there will be an “X” in place of one of those numbers, which means the flashlight hasn’t been tested for protection from solids (if the X is where the first number should be) or liquids (if it’s where the second should be).

For the first number, protection from solids, the highest rating, 6, indicates the light should be impenetrable by dust and sand. The highest value for the second number, representing protection from liquid, is 8. The flashlight can be submerged in water deeper than 1 meter for longer than 30 minutes, with no harmful effects.

A flashlight’s IP rating gives a partial picture of its durability. You’ll also want to take into account things like the materials used—ranging from lightweight but less-than-durable plastic to rubberized enclosures to heavy-duty anodized aluminum—and whether the flashlight floats in water in addition to being waterproof, not to mention the warranty.

As our first-hand testing showed, manufacturer estimates for flashlight specs are relatively accurate, especially regarding the peak brightness. It’s important to keep in mind that there are a variety of factors that can influence a flashlight’s moment-to-moment performance, such as its battery life and how long it has run in the past few hours.

As we mentioned, it is normal for flashlights to only shine at peak brightness for a few minutes before sliding back to the middle of their range. The good news is your visibility won’t suffer for that.

That depends on how you’re using your flashlight. Manufacturer Nitecore suggests a range of 1 to 300 lumens should be enough to light up a room or an intermittently lit outdoor area. Look for 300 to 980 lumens for walking in the dark without any additional light sources. Mechanics and other workers who need to see precise details in complete darkness might go a little higher, say 1,000 to 1,300 lumens.

Hunters or law enforcement might use brighter flashlights than that, but it really depends on the task. Furthermore, it’s important to remember that powerful flashlights can be disruptive to other people and wildlife, so choose your light carefully.

Flashlight enthusiasts often recommend making a flash part of your “everyday carry,” keeping it on you at all times as you would with your keys or smartphone. Personally, we recommend being proactive and keeping it around whenever or wherever you think there’s a chance you may need some extra light. For example, if you’re going on a hiking trip or evening walk, it’s a no-brainer.

It’s never a bad idea to stash a flashlight on each floor of your home in case of a power outage or other emergency. That way, you can easily grab it without going up or down stairs in the dark. It’s best to keep them in a place that you know you’ll remember and is easy to find in the dark, such as a small drawer.

We also stronglyrecommend keeping a flashlight in your car, as you never know when you might have a mechanical issue at night, and you’ll want to save your phone battery.

Separately, FEMA and The Department of Homeland Security recommend that you keep an emergency kit with a flashlight and other essentials in a cool, dry place somewhere at home, as well as in your car. In order to keep the kit intact and ready for an emergency, the flashlight in your emergency kit should be a backup, not your primary flashlight.

#6368. Quitting statins after age 70 initially appeared to be safe, yet heart attacks, strokes, and deaths increased after four years off those meds

A trial of adults aged 70 and older without cardiovascular disease found that stopping preventive statins may carry greater long-term risks.

When adults aged 70 and older stopped taking statins for preventing a first heart attack or stroke, they did not see a significant jump in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths two years later.

A research team followed participants for a median of 103 weeks, and up to four years for some.

During that time, 12.7 percent of the group that stopped taking statins suffered a heart attack, a stroke, or death. That compares with 9.2 percent of the group that continued taking them.

The results were presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published the same day.

Named STREAM, the trial enrolled 1,880 adults aged 70 or older with no known cardiovascular disease. The name stands for statin discontinuation as prevention among the elderly and multimorbid.

Every participant was taking a statin to lower cholesterol as primary prevention. That term means the drug is meant to head off a first such event, not a second one.

Each also had at least two chronic conditions, such as a past cancer or lung disease. The average age was 77, and 47 percent of the group were women.

Of those enrolled, 938 were randomly assigned to stop the drug and 942 to carry on.

STREAM ran from November 2021 to April 2026 at 24 clinical centers in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. Hospitals in Bern, Lausanne, Geneva, Zurich and Basel were among the Swiss sites.

The main outcome combined three events: a nonfatal heart attack, a nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause.

During the first two years, 100 people in the group that stopped and 77 in the group that continued had one of them. That works out to 10.7 percent against 8.2 percent.

STREAM was built as a noninferiority trial, a design that asks whether stopping is not meaningfully worse than continuing. The two-year difference stayed within the limit set in advance.

Outcomes were judged by reviewers who did not know which group a patient belonged to, according to the University of Bern, which led the project.

Patients and their doctors knew the assignment, because STREAM was run open-label.

Its rationale was that the value of these drugs is uncertain after age 70 in people with no heart disease. Side effects and risky combinations of drugs are also common in that age group.

Across the full follow-up, 119 events occurred among those who had stopped, against 87 among those who had continued. The counts come from the AHA’s late-breaking science report.

The design centered on the two-year comparison.

Nicolas Rodondi led the work. He is professor of primary care and internal medicine and director of the Institute of Primary Health Care at the University of Bern.

He estimated that over two years, one additional major cardiovascular event or death would occur for every 40 people who stopped their statin.

The association’s report notes that the estimate requires further investigation.

A second set of measures looked at how people felt. Pain, quality of life, fall risk and muscle weakness showed no difference between the two groups.

Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age, was also no more common in one group than the other. Reports of muscle pain were no different either.

Roughly 14 percent of participants crossed over along the way. Some who had stopped restarted, and some who had continued quit.

Extra analyses that took those switches into account did not change the result.

“Our findings provide information for shared decision-making about cautious statin discontinuation when statins are used for primary prevention only,” Rodondi said.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) advises a statin for some adults aged 40 to 75. They must have at least one risk factor and a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10 percent or more.

When that risk falls between 7.5 percent and 10 percent, it tells clinicians to offer the drug selectively, because the likely benefit is smaller.

For adults 76 and older, the task force concluded that the evidence is insufficient to weigh the benefits and harms of starting one. The recommendation dates from August 2022 and replaced a 2016 version.

Its advice turns on a patient’s overall risk, not on LDL cholesterol alone, and it addresses starting a statin. STREAM tested the opposite question: what happens when older adults already on a statin stop.

“Although deprescribing inappropriate drugs in older adults appears to be safe, the results of our trial suggest that additional randomized trials of discontinuation are needed for specific drugs,” Rodondi said.

The study was published in the journal The New England Journal of Medicine.

#6367. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Warming has intensified El Niño’s impacts on weather around the globe, making it harder to prepare

Large waves, driven eastward by the strengthening El Niño in the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, battered the city of Oceanside California (shown) on October 9.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento.  And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”

#6366. Astronauts could turn everyday trash and moon dust into something surprisingly useful

Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.

Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.

The ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere. On the moon, part of that waste might be put to use as insulation.

Paper fibers have now been ground together with imitation moon dust by a team of chemists.

The mixture was dried into an aerogel, an ultralight solid made mostly of empty space. Very little heat passes through such a material.

According to the results, some insulation for a lunar base could be made on site. Two ingredients would be needed, and both should be plentiful there: waste paper and the ground outside.

The recipe was developed by Alexander Wei, a chemistry professor at Purdue University, and graduate researcher Jacob Staker. Their colleagues included researchers at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

Wei said a lunar settlement will generate waste rich in cellulose, the plant fiber found in paper and cardboard packaging.

“And I can guarantee that astronauts on the moon will never run out of moon dust,” Wei added.

For now, the aerogels exist only as samples made on Earth. A manufactured stand-in was used for lunar soil, and the paper was clean laboratory filter paper.

The final drying step relied on a method the team considers less practical on the moon than freeze-drying.

Between 60% and 70% of wastepaper by weight is cellulose. When cellulose is torn into much finer threads, it can strengthen a material in ways the original fibers cannot.

A stand-in for lunar soil, or regolith, has already been mixed with recycled plastic by other engineers. Wei’s team paired the dust with paper instead and used it as a grinding aid.

Filter paper was first shredded in a food blender. The team then loaded it into a mill together with water, ceramic cylinders, and a powder called Lunar Highlands Simulant.

This powder is made from Earth rock to match soil from the moon’s highlands.

For two hours, the jars were spun at an acceleration about 60 times that of Earth’s gravity.

The team expects a mill of this kind to work in the moon’s weak gravity.

The paper fibers were thinned by the ceramic cylinders alone. Once dust was added, they became much thinner still.

The most common fiber width fell to about 4 millionths of an inch (0.1 micrometers).

Fibers milled with dust were eight times thinner than those milled without it. They were also at least 30 times thinner than the original paper fibers.

The milled mixture was frozen in small molds, and its water was replaced with alcohol.

The team then removed the alcohol with pressurized carbon dioxide, which is a standard way of drying aerogels.

“Imagine an aerogel as a high-tech thermos for a lunar base,” Staker said. “Most of it consists of empty space that insulates the interior, helping it maintain the temperature of what’s inside.”

Empty space accounted for 79.3% to 98.6% of the volume in these samples.

In total, 18 batches were made, and the recipe was varied between them. Cellulose made up 1% to 9% of the wet mixture by weight. Dust made up 25% to 75% of the finished aerogel.

Insulation is rated by its thermal conductivity, which describes how easily heat passes through a material. A lower value is better.

The batches scored between 30 and 45 milliwatts per meter-kelvin when measured in air.

An earlier attempt had produced a freeze-dried aerogel of imitation regolith and natural polymers. Its lowest reported figure was 70 in the same units.

The best new batches therefore had less than half the thermal conductivity of the earlier material.

The best insulation came from the batches with the least cellulose. Among the 18, the lightest batch was made from a mixture with 1% cellulose. Its conductivity of 30.9 was the lowest in that group.

When exposed to the moon’s near-vacuum environment, the pores would contain virtually no gas.

The team expects the aerogels to insulate better under those conditions. Several times less heat is conducted by other aerospace aerogels in a near-vacuum than in air.

Temperatures on the lunar surface can reach 266°F (130°C). That heat is a problem for many of the organic materials used in aerogels.

A sample heated in nitrogen did not start to break down until about 653°F (345°C).

Insulation and stiffness responded to the recipe in opposite ways. Heat was generally blocked best by the low-cellulose batches.

However, those batches were also soft, and they shrank the most during drying.

A batch made with 1% cellulose came out 52% narrower than its mold. Only 3.2% shrinkage was seen in a batch made with 9% cellulose.

The stiffest batch was also made with 9% cellulose. Under compression, it was nearly 300 times stiffer than the softest batch.

“Rather than trying to make the world’s best aerogel, we’re looking for the sweet spot where we can get the properties we need with the limited resources we have available,” Wei said.

To look for that balance, the team fitted a statistical model to the 18 batches. Three recipes suggested by the model were then made and tested.

Dust would be far more plentiful on the moon than waste paper. For that reason, one recipe was required to be at least 60% dust by weight.

A figure of 61.2% was suggested by the model. The resulting aerogel had a conductivity of 30.5, which was the lowest in the study.

The same aerogel shrank by about half. It also did not meet the standards for the strength test.

A second recipe was balanced across six measured properties. It insulated nearly as well, at 30.8, and shrank by 18.5%. This aerogel was stiff enough to be tested, but only 25% of it was dust.

The aerogels have not yet been made the way a lunar crew would make them. The team wrote that freeze-drying would be far more practical on the moon than the carbon dioxide method.

According to Wei, the lunar surface offers a natural vacuum and subfreezing temperatures at night. Wei said the water removed from the aerogel could also be recovered and reused.

However, this kind of material can be damaged by freezing. Growing ice crystals pack the fibers and dust together.

That packing is known to lower the quality of cellulose aerogels. To slow the growth of the crystals, the team proposed adding simple alcohols or sugars.

Only one kind of imitation dust was used, and the paper was not real trash. Every heat-flow measurement was taken at 73°F (23°C) in air.

For the weakest recipes, additives known to strengthen cellulose aerogels should be tested, the team suggested.

Freeze-drying is now being studied by the team for its next batches. Those tests should show whether a freeze-dried aerogel can insulate as well as the samples made so far.

The full study was published in the journal ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.
