#6365. The 9 Best Binoculars, According to Our Tests and Research

See the world in greater detail with one of these recommended models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Despite ubiquitous satellite imagery, incredible smartphone cameras, and a video doorbell on almost every house, there’s still incredible power in witnessing something with your own eyes. Unfortunately, despite eyesight being our dominant sense, our optics have some real limitations. Binoculars are considered relatively old technology, but they’re still recognized as the best tool to reach for when identifying a far-off animal or examining details on a backyard bird.

Hunters use binoculars to spot and pick out details on their quarry thousands of yards away, birders confirm species they’re identifying, and stargazers zoom in on constellations. They’re also just handy to keep in your house or even your vehicle for those moments when you just want to “see for yourself.”

You can extend your vision with telescopes, spotting scopes, and even zoom camera lenses, but the comfort and ease of use are why binoculars have such enduring appeal. Monocular devices—spotting scopes, for instance—can put strain on your eyes after only a few minutes, while binoculars offer a much more natural extension of normal vision, making them more comfortable for long sessions and easier for beginners to use. Binoculars are also lighter than those similar devices, which makes them packable and portable for trips into nature where they offer a more intimate look at shy creatures.

The challenge in shopping for a pair of binoculars is the sheer number and diversity of options from big, high-powered zooms that require a tripod to pocket-sized budget versions and everything in between. To help you narrow your search, we dive into how to select a pair that fits within your price range and how you intend to use them. We also share our favorites from years of testing in the field.

I’m a lifelong hunter and wildlife enthusiast who uses binoculars year-round for hunting as well as volunteer wildlife surveys for bighorn sheep and goats. Long hours behind glass, as well as more than a decade of testing dozens of pairs of binoculars in the field for editorial reviews, have informed my picks, along with conversations with brand representatives and optics dealers. For this update of my long-running guide, I tested six new pairs of binoculars that are new releases from established optics brands. Not all of them made the cut here, but several did, including the Nikon Trailblazer II 10x25, the first time I enjoyed a microcompact binocular enough to include it.

The new Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD binoculars deliver premium-enough outdoor optics while maintaining a price point almost everyone can stomach. The BX-2 Alpine HD, which occupied that exact niche for years, did it well enough that it became my favorite binocular in the midrange category and my everyday hunting optic.

This is a compact, lightweight binocular with good clarity and low-light performance, which makes it a solid choice for basically everyone from birders to stargazers, even though Leupold tends to market mostly to hunters and target shooters. While not the cheapest bino on the market, it’s worth the upgrade over the lowest-tier optics and, like any Leupold optic, comes with a lifetime warranty, meaning it could conceivably be the last pair you’ll ever buy.

The BX-3 doesn’t reinvent anything, but Leupold subtly refined the binos, updating coatings, tweaking ergonomics, and adding a few quality-of-life improvements while keeping the same general form factor, magnification options, and modest price point that made the BX-2 so successful in the first place.

The price jumped up slightly with the release of the BX-3, so while I’d buy the BX-3 for the improvements if you’re paying full price, retailers appear to be deeply discounting the existing stock of BX-2s, so it’s worth considering the older model if there’s a great price on it, at least until retailers run out of the now-discontinued model.

Read the Full Review of the Leupold BX-3 Here

Zeiss is synonymous with good glass in consumer camera lenses and sport optics, so the mid-tier-priced Terra ED 10x42 binoculars are somewhat of a surprise in the manufacturer’s lineup. I’ve tested several higher-end Zeiss binoculars, which were unsurprisingly great given their price tags, but finding nearly as good clarity and color in this $500 pair was unexpected.

While $500 isn’t cheap for most casual binocular buyers, I’d argue getting Zeiss quality at this price presents a serious value if you’re looking for good glass but aren’t ready to put down a mortgage payment to get it.

The 10x42 Terra ED uses ED glass and Zeiss's hydrophobic multicoating to produce a bright, high-contrast image that will feel like a serious upgrade to budget options. It's not going to match the edge-to-edge perfection or low-light performance of Zeiss's flagship binoculars, but it delivers enough optical quality to be an obvious jump in clarity for the investment.

The 10x42 configuration is a versatile middle ground for hunting, hiking, birding, and general wildlife observation. The Terra ED has a 330-foot field of view at 1,000 yards and a 5.3-foot close focus, so it is adequate for birding, casual stargazing, and wildlife watching. At 25.6 ounces, it's also light enough to carry comfortably in a chest harness (not included) for long stretches without pulling on your neck.

The fiberglass-reinforced housing is waterproof and nitrogen-filled to minimize fog and condensation outdoors. The hydrophobic coating helps keep moisture from becoming a major distraction when you're using the binoculars in wet weather or going between temperature extremes. The large focus wheel is also easy to find and operate quickly.

The Terra ED isn't the cheapest 10x42 on the market, but that's not really the point. It's a relatively affordable way into a serious optics brand, and the difference is visible when you use them side by side with cheaper binos.

Most hunters don't need the biggest or most expensive binoculars they can buy, but many with the budget and obsession with the sport will spend thousands hoping expensive optics can buy success. While $3,000 binoculars are overkill for most, hunters do ask a lot of their optics. Early morning and late evening light and long distances expose the weaknesses of lower-quality glass, so many hunters get the advice to buy the best glass they can afford.

While the top-tier binoculars are undoubtedly better, there’s a mid-tier sweet spot that gives you most of the performance of those four-figure binos at a fraction of the price. The Vortex Viper HD 10x42 binoculars are squarely there. Vortex’s Triumph binoculars are our Best Budget pick above for the value they provide at $100, but dedicated hunters who get up early and stay out late will eventually want to upgrade.

The Viper HD 10x42s have a list price around $729, but can be found at most retailers for closer to $500, a good value for the upgrade. Still, that’s $400 more than the Triumph, so you’ll want to be sure you value the improvements. The benefits over cheaper options are better light transmission and reduced distortions such as chromatic aberrations. If you’ve used cheaper binos, you’ve seen off colors such as purple fringes on trees. In broad daylight, this isn’t a problem you can’t adjust your eyes to, but in low light and longer distances it can result in straining and struggling to tell a stump from a bear or deer.

A relatively low 24.9-ounce weight and compact form factor enabled by the roof prism design make these comfortable to carry in a chest harness over long days in the field or a tree stand. The rubber housing offers satisfactory grip and I notably appreciated the underside thumb grooves, though they don’t look as high-end as magnesium housings. The included chest harness is capable enough, but will be a throwaway for hunters who already own a specialized hunting chest rig.

Turned off by cheap compact binoculars in the past? These are worth it. They offer quality optics with powerful-enough magnification for bird-watching, hunting, and a range of everyday uses. In addition, they’re sealed, so they're waterproof and fogproof, and there is a lifetime warranty on the optical parts so you won’t need to replace them if you drop these binos even once.

Nikon’s Trailblazer II 10x25 compact binoculars make some compromises on field of view and low-light performance, but on the plus side, they’re small enough to fit in your pocket. These are binoculars you can toss in a daypack for when you want them, rather than committing to positioning them on you, front and center, and dealing with the weight.

The trade-off, however, is the 25mm objective lens. There's simply less glass available to gather light than you'll get with a 42mm binocular, and the field of view isn’t bad but feels cramped if you’re used to bigger binos. The 10mm eye relief also isn't particularly generous for eyeglass wearers. But for quick looks during daylight, the compact size makes these much easier to have on you when you need them.

Bigger is typically better when it comes to optical performance in binoculars, but there is always a give-and-take. With standard 10x42 or larger binoculars, you get better performance, but usually at least a pound of weight and a bulky item. Bird-watchers and hunters use chest harnesses to distribute the weight and keep them accessible, but that’s a commitment you don’t always want for a casual hike.

The Trailblazer II has a more palatable price at $130 than you’ll find with larger binos with similar optical quality, making these a no-brainer if you’re shopping for casual use.

Like Leupold, Vortex has a great reputation, in large part due to its accommodating lifetime warranty program—a comfort to those of us who are hard on our gear. One challenge with Vortex is the sheer number of lines and models, but the newer Triumph line is easy to understand: it’s the brand’s cheapest pair of binoculars in the 10x42 build and arguably its best value at $100. While the optical clarity and quality aren’t on par with that of the more expensive lines, the Triumph does surprisingly well, especially in daylight.

Like most cheaper binos, the clarity falls off the closer you get to the edges of the field of view, but is sharp and color-true in the center. Yes, you can spend less, but I wouldn’t recommend it, having tried a lot of $25 to $50 binoculars over the years. Despite the attractive price, the Triumph ships with a case, harness, and neck strap as well.

Full Vortex Triumph 10x42 Binoculars Review

Nikon is best known for its cameras and lenses, but this Japanese optics brand makes a wide range of excellent binoculars as well. I’ve tested several models over the years, but the Monarch M7 stands out for the optical clarity it delivers at a mid-tier price point.

Nearly any pair of binoculars will work for birding, but for most species, you’ll be in trees and fairly close quarters where higher magnifications can make it harder to spot and track birds with the more zoomed-in view. Even when you spot a bird, even the slightly tighter 10x magnification can make it harder to follow flight.

The 8x42 version of the Monarch M7 binos gives you enough magnification to confirm details without spooking wildlife, but the wide field makes it easier to track them. The M5 series is also good and about $200 cheaper, but it has a narrow field of view even in the 8x42 configuration.

Like most binoculars, they’re nitrogen-purged and O-ring sealed, which just means they’re waterproof and fogproof. (Note: Fogproof only means there won’t be interior fog. You can still steam up the glass if, for example, your face is warm and the air or binos are cold.)

More money can, of course, get you even better glass from Nikon and other companies, but this is one of the best mid-tier options that delivers a clear and comfortable birding experience. Less money will downgrade your clarity, but cheaper and smaller options that weigh and cost much less abound if those are your priorities. (The entry-level Nocs Provisions Standard Issue 8x25 binos, for example, weigh about half as much.)

There are times when 10x binoculars simply aren't enough—and that’s especially true in Western hunting country where the animal you're looking for might be thousands of yards across a canyon. A 15x binocular like Maven's C.4 gives you considerably more reach while retaining the depth perception and comfort of looking through both eyes.

Extra reach is the reason to buy these. At 15x, details that can be frustratingly ambiguous through a conventional 10x42 become much easier to pick apart. I've found high-power binoculars particularly useful for searching large expanses of terrain where the ability to use both eyes makes extended glassing considerably more comfortable than squinting through a spotting scope. At distances of a mile or more, you’ll still want a spotter that’s 20x and up, but the 15x is a meaningful middle ground that’s wide enough to use in a forest, but reaches far enough for big mountain hunting.

The C.4 combines 15x magnification with large 56mm objective lenses, giving it a 215-foot field of view at 1,000 yards. This is noticeably tighter than, for example, the 342-foot field of view of the Leupold BX-3 10x42s, but that’s by design and the trade-off for 50 percent more zoom.

The other big trade-off is the weight and size. At 45 ounces, they’re still lighter than a spotting scope, but you’ll likely also be carrying a tripod, which adds several pounds to your pack. Compare this to 10x42s, which are usually 1 to 2 pounds total, and it’s a big difference. Still, if you’re using binoculars to cover big mountain distances and need the clarity and zoom to identify animals precisely, it’s likely a weight penalty you’ll be willing to pay.

The ED glass and phase-corrected, dielectric-coated prisms produce a surprisingly sharp image, and the 92 percent light transmission is key around dawn and dusk—impressive for the price. Most high-quality, high-power binoculars are at least four figures, but Maven delivers the C.4 for $550. Unlike the rest of its line that uses Japanese and Chinese components that are assembled in Wyoming, the C.4 is produced entirely in China. Despite this difference, I didn’t notice a sharp drop-off in build or optical quality from other Maven binos I’ve tested.

There's a catch: These aren't really handheld binoculars. At 45.1 ounces, the C.4 is almost twice the weight of many conventional 10x42s, and 15x magnification makes even small hand movements obvious. I used the C.4 handheld fine for short periods, but the size and weight wear on your stability much faster than lightweight hunting binos. Once mounted, however, the extra weight only affects your pack and the C.4 becomes a remarkably capable long-distance optic.

Any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

Celestron is a budget binocular brand, but its SkyMaster series is astro-focused and worth a look if you’re focused on stars. The massive objective lenses, high magnification, and Porro prism combine for a heavy build, but one that’s designed for night use at the distance of light-years.

The 25x magnification won’t be much good for backyard bird-watching or any handheld use, but they’re designed for tripod mounting, and for use as a stationary sky-watching setup that’s more comfortable for longer sessions than telescopes.

Going with binoculars for sky watching, especially ones as zoomed-in as these, adds a layer of dimensionality that’s lost looking with the naked eye (or with one eye as with telescopes). Unlike cheap Amazon optics brands, Celestron has friendly price points but still gives you a lifetime warranty. If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

Any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

Yes, this is an article about binoculars, but I humbly present the little-known monocular as a better tool for certain jobs. Like spotting scopes, monoculars aren’t as natural to use since you have to close one eye and miss out on the depth of a stereo picture. However, there are times when the weight and bulk of binos mean you leave them at home even though you might want them in the field.

I personally carry this Nocs Field Tube monocular every time I go backcountry skiing and find it quite literally worth its weight for scouting potential approach and descent lines, using it to pick out details about snow quality, avalanches, and terrain that my naked eye regularly misses. It’s also easy to throw in a pack or pocket for casual hikes or pre-hunting season scouting walks where I never know when I might want a closer look at something but am not motivated enough to harness up with my binoculars.

There aren’t a lot of companies making monoculars, but Nocs has several options. I love the 8x32 size of the Field Tube, but you can get a 10x32 version that offers a bit more zoom but a slightly narrower field of view in the same size package. There’s also the newer 8x32 Zoom Tube that’s significantly cheaper and slightly lighter and smaller but isn’t fully waterproof.

Not everything we test or like ends up in our buying guide, but some are products that still warrant a mention. Here are a few.

Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42: These budget binos fall between the Triumph and Viper models we recommend above. They’re solid optics for the cost, but in a no-man’s-land for the price. If you’re on a tight budget, the Triumph 10x42s are less than half the price and nearly as good. And if you’re looking to upgrade to the mid-tier, it’s worth saving up for the Vipers or the Zeiss Terra ED 10x42s for a more noticeable jump in quality in a compact all-arounder.Nocs Field Issue 10x42: Give us some fun colors and a grippy, overmolded texture like on these 10x42s. But similar to the Vortex Crossfire, they’re not enough of an improvement on our best budget pick to justify double the cost. If you like the design that stands out from a crowd of bland black options, you won’t be disappointed, but we prefer to pay for performance.Zeiss SFL 12x50: These are awesome high-end binoculars that pack a little extra zoom as well as a large, 50mm objective lens that pulls in extra light for early and late. They also are incredibly compact and light despite their specs. The problem is the $2,000 price tag that puts them out of reach of most casual users. They’re really good, just not 10 times as good as a solid $200 pair from our list above.

The magnifications of most consumer binoculars are fixed (i.e., not zoomable), making it one of the most important decisions for buyers. More isn't always better and can feel claustrophobic in tight quarters such as trying to track a small bird in dense forest, while wider-angle, lower-power lenses can feel underpowered if you're trying to see across longer distances.

Most binos range between 7x and 18x. Much less than 7x isn’t enough of an effect to bother with for most applications, while 15x and up becomes difficult to use without a tripod. In general, lower-power binoculars are a better fit if you’re mostly glassing shorter distances, such as in forests, and don’t need precise detail. Higher-power binoculars make sense if you’re looking to avoid also carrying a spotting scope and glassing longer distances up to a mile or need precise detail for identifying wildlife.

Objective lens diameter is the size of the lens farthest from your eyes and impacts the field of vision you get, as well as how bright the image is since, generally, bigger lenses capture more light. Jeremy Bentham, senior manager of SRO Sales & Operations for Nikon, explains the trade-offs associated with objective lens size.

“One of the key things that needs to be decided is brightness versus weight,” he says. “Larger objective lenses allow more light into the optic but are also heavier to pack and carry with you.”

Objective lens sizes in binoculars range anywhere from 20 mm to 100 mm, but the common sizes are mostly in the 30 mm to 60 mm range. I find ultracompact binoculars of less than about 30 mm annoying to use for more than a quick look at something nearby since the field of view is small and it can be harder to keep in position on your eyes. On the other end of the spectrum, most binoculars larger than about 55 mm become heavy and unwieldy if used without a tripod.

Binoculars are listed by size spec, where the first number is magnification and the second is objective lens diameter. Probably the most common size is 10x42, which permits a big enough field of view and magnification for viewing things as near as 15 feet but still allows you to spot larger objects such as wildlife as far as a mile away.

For backcountry hunters and hikers, weight is one of the most important considerations in a binocular. You need to balance the desire for a larger, brighter optic with your ability and interest to carry it around your neck over long distances. For me, anything heavier than about 35 ounces is too much to carry in a chest harness when actively hunting and covering several miles a day. If you’re a hunter or hiker who doesn’t need ready access to your binoculars and can keep them in a pack until you need them at specific spots, you may be able to tolerate heavier options.

Even folks who mostly use binoculars at home or from a vehicle need to consider weight. Heavier binoculars are harder to use for longer periods of time since your arms and shoulders do eventually fatigue and become shaky. If you’re mostly using binoculars on a tripod (a must for higher-magnification binos), you may want to prize optical quality over weight savings.

Aside from range-finding binoculars, most have surprisingly little tech as we usually think of it in terms of electronics and connectivity. What makes great binoculars hasn’t changed much over the years and still boils down to quality glass and craftsmanship.

Where tech does show up is in the glass quality and the coatings used. High-tech coatings are used to make colors true, enhance brightness, and protect your expensive lenses. Coatings and glass often use nonstandardized terms such as ED, HD, and UHD glass, or proprietary branding such as LotuTec or Swarobright, making it hard to compare apples to apples when talking about something as subjective as optical quality. What you can look for is whether lenses are “fully multi-coated,” meaning that all glass surfaces have multiple coatings for durability and performance, whatever the branding.

#6364. Flying squirrels have an unusual habit that may shape entire forests

Flying squirrels in China may influence where young trees grow by storing nuts in branches instead of underground.

Squirrels help oak forests grow by burying acorns and forgetting about them. But two species of flying squirrel in southern China have a different way of storing food.

Instead of burying nuts, they tuck them between small branches. A new study suggests that this habit may affect where young trees grow.

Researchers found fewer seedlings a short distance from parent trees. But their numbers increased again about 66 feet (20 meters) away, where squirrels often store their nuts.

Scientists have usually linked this pattern to tree diseases. The new study suggests that squirrels may also play a role.

The work was carried out by Xuelian Tan, Han Xu and their colleagues at the Research Institute of Tropical Forestry. This institute is part of the Chinese Academy of Forestry in Guangzhou.

The study was a field survey of two tree species in a single forest. It therefore shows a match between stored nuts and seedlings rather than proof that the squirrels planted them.

The research took place in Jianfengling, a forest within the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park on Hainan Island.

The forest averages about 67°F (19.7°C), and about 97 inches (2,461 millimeters) of rain falls there each year. In total, 992 species of free-standing trees and shrubs have been recorded in the forest.

Two of these trees are Cyclobalanopsis edithiae and Cyclobalanopsis patelliformis, which are close relatives of oaks. Their nuts are smooth and are not covered by the small cup at their base.

Many animals feed on these nuts. Their slick surfaces make them difficult to hold in place on a branch, however.

The flying squirrels solve this problem by gnawing grooves into the nuts, allowing them to wedge their food between branches.

The grooves differ between the two kinds of nut. Oval C. edithiae nuts usually receive one zigzag groove around the middle. Flatter C. patelliformis nuts, on the other hand, may carry up to 20 grooves on the underside.

Most stored nuts sat 33 to 82 feet (10 to 25 meters) from the nearest possible parent tree. Photographs in the new study show squirrels returning to collect their nuts.

Another image shows a gnawed nut that had fallen to the forest floor and begun to sprout.

The importance of this behavior is linked to an older idea about how tropical forests work. During the early 1970s, the ecologists Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell observed a pattern among tree seedlings.

Young trees, they noticed, were seldom found close to adults of their own species. The pair put this down to disease and pests.

Fungi and plant-eating insects that target one tree species spread from an adult tree to the seedlings around it.

Seedlings close to the parent are therefore more likely to die. Most seeds, however, land near the parent tree in the first place.

When both effects are combined, most surviving seedlings would be expected at a middle distance from the parent.

Ecologists refer to this process as conspecific negative density dependence. In simpler terms, plants tend to do poorly when they are surrounded by their own species.

This effect helps prevent any single species from dominating a forest. It is one reason why a rainforest can support so many different kinds of trees.

An earlier study in one of the Jianfengling plots detected the effect in 89% of tree species.

Where a seedling ends up hinges on two separate events. A seed has to land somewhere, and the young plant has to survive in that spot.

Seed-carrying animals can shift the first of these. Whether they could mimic the disease pattern on their own had gone largely untested.

Twenty parent trees anchored the survey. On ten of them, squirrels had lodged nuts in at least one direction.

The other ten were bare on all four sides. Each of the first ten trees got two survey lines.

One pointed toward the stashed nuts, and the second ran off where no nuts hung. A single line from each bare tree, comparable in trunk size, formed a second point of comparison.

Markers went down every 16 feet (5 meters), stopping at roughly 100 feet (30 meters). Beside each marker lay three plots about a yard (1 meter) square. Every seedling inside those plots was tallied.

Seedlings along the test lines were most plentiful beside the parent tree. Their numbers, however, fell away at 16 and 33 feet (5 and 10 meters).

At 49 and 66 feet (15 and 20 meters), on the other hand, the counts climbed once more. Farther out they declined again, and the comparison lines showed no second rise at all.

The 66-foot mark stood out in particular. There, the test lines held more seedlings than both comparison groups. The difference was statistically significant.

This is, notably, the very band of distances in which the squirrels hang their nuts. Beside the trunk itself, the test lines also held more seedlings, though only relative to the second group.

The authors offered a simple explanation, namely that trees ignored by squirrels may produce fewer nuts. Fewer nuts would mean fewer seedlings and, in turn, fewer squirrel visits.

Comparisons on two sides of the same tree therefore mattered, since seedling numbers vary widely from tree to tree.

Disease, for its part, ought to leave more damage on saplings close to the parent. Fine roots from 33 young trees were therefore examined, 15 of one species and 18 of the other.

The trees grew at different distances from adults. Each sapling’s root samples were inspected at 100 points under a microscope for lesions, which can indicate infection.

The level of damage, however, showed no clear trend with distance.

Fungi are not cleared by this result. Root lesions, the authors wrote, may not reflect the full pressure that pathogens place on seedlings.

They also wrote that “our results do not imply that pathogens are unimportant.”

Squirrels that move nuts are, in their account, one more possible influence on where seedlings take root.

Tan and Xu’s team has not confirmed whether squirrels directly help new trees grow. Other animals and local growing conditions may also play a role.

Changing how squirrels store nuts could provide stronger evidence, but such experiments are difficult in the wild.

The researchers suggest tracking seedlings over several years to see whether the nuts grow into healthy trees. Future studies could also examine other animals and forests.

The full study was published in the journal Forest Ecosystems.

Archaeologists have found the remains of a 2,900-year-old sanctuary on an island mountaintop, where ancient Greeks may have worshipped the goddess Artemis.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The discovery of a 2,900-year-old mountaintop sanctuary on a Mediterranean island shows the ancient Greek veneration for high mountains and their link to the Greek gods, archaeologists say.

The sanctuary was found during new excavations on Euboea, a very large island only about 30 miles (50 kilometers) northeast of Athens. The sanctuary did not include any buildings, such as a temple. Archaeologists think it was used for offerings and feasting by worshippers for hundreds of years, from about the ninth century B.C. until the first or second century A.D., during Imperial Roman times.

"We know that in the ancient Greek world, religious life was not limited to large temples and urban sanctuaries," excavation leader Chloé Chezeaux, an archaeologist at the Swiss School of Archeology in Greece, told Live Science in an email. "There were also many places of worship in the countryside and in the mountains."

Chezeaux led the excavations this year near the summit of Elatias, one of the highest peaks of Mount Olympus on Euboea. It is not, however, the mainland Mount Olympus traditionally regarded as the abode of the Greek gods.

Chezeaux said that her team first spotted signs of the sanctuary during an archaeological survey in 2025. In excavations throughout Greece, "mountaintop sanctuaries are not uncommon," she said. "The problem is that these sanctuaries often left very little archaeological evidence, sometimes with no visible structures at all, which makes them particularly difficult to identify."

Archaeologists found the sanctuary during a survey in 2025 and first excavated it in 2026.

The sanctuary on the Euboean Olympus, however, has yielded "an exceptional concentration of pottery," she said. The earliest is from at least the ninth century B.C., during the early Greek Geometric period — named after the distinctive patterns on ceramics of the time.

"This means that people were coming to this summit over several centuries, perhaps even for more than a thousand years," Chezeaux said.

The sanctuary was used in ancient times mainly by people from the nearby city of Eretria, where the Swiss School of Archaeology is now based.

"Reaching the summit is quite a physical challenge even today," Chezeaux said. "The final part of our ascent involves walking about 3 kilometres [1.8 miles], with an elevation gain of 650 metres [2,130 feet]"

Researchers now reach the summit from the nearest mountain pass in about an hour, but "it's difficult to estimate how long the journey would have taken in antiquity," she said. "Travel conditions were different, we don't know which routes people followed, and … not everyone visiting the sanctuary necessarily came from the city of Eretria."

The effort required to get to the mountaintop is part of the mystery.

"People were willing to devote considerable time and energy to reaching these places, and in our case they seem to have done so over many generations," Chezeaux said. This raised questions of what the mountain meant to worshippers, and why this particular summit remained important for so long, she said.

The immortal Greek gods of ancient myths were said to watch the affairs of mortal humans from their home on the summit of a different Mount Olympus, in a mountain range between the northern Greek regions of Thessaly and Macedonia. The highest mountain in Greece, it stands at over 9,500 feet (2,900 m) high, while the Euboean Olympus is almost 3,800 feet (1,100 m) high, and the Elatias peak on it is about 100 feet (30 m) lower than its highest peak.

The Mount Olympus in northern Greece is the highest of several mountains with that name.

The tradition of the northern Olympus on mainland Greece dates from the poems of Homer and Hesiod, which were written in about the eighth century B.C. But the name Olympus was already widespread for high mountains, and modern Greece has several mountains bearing this name.

Chezeaux said religious ceremonies were often held at the sanctuary high on the Euboean Olympus, as well as at other sites on the island.

"In antiquity, Eretria had a very rich religious life, with sanctuaries both within the city and throughout its territory," Chezeaux said. "Mount Olympus dominates much of the surrounding region, and its prominent position probably played a role in the choice of this location."

High mountains held particular significance for the ancient Greeks, and the journey to reach the sanctuary may have been part of the religious experience, she noted.

The excavation team has yet to find an altar at the sanctuary. While the chief Greek god Zeus is traditionally associated with mountaintops, an inscription at an ancient site in Eretria mentions "Artemis Olympia" — an epithet that suggests the wild nature goddess Artemis was worshipped at the mountaintop sanctuary.

The remains of offerings found in crevices at the site include bones from sheep and goats.

"Several of them show signs of burning, sometimes at very high temperatures," Chezeaux said. "These finds naturally suggest practices involving animal sacrifice and ritual meals, which played an important role in ancient Greek religion."

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6362. Standard fertility tests may be missing an important clue about sperm health

Retained mitochondrial DNA in mature sperm has been linked to longer times to pregnancy, even among men with normal semen test results.

Men in couples who struggle to conceive are usually sent for a semen analysis. The test measures sperm count, concentration, shape and movement. Normal results do not guarantee a quick pregnancy.

A study of 327 men with normal semen results has now pointed to one extra factor. Some of their mature sperm still carried mitochondrial DNA.

This DNA belongs to the mitochondria, the parts of a cell that make energy. Couples needed more time to conceive when the man’s sperm held more of it.

The study was carried out at the Wayne State University School of Medicine in Detroit. It was observational, so a link was found but a cause was not established.

The senior author was J. Richard Pilsner, a professor at Wayne State’s C.S. Mott Center for Human Growth and Development.

“These findings provide an important new window into the male contribution to reproductive success,” Pilsner said.

Almost every cell in the body contains mitochondria. Energy for the cell is generated within these small compartments.

Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA, which carries 37 genes. In humans, it is passed on through the mother.

R. E. Giles and colleagues reported this maternal pattern in PNAS in 1980. Defects in these genes underlie several inherited diseases, and mitochondrial donation has been used to prevent their transmission.

Mitochondria are retained by the egg. According to a separate study, women’s egg cells keep this DNA largely free of age-related damage.

In sperm, a different process is assumed. Most paternal mitochondrial DNA is thought to be eliminated during sperm production.

That assumption sat awkwardly beside earlier data. Higher sperm mitochondrial DNA had been associated with lower semen quality and with longer times to pregnancy.

Two sources were proposed for the excess DNA. Ordinary body cells may have contaminated the samples, or immature sperm cells may have been present.

Purified, frozen sperm from the LIFE Study were analyzed by the Wayne State team. Couples in that cohort had been enrolled before conception and followed while they attempted pregnancy.

Female partners kept daily journals. Time to pregnancy was then calculated in menstrual cycles.

Inclusion was restricted to men who met the 2010 WHO criteria for sperm count, concentration and shape. Of these, 327 were analyzed.

Mitochondrial DNA was quantified by digital PCR, a method that detects and counts individual copies of a target sequence.

Values ranged from 0.5 copies at the lower end to 49.0 copies at the upper end.

Bulk measurements cannot indicate which cells contain the DNA. Imaging of individual sperm was therefore required.

Samples from 18 men were selected at random, six from each of the low, moderate and high groups. Fluorescence in situ hybridization, which labels a chosen DNA sequence with a glowing tag, was adapted for sperm.

Image scoring was performed blind to group. A total of 50 sperm per participant were assessed.

Signal was located in the midpiece, a segment between the head and the tail. Mitochondria are arranged in a sheath around this segment.

Distinct spots were resolved around the midpiece in three-dimensional microscope images. Signal was not localized to the head or tail.

Jeffrey Mann, the study’s first author, is a postdoctoral fellow at Wayne State. He described the meaning of the images.

“Directly visualizing mitochondrial DNA within the sperm midpiece provides compelling evidence that the mitochondrial DNA detected by polymerase chain reaction reflects DNA retained within mature sperm,” Mann said.

Men with higher DNA levels had a larger share of glowing sperm. The correlation between the two measures was 0.87, where 1 would be a perfect match.

In men with moderate or high mitochondrial DNA levels, the glowing signals covered a larger area of the sperm midpiece than in men with low levels.

Sperm within a single sample differed from one another. In high-group samples, glowing sperm were found beside sperm with no signal.

A high reading appears to reflect a mixed population. Some sperm kept their mitochondrial DNA, while others removed it as expected.

DNA levels were then compared with the time each couple took to conceive. Higher levels were linked to a lower chance of pregnancy per menstrual cycle.

The team reported a fecundability odds ratio of 0.79. Values below 1 indicate lower odds of pregnancy per cycle as levels rise.

Differences between the low, moderate and high groups were unlikely to be due to chance. The link remained after adjustment for both partners’ age, body mass index and smoking.

Pilsner linked the imaging and pregnancy results.

“For the first time, we directly visualized mitochondrial DNA retained within mature sperm and showed that this feature is associated with lower likelihood of achieving pregnancy, even among men with normal semen parameters,” Pilsner said.

The team views the measure as a possible addition to routine semen analysis. A separate study found that body fat can lower sperm counts in men of normal weight.

“These findings suggest that conventional semen analysis may miss molecular signatures within sperm that provide important information about couples’ ability to conceive,” Pilsner said.

The study did not prove that retained DNA slows pregnancy. Only an association was shown.

Men with abnormal semen results were excluded. This limited the influence of other sperm problems on the findings.

The results cannot yet be extended to men with abnormal semen or diagnosed infertility.

Some factors were not measured. These included how often couples had sex, which also affects time to pregnancy.

The probe detects specific DNA sequences. Whether each spot represents a complete mitochondrial genome or a fragment is still unknown.

Imaging was performed on only 18 men. The microscope images have been posted online for other researchers.

Future studies could test a link with TFAM, a protein that packages mitochondrial DNA. Retention in men with abnormal semen results could also be examined.

“This finding opens new questions about the molecular mechanisms that allow some sperm to retain mitochondrial DNA,” Mann said.

Normal semen results may not give a complete picture of male fertility. Leftover mitochondrial DNA in sperm could be worth measuring alongside the standard tests.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6361. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”

#6360. The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.

Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.

When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each new pad. Within a few weeks, these are shed again.

A team in Israel found that these leaflets behave like the leaves of a common garden plant. Carbon dioxide is taken in by them during the day.

The researchers estimate that they supply about a fifth of the carbon a young pad needs for growth.

So the cactus has two ways of gathering carbon rather than one. Older pads collect it after sunset, and the leaflets add to the supply once the sun is up.

The research was conducted by scientists at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Israel. They worked with researchers from the Gilat Research Center of the Volcani Institute.

Potted plants of Opuntia ficus-indica were grown for the experiments. This is the prickly pear species that is cultivated on farms.

The plants were kept in a net house on BGU’s desert campus at Sde Boker. They were watered every day for a year.

Ilya Gelfand is a professor at BGU’s Jacob Blaustein Institutes for Desert Research and a co-author of the study.

“The cactus effectively has two gears,” said Gelfand. “Most of the year it runs in saving mode and breathes at night to hold on to every drop.”

“When water arrives, it switches on a second, faster gear: temporary leaves that work by day like a regular plant. When the good times end, it simply drops them.”

In most plants the tiny pores on the leaves are opened during the day.

Carbon dioxide enters through them and is used by the plant to build sugars. Water is lost through the same openings, and that loss becomes costly in hot desert conditions.

Cacti, agave and many other succulents get by on less water because their pores open at night instead. The carbon dioxide is stored as an acid until the following morning.

The pores then close, and carbon dioxide released from the stored acid is used to make sugars with the help of sunlight.

This strategy is known as crassulacean acid metabolism or CAM. Mature prickly pear pads rely on it so heavily that scientists classify the species as a full-time CAM plant.

The prickly pear is also an important crop that is grown on about 6.4 million acres (2.6 million hectares) worldwide.

Much of this area lies in drought-prone parts of Africa and South America. In these regions the plant is used for food and livestock feed and for slowing desertification.

Until this project, nobody had examined the leaflets as working organs. Each one measures only about 0.4 inch (10 millimeters) in length.

Around 150 of them can be carried by a single new pad, and they fall off after about six weeks.

The study was led by Patrick Mdemba, who is a doctoral student at BGU. Pores were the first thing he and his colleagues examined.

Clear nail polish was brushed onto pads and leaflets at five different times of the day. After the polish had dried it was peeled away and examined under a microscope. Each thin film preserved an impression of the pore openings.

The older pads opened their pores at night, which was the expected result for a CAM plant. The leaflets showed the opposite pattern. Their pores were opened in the morning and closed after dark, as in a typical leafy plant.

Young pads that were two weeks old did not follow either pattern. Their pores were found to be open at every time the team checked.

Acid build-up between dusk and dawn was then measured in each tissue. A large amount was stored overnight in the older pads.

The young pads stored more acid as they grew older. In the leaflets no significant difference was seen between the dawn and dusk readings.

Mdemba’s team also looked at the carbon inside the leaflets. Carbon in nature comes in a lighter form and a heavier form. Cactus pads that feed at night build up more of the heavier one.

In week-old leaflets the carbon looked much like the carbon in the pads. The mother pad had probably supplied it. Five weeks later the leaflets held noticeably more of the lighter form that daytime leaves collect.

For a second test the researchers sealed whole plants in a clear box almost 4 feet wide. They filled it with carbon dioxide made from the heavier form. One run lasted from 10 a.m. until noon, after the pads had closed their pores.

The marked carbon was found in the leaflets. The pads on those same plants gained no significant amount.

Next came leaflets with no pad at all. Mdemba cut them from pads less than a week old and kept them in sealed jars on a sugar-free gel.

In sunlight the carbon dioxide in each jar went down. Under aluminum foil it went back up. The cut leaflets also grew heavier until about day 15.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch as the leaflets.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch.

The team then worked out a carbon budget. A pad with about 150 leaflets gets roughly 0.12 grams of carbon a day from them. A 1998 study put a growing pad’s daily need near 0.6 grams. So the leaflets supply about 20% of it.

The leaflets covered their own growth first. What was left over went to the young pad.

Mdemba then took the leaflets away. All of them were cut off some young pads. On other pads they were left on but painted with clear nail polish, which sealed their pores.

Pad size was checked every five days. By day 25 both groups were about a third smaller in area than normal pads. Pads with no leaflets also weighed about 38% less at three weeks.

Without working leaflets, then, a new pad grew more slowly.

“That lets the cactus grow quickly whenever the desert briefly allows it, without giving up its ability to survive drought,” said Gelfand.

Desert rain tends to arrive in short bursts. For desert plants the timing of that water can matter a great deal.

Some desert shrubs drop their leaves when life gets hard. The prickly pear makes its leaflets in the wet weeks and drops them within about two months.

Every plant in the study got water daily. That may have made the leaflets look more important than they would be in a dry field. Well-watered pads may rely less on their night feeding.

The authors listed other limits too. They did not measure the two enzymes that capture carbon in each system. Gas exchange was not followed over a full 24 hours. Their conclusions come from pores, acid and carbon tracers instead.

They recommend measuring those enzymes in leaflets and young pads, along with gas readings around the clock.

Plants under drought stress should be tested as well. That work could show how much the leaflets matter when a wet spell is short.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Botany.

#6359. The 8 Best Electric Scooters Built for the Daily Commute—And Beyond

These reliable models give you a comfortable, safe commute and offer good range, top speeds, and anti-theft features.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Instead of driving for every short trip to the store or commute to work, hop on an electric scooter and zoom through your neighborhood. Electric scooters are easier to ride than electric skateboards and more portable than electric bikes, so they’re a great alternative for city-dwellers who don’t have the space for a car or would prefer a smaller mode of transportation for short distances.

These days, there are plenty of affordable and durable electric scooters available. Options range from electric scooters built for just a few miles of daily commuting to ones designed to handle uneven trails, high speeds, and long distances. We tried out electric scooters on our own commutes to find the best.

What Are the Laws for Riding E-Scooters?In many areas, electric scooters aren’t allowed on sidewalks, so check whether you need to ride in bike lanes before you jet around. Some areas have speed limits on small electric vehicles like scooters and e-bikes. For instance, in Florida, e-scooters with seats must be registered and have a title and license plate, so check your local laws before you opt for one of our seated options. Similarly, there are some restrictions based on battery size and type.

If you’re looking for a scooter that can do just about everything well—with a long range to boot—check out the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max. It can go up to 40 miles on a single charge, handle slopes up to 22 degrees, and carry riders up to 265 pounds.

Its 10-inch pneumatic tires are great at absorbing bumps in the road, and it folds easily for storage. The tires are “self-sealing,” meaning an interior liner will automatically fill in punctures for a short-term patch. It’s not a permanent solution, but even if you roll over a nail or sharp rock, you’ll be able to continue driving without stopping for an immediate replacement. At just over 40 pounds, this Ninebot is heavier than some commuter scooters. But some of that comes from the bigger battery for extended range.

While 40 miles won’t take you on long-range adventures, it should last for multiple weeks of scootering around town. The Ninebot is the second most expensive of the scooters we recommend. But considering how well-rounded this e-scooter is, it’s the best for most people.

The GoTrax XR Elite needs to be on your radar if you’re looking for an electric scooter that doesn’t take a bite out of your wallet. At just 32 pounds, it’s one of the lightest and easiest to carry among the scooters here. This is further amplified by the foldable design and slender frame.

This scooter has an estimated range of 16 miles, a top speed of about 15 miles per hour, and a max incline of 15 degrees. What really sets it apart from the others is the affordable price given the quality performance. This costs about $400 less than the Segway Ninebot Kickscooter Max.

While the XR Elite isn’t built for long distances or top speeds, it’s a perfect choice for puttering around town. Moreover, its battery charges in just four hours, allowing you to get around sooner if need be.

Very few electric scooters offer the balance of affordability and performance that the Gotrax G3 Max does. With a maximum range of 37 miles, the scooter is ideal for daily commuting back and forth to work without the constant need to recharge.

Beyond this, the scooter is equipped with a number of features that caught our eye, including the integrated number lock on the body that dissuades thieves by preventing them from actually being able to unfold and ride the scooter without the right code.

The G3 Max also comes with an LED display showing your speed, speed modes, mileage, and battery life. There’s an LED headlight for riding at night too.

Full Gotrax G3 Max Electric Scooter Review

Don’t confuse this electric scooter with a bike or moped. Built with a seat and basket, the Flex Ultra from Gotrax is more than just a quick commuter.

When testing this scooter, I took it from Central Park all the way back to my apartment in Brooklyn. I had my backpack, which weighed over 20 pounds, in the basket, and I sat on the seat for the majority of the trip.

What I noticed immediately was the zip of the motor as I got close to 20 miles per hour on straightaways and churned up the incline of the Queensboro Bridge without losing momentum. I also have to admit that I loved the seat. Instead of standing for over 30 minutes on the ride back, I could rest a bit more while still making better time than I would on the subway.

The throttle is responsive, and the larger 14-inch wheels stood up well to the potholes on the streets and cracks on the pavement. While its size prevents it from being an easy storage item in a closet—even though it folds—this electric scooter comes with the power, comfort, and convenience for quick grocery trips and long city commutes alike.

With a 34-mile range and a top speed of 20 miles per hour, the Ninebot E3 Pro is an ideal commuter scooter balancing speed and range. It’s also quite durable, with an alloy frame boasting an IPX5 water resistance for riding through puddles, rain, and even mud.

Furthermore, the electric scooter is a relatively quick charge, going from zero to fully charged in 7 hours. This means you can plug it in overnight and ride out in the morning on a full charge with no worry. Alongside an LED headlight, the scooter comes with lighting underneath the board so you’ll have full visibility at night.

The headlight and under-board lighting are paired with real turn signals as well, so you don’t have to take your hands of the handles to let drivers around you know which direction you’re headed.

Full Segway E3 Pro Electric Scooter Review

This lightweight and affordable scooter won’t take you everywhere with just a 16 mile range, but you can take it anywhere you please. The scooter is small enough to fold up and carry without feeling like it’s dragging on your arm after a few minutes.

While it won’t exactly disappear under a desk, it’s probably one of the few that will fit with ease in a storage closet or under the bed at home. At the same time, you can toss it in the back of your trunk and take it out whenever you go to the park.

The hollow tires also mean you’ll never run flat and don’t need to worry about inflating them after a few winter months out of use.

Have you ever wanted to take a load off while riding but don’t want a permanent seat? The Gotrax Eclipse offers the best of both worlds. The electric scooter comes with a detachable seat so you can plop down if you know you have a long ride ahead, but can take it off and leave it at home when portability and foldability take priority.

The scooter is more than just the seat as well. With a top speed of 25 miles per hour and a max range of 38 miles, this is a performance-focused option that is great for longer commutes and open streets.

At the same time, the electric scooter has a small rear shelf that can be used to securely tie down small packages and backpacks so you can actually use it for carrying more than just yourself.

Reaching speeds of over 30 miles per hour and boasting a range of 45, this electric scooter from Segway is aptly named the SuperScooter GT3. This heavy-duty option is designed with performance as the end all, be all priority. In fact, in combination with its 11-inch self-sealing tires, the SuperScooter GT3 is one of the few electric scooters that is legitimately well-equipped to handle gravel, dirt, and general off-road adventures.

Beyond pure power and battery, the electric scooter comes with one of the most useful displays that we’ve found. The full color screen comes with smart technology that connects to your phone so you can receive notifications and access navigation routes in real time.

That said, before you click buy, make sure it’s actually legal to ride in your city. Electric scooters of this speed and size are often highly regulated and illegal to ride in densely populated cities across the United States.

An electric scooter’s range is based on battery and motor size and is impacted by a number of factors, including rider weight, weather conditions, surface type, and incline of the roads you travel on. The ranges we include are based on the manufacturers’ claims, and your real-world use will vary.

Many scooters get up to 10 miles, while some can last for up to 40 miles or more on a single charge. Some have various drive settings that help you get the most juice out of your battery based on the type of ride you’re on. For instance, if you’re trying to conserve power for a longer trip, many options have a low-power or eco mode, which reduces top speed or acceleration for the sake of saving the battery. Furthermore, if you want to extend your scooter range as much as possible, consider routing yourself on smooth flat roads with little incline that don't require lots of stopping and starting.

Most of the e-scooters we recommend top out between 15 and 20 mph. That should be fast enough to zip along city streets and paths without feeling like you’re falling behind.

The only exception to this speed range is the Navee XT5 electric scooter, which reaches a top speed of 31 mph. However, if you’re seeking a quicker commute or more of a thrill, there are other e-scooters that reach speeds up to 60 mph. We didn’t recommend any of those because many states and cities have banned them or require you to gain an additional license to use them.

Electric scooters often have motors with a power rating between 250 and 350 watts. This is enough for most daily city commuting. If you’re a heavier person or expected to ride up steep inclines, you may want to opt for a scooter with a larger, more powerful motor. High wattage motors offer significantly more torque and acceleration but typically come at a premium. Their size also makes them heavier than lower wattage motors, which can make the scooter more cumbersome to carry or transport when not in use.

Almost all electric scooters have rubber tires, whether they’re solid, tubeless, or tires with inner tubes. Solid rubber tires are the longest-lasting and are ideal for those making shorter rides on smooth streets, but they also absorb less shock than their tubeless counterparts.

Tires with inner tubes were more common in the past, but we’re starting to see more tubeless and tube-ready tires today. Both tubeless and tube-ready tires can suffer punctures, but offer more cushioning during a ride than solid rubber models.

If you plan on riding a scooter in the early morning or night, look for a scooter with good front and rear lights. It’s also a good idea to look for a scooter with a horn or bell to warn bikers, pedestrians, and other scooter riders that you’re approaching. Some high end scooters also come with board lights and turn signals for additional visibility in the dark.

All scooters should have good brakes as well. Some only have them on one wheel, but more powerful scooters that need to decelerate quickly should have front and back brakes, and possibly a motor brake so you don’t go flying down a hill faster than intended. Motor brakes can also provide some regenerative braking, extending the scooter’s range slightly as you ride.

Some other extras to look for on electric scooters are items like seats or baskets. These are great to have if you prefer a seated ride and/or if you plan on using the scooter for errands, like grocery shopping.

In selecting these electric scooters, we rode multiple options. We used the scooters in daily work commutes to test their power, speed, range, and comfort over distance. This included trips over long bridges, on steep inclines, and many times, on streets without bike lanes. We also gauged how the acceleration and brakes felt in our hands, and how smooth the scooter stayed when riding over bumps or uneven asphalt.

For scooters we haven’t tested yet, we based our picks on research, evaluating the opinions and ratings of professional reviewers, as well as checking out customer reviews and rankings, and evaluating each model’s most important specs like wattage, range, and safety features. We chose reputable brands, selecting electric scooters that are not only the highest-performing models on the market, but also the easiest to find in stock.

Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer.

The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios, demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking.

This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip, which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests, for an error rate of 0.0772%.

The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server.

In a statement, Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years."

"A scaled-up version of this system could reach the reliability required for useful fault-tolerant computation at a feasible size — less than a million physical qubits — which improves the outlook for practical quantum computing," added Blume-Kohout, who was not involved in the research.

Preserving the fragile information stored in qubits is one of quantum computing's greatest challenges and presents a major barrier to making systems practical.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Qubits, the most basic units of quantum information, are extremely sensitive to interference. Their delicate quantum states can be easily disturbed by heat, vibrations and other forms of environmental "noise," and if this happens in the middle of a calculation, the result becomes far less reliable — if it survives at all.

Quantum error correction has become a focal point for researchers for this exact reason. It introduces redundancy to quantum systems to ensure that small, potentially manageable errors don't wipe out entire calculations.

This involves spreading quantum information across multiple physical qubits to form a "logical" qubit. If a single qubit loses its quantum state due to interference, the redundancy provided by the logical qubit helps to keep the information it collectively stores intact.

The challenge is packing enough qubits into computers to ensure redundancy for longer, more complex calculations. This presents something of a catch-22: Adding more qubits provides more redundancy, allowing for larger quantum systems, but it also increases the opportunity for errors.

Unlike Google's Willow processor, which is based on superconducting circuits, Helios uses electrically charged barium ions that can be dynamically rearranged.

By shuttling ions around the processor, scientists can unite different pairs of qubits, allowing them to exchange information directly. That way, it doesn't have to pass through multiple qubits — a process that can introduce additional errors.

The team also developed a technique called "leakage repumping," which uses precise, split-second laser pulses to bring qubits that have slipped out of their information-storing quantum state back into a usable state.

To test how effectively Helios could correct errors as more physical qubits were added, the researchers used a type of error-correcting code known as a color code. They tested three progressively larger versions ‪—‬ known as code distances 3, 5 and 7 ​​—‬ which could correct one, two and three physical-qubit errors, respectively.

They found that Helios became substantially more reliable as they added more physical qubits. Each increase in code distance reduced the likelihood of an uncorrectable error by roughly 12 times. At the highest level tested (distance 7), Helios achieved a record failure rate of approximately one uncorrectable error per 200,000 rounds.

In the study, which has not been peer-reviewed yet, the scientists suggested that future quantum computers using the same technology as Helios could achieve extremely low error rates without needing an impractically high number of physical qubits.

According to estimates from Quantinuum representatives, a future trapped-ion system could support 100 logical qubits using approximately 30,000 physical qubits, compared with around 900,000 for a competing superconducting system.

"There is still substantial engineering ahead to scale to much larger systems and integrate all the elements of fault-tolerant computation, but this work demonstrates that our underlying hardware and error-correction approach can deliver the exponential improvement in reliability that large-scale quantum computers will depend upon," Dave Hayes, director of computational design and theory at Quantinuum, told Live Science in an email.
